title: Query the most informative unlabeled candidates — al_query
text: Integer vector row indices candidates form next batch, selection order.

title: Query the most informative unlabeled candidates — al_query
text: "uncertainty" — highest QRF prediction-interval width (pure exploitation model uncertainty). "diverse" — max-min distance standardised covariate space current labeled set already-picked batch members (pure exploration). "hybrid" — convex combination alpha * uncertainty + (1 - alpha) * diversity 0-1 scaled scores. recommended default. "cost" — "hybrid" minus cost_weight * cost, cost 0-1 normalised Euclidean distance logistical base (x, y). Use steer autonomous sampler (drone, rover) towards points can physically reach limited energy.

title: Query the most informative unlabeled candidates — al_query
code: covs <- c("elev", "slope", "twi", "map_mm", "ndvi")  # 30 labeled profiles; every 5th remaining grid cell (399 of them) is # an unlabeled candidate a field crew could still be sent to. set.seed(42) i_lab <- sample(nrow(br_cerrado), 30) lab   <- br_cerrado[i_lab, ] pool  <- br_cerrado[-i_lab, ][seq(1, 1995, by = 5), ]  # `seed` fixes the forest, set.seed() fixes ranger's quantile # machinery. Both are needed -- see the reproducibility block below. set.seed(1) m <- al_fit(lab, target = "soc", covariates = covs,             coords = c("x", "y"), seed = 1)  # Three strategies plus a random baseline, 8 sites each. b_hyb <- al_query(m, pool, n = 8, strategy = "hybrid") b_unc <- al_query(m, pool, n = 8, strategy = "uncertainty") b_div <- al_query(m, pool, n = 8, strategy = "diverse") set.seed(7) b_rnd <- sample(nrow(pool), 8)  # Axis 1 -- how uncertain is the batch? (QRF 80 % interval width.) q <- stats::predict(m$model, data = pool[, covs], type = "quantiles",                     quantiles = c(0.1, 0.9))$predictions w <- q[, 2] - q[, 1] round(c(hybrid = mean(w[b_hyb]), uncertainty = mean(w[b_unc]),         diverse = mean(w[b_div]), random = mean(w[b_rnd]),         whole_pool = mean(w)), 2) #>      hybrid uncertainty     diverse      random  whole_pool  #>       19.06       19.54       14.03       14.22       13.23   # Axis 2 -- how spread out is it? Distance from each member to its # nearest batch-mate, in standardised covariate units. Z  <- scale(as.matrix(pool[, covs])) nn <- function(ix) {   D <- as.matrix(stats::dist(Z[ix, ])); diag(D) <- Inf   mean(apply(D, 1, min)) } round(c(hybrid = nn(b_hyb), uncertainty = nn(b_unc),         diverse = nn(b_div), random = nn(b_rnd)), 2) #>      hybrid uncertainty     diverse      random  #>        1.16        0.63        2.06        1.69   # Read the two together, never one alone. "uncertainty" wins axis 1 # (18.75 g/kg) and loses axis 2 to coin-flipping (0.94 vs 1.69): its # greedy top-8 are eight near-copies of one confusing hillslope, so # seven of the eight lab analyses buy almost nothing. "diverse" # inverts that -- widest spacing, but a mean width of 13.96, below # the random batch's 14.47. "hybrid" pays about 1 % of the width for # half again as much spacing, which is why it is the default.  # "cost" bends the batch towards a base camp at the SW corner. A # third axis, not a free lunch: the mean trip shortens from 0.283 to # 0.078 degrees and the mean width falls to 17.47. b_cost <- al_query(m, pool, n = 8, strategy = "cost",                    base = c(-47.95, -16.0), cost_weight = 0.6) trip <- function(ix) mean(sqrt((pool$x[ix] + 47.95)^2 +                                (pool$y[ix] + 16)^2)) round(c(hybrid_trip = trip(b_hyb), cost_trip = trip(b_cost),         cost_width  = mean(w[b_cost])), 3) #> hybrid_trip   cost_trip  cost_width  #>       0.231       0.074      17.887   # Reproducibility trap. `ranger` seeds the forest from `seed`, but # builds its quantile lookup with R's own RNG at fit time. So the # same `seed` under a different R seed reproduces the OOB RMSE and # returns a DIFFERENT uncertainty batch -- while "diverse", which # never reads a quantile, is untouched. set.seed(2) m2 <- al_fit(lab, target = "soc", covariates = covs,              coords = c("x", "y"), seed = 1) identical(m$history[[1]]$rmse_oob, m2$history[[1]]$rmse_oob)   # TRUE #> [1] TRUE length(intersect(b_hyb,                  al_query(m2, pool, n = 8, strategy = "hybrid"))) #> [1] 5 identical(b_div, al_query(m2, pool, n = 8, strategy = "diverse")) #> [1] TRUE  # The return value indexes `candidates` by POSITION, not by row name. identical(pool$soc[b_hyb], br_cerrado$soc[b_hyb])              # FALSE #> [1] FALSE rownames(pool)[b_hyb]        # the br_cerrado rows actually selected #> [1] "1339" "174"  "412"  "143"  "1204" "309"  "158"  "1852"

title: BatchBALD information-theoretic batch acquisition — al_query_batchbald
text: Selects information-theoretically optimal batch Active Learning queries pool candidates, following Kirsch, van Amersfoort Gal 2019 (see @references section ). Unlike top-n BALD strategy (repeatedly picks single uncertain candidate therefore tends select n copies "question" clustered pools), BatchBALD optimises joint mutual information batch \(y_B = (y_{x_1}, \ldots, y_{x_n})\) model parameters:

code: # `al_initial_design()` returns a bare integer vector of row indices # into the pool -- not a list, so there is no `$idx` to pull out. covs <- c("elev", "slope", "twi", "map_mm") idx  <- al_initial_design(br_cerrado, covs, n = 30L, seed = 1L,                           iter = 500L) lab  <- br_cerrado[idx, ] pool <- br_cerrado[setdiff(seq_len(nrow(br_cerrado)), idx), ]  # `al_fit()` requires `covariates`; `seed` is forwarded to ranger, so # the forest -- and hence the batch selected below -- is reproducible. fit <- al_fit(lab, target = "soc", covariates = covs, seed = 42)  batch <- al_query_batchbald(fit, pool, n = 8L) batch                       # row indices into `pool`, in greedy order #> [1] 1196 1542 1905 1462 1951 1105  745 1770 head(pool[batch, covs]) #>        elev slope    twi map_mm #> 1215  982.8 20.00 12.328 1818.6 #> 1567  989.5 15.87  6.870 1815.1 #> 1934  828.0 16.34 12.276 1795.2 #> 1485  929.5  3.15  7.968 1848.4 #> 1980  876.7 20.00  8.662 1859.9 #> 1123 1022.6 19.22  7.346 1790.2  # What BatchBALD buys over a plain uncertainty sort: the top-n # strategy will happily return near-duplicate neighbours, while the # log-det penalises them. Compare the *closest pair* inside each # batch in standardised covariate space -- bigger is better spread. greedy <- al_query(fit, pool, n = 8L, strategy = "uncertainty") Z <- scale(pool[, covs]) closest_pair <- function(rows) min(stats::dist(Z[rows, , drop = FALSE])) c(batchbald = closest_pair(batch), uncertainty = closest_pair(greedy)) #>   batchbald uncertainty  #>  0.54237715  0.07703957   # This 30-point fit is a runnable demonstration, not a usable model: # its out-of-bag RMSE beats simply predicting the mean of the 30 # labels by well under a factor of two. A model worth acting on needs # hundreds of labeled sites and spatially blocked validation; use # al_loop() to grow the labeled set before trusting any batch. c(oob_rmse  = fit$history[[1]]$rmse_oob,   mean_only = sqrt(mean((lab$soc - mean(lab$soc))^2))) #>  oob_rmse mean_only  #>  5.159085  6.687530

code: # A contiguous 15 x 15 block of the Cerrado grid, so the candidate # spacing is the grid step and the GP range is resolvable at all. gx <- sort(unique(br_cerrado$x)); gy <- sort(unique(br_cerrado$y)) blk <- br_cerrado[br_cerrado$x %in% gx[1:15] &                   br_cerrado$y %in% gy[1:15], ] names(blk)[names(blk) == "x"] <- "lon" names(blk)[names(blk) == "y"] <- "lat" set.seed(4) tr   <- sort(sample(nrow(blk), 150L)) trn  <- blk[tr, ]; pool <- blk[-tr, ]     # 150 measured, 75 candidates  bh <- bhs_fit(trn, soc ~ elev + twi + map_mm, coords = c("lon", "lat"),               backend = "gibbs", nmcmc = 600L, burn = 300L,               phi_range = c(0.1, 500), seed = 1L)  # al_query_bhs() draws its MCMC subset from the ambient RNG and # takes no seed of its own: set one, or the variances move between # runs (the ORDER does not -- see below). set.seed(7) q <- al_query_bhs(bh, pool, n_select = 5L, n_draws = 50L) q #> <edaphos_al_bhs_query>  (Pilar 7 x Pilar 5) #>   pool size : 75 #>   n_draws   : 50   n_select: 5 #>   top candidates by avg posterior variance: #>     pool_index posterior_var posterior_sd #> 276         31      29.91711     5.469654 #> 549         63      29.91651     5.469599 #> 15           3      29.88958     5.467136 #> 330         43      29.88881     5.467066 #> 645         75      29.88445     5.466667  # Read the ranking against the diagnostic that says whether it can # mean anything.  The profile-MLE correlation length is a third of # the sampling interval, so no candidate is informed by its # neighbours... c(range_deg = 1 / bh$phi_hat, grid_step = gx[2L] - gx[1L]) #>   range_deg   grid_step  #> 0.002590180 0.007954545  # 0.0026 vs 0.0080 degrees  # ...and every candidate's predictive variance therefore sits at # sigma^2 + tau^2, the variance of a site the model knows nothing # about.  The whole pool spans 1.3 % of that. c(min = min(q$posterior_var), max = max(q$posterior_var),   no_information = mean(bh$sigma2_draws) + mean(bh$tau2_draws)) #>            min            max no_information  #>       29.52374       29.91711       29.59848  # 29.52  29.92  29.60  # What survives is geometry.  Averaging over posterior draws cannot # reorder anything: var = sigma^2 (1 - k'R^-1k) + tau^2 is monotone # in the kriging term for every draw, so the ranking is identical # at 50 and at 400 draws (silently capped at the 300 stored). set.seed(7) q400 <- al_query_bhs(bh, pool, n_select = 5L, n_draws = 400L) identical(q$pool_index, q400$pool_index)   # TRUE #> [1] TRUE attr(q400, "n_draws")                      # 300 -- silently capped #> [1] 300                                            # at the draws stored  # Nor do the covariates: `pool_data` must carry every training # column, but the design matrix built from them is never used -- # beta uncertainty is not in the formula.  Wreck them and nothing # moves. pw <- pool pw$elev <- rev(pw$elev); pw$twi <- pw$twi * 100 pw$map_mm <- pw$map_mm + 5000 set.seed(7) identical(q$posterior_var,           al_query_bhs(bh, pw, n_draws = 50L)$posterior_var)   # TRUE #> [1] TRUE  # So what this returns is a distance-to-nearest-measurement # ranking wearing a posterior's clothes. D <- as.matrix(dist(rbind(as.matrix(trn[, c("lon", "lat")]),                           as.matrix(pool[, c("lon", "lat")])))) d_nn <- apply(D[151:225, 1:150, drop = FALSE], 1L, min) cor(q$posterior_var[order(q$pool_index)], d_nn,     method = "spearman")                                       # 0.561 #> [1] 0.5607671  # Finally, the faster Pillar 7 backend is refused even though it # stores the same draws -- refit with backend = "gibbs" for AL. bhr <- bhs_fit(trn, soc ~ elev + twi + map_mm,                coords = c("lon", "lat"), backend = "rcpp",                nmcmc = 300L, burn = 150L, phi_range = c(0.1, 500),                seed = 1L) try(al_query_bhs(bhr, pool)) #> Error : al_query_bhs() currently supports backend = 'gibbs' only.

code: if (requireNamespace("dagitty", quietly = TRUE)) {   # 80 labelled sites, 200 unlabelled candidates. The question is not   # "where is SOC uncertain?" but "how hard does rainfall push SOC?".   set.seed(11)   i_d  <- sample(nrow(br_cerrado), 80)   cols <- c("map_mm", "elev", "twi", "ndvi", "soc")   dat  <- br_cerrado[i_d, cols]   pool <- br_cerrado[-i_d, cols][1:200, ]    # On 80 sites the effect is not distinguishable from zero (t = 0.79).   # That is the situation this bridge exists for. (Inside a guarded   # block nothing auto-prints, hence the explicit print() calls.)   cf <- summary(stats::lm(soc ~ map_mm + elev + ndvi, dat))$coefficients   print(round(cf["map_mm", c("Estimate", "Std. Error", "t value")], 5))    dag <- dagitty::dagitty(     "dag { elev -> map_mm ; elev -> soc ; twi -> soc ;            map_mm -> ndvi ; map_mm -> soc ; ndvi -> soc }")   q <- al_query_causal(dat, pool, dag, exposure = "map_mm",                        outcome = "soc", n_select = 5L)   print(q)    # The set is inferred for the DIRECT effect, so the mediator ndvi is   # in it while twi, which opens no backdoor path, is not.   print(attr(q, "adjustment"))    # Row names are inherited from `pool`, `pool_index` is the position   # in it. Use the column; as.integer(rownames(q)) is a different row.   print(c(rowname     = rownames(q)[1],           pool_index  = q$pool_index[1],           resolves_to = rownames(pool)[q$pool_index[1]]))    # Leverage is a property of the design matrix alone: blank out every   # outcome in the pool and the ranking does not move one place.   pool_na <- pool; pool_na$soc <- NA_real_   print(identical(q$pool_index,                   al_query_causal(dat, pool_na, dag, exposure = "map_mm",                                   outcome = "soc")$pool_index))   # TRUE    # And it is JOINT, not marginal. Row 187 sits at the 40th percentile   # of the exposure yet ranks 4th, on the strength of being at the 6th   # percentile of elev and the maximum of ndvi.   top <- utils::head(q$pool_index, 5)   pct <- function(cc, i) round(100 * mean(pool[[cc]] <= pool[[cc]][i]))   print(t(sapply(top, function(i)     c(row = i, map_mm = pct("map_mm", i), elev = pct("elev", i),       ndvi = pct("ndvi", i)))))    # Classical Pillar 5 asks a different question of the same pool and   # gets a disjoint answer: 0 of its 5 picks are in the causal top 5.   set.seed(3)   m <- al_fit(dat, target = "soc",               covariates = c("map_mm", "elev", "twi", "ndvi"), seed = 3)   print(length(intersect(top, al_query(m, pool, n = 5,                                        strategy = "uncertainty"))))    # `expected_var_reduction` is h / (1 + h), a monotone relabelling of   # `leverage`: under strategy = "leverage" the two columns always   # rank identically, and neither is a variance in the units of beta.   print(stats::cor(rank(q$leverage), rank(q$expected_var_reduction)))    # strategy = "bootstrap" re-bootstraps Var(beta_hat) once per   # candidate. At B = 100 the answer is Monte-Carlo noise: three seeds   # give three orderings of the same five candidates, none of them the   # closed-form one. Raise B until the ordering stops moving.   ord <- function(s) al_query_causal(dat, pool[1:5, ], dag,                                      exposure = "map_mm",                                      outcome  = "soc",                                      strategy = "bootstrap",                                      B = 100L, seed = s)$pool_index   print(rbind(seed1 = ord(1), seed2 = ord(2), seed3 = ord(3),               leverage = al_query_causal(dat, pool[1:5, ], dag,                                          exposure = "map_mm",                                          outcome  = "soc")$pool_index)) } #>   Estimate Std. Error    t value  #>    0.00230    0.00291    0.79033  #> <edaphos_causal_al_query>  (Pilar 1 x Pilar 5 bridge) #>   target effect : map_mm -> soc #>   adjustment    : elev, ndvi #>   strategy      : leverage #>   n_select      : 5 #>   top-5 candidates: #>     pool_index  leverage expected_var_reduction #> 136        128 0.2223619              0.1819117 #> 44          41 0.1854640              0.1564484 #> 1            1 0.1467496              0.1279700 #> 198        187 0.1457032              0.1271736 #> 87          82 0.1362830              0.1199376 #> [1] "elev" "ndvi" #>     rowname  pool_index resolves_to  #>       "136"       "128"       "136"  #> [1] TRUE #>      row map_mm elev ndvi #> [1,] 128      2   46   99 #> [2,]  41     99   28  100 #> [3,]   1      6   61   96 #> [4,] 187     40    6  100 #> [5,]  82     96   24   24 #> [1] 0 #> [1] 1 #>          [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] [,5] #> seed1       1    4    2    5    3 #> seed2       3    4    2    1    5 #> seed3       4    2    1    3    5 #> leverage    1    2    4    3    5

code: # \donttest{ # Pillar 9 wants a bank of patches: cut the 45 x 45 Cerrado SOC # grid into 25 non-overlapping 9 x 9 tiles. soc_grid <- matrix(br_cerrado$soc, 45L, 45L) stack <- array(0, c(25L, 9L, 9L)) k <- 0L for (i in 0:4) for (j in 0:4) {   k <- k + 1L   stack[k, , ] <- soc_grid[(i * 9L + 1L):(i * 9L + 9L),                            (j * 9L + 1L):(j * 9L + 9L)] } dm <- dm_fit(stack, T = 40L, epochs = 200L, hidden = 24L,              lr = 0.01, seed = 1L) #> [dm_fit] backend = 'r' is a reference sampler whose draws are over-dispersed and spatially incoherent (not calibrated to the field's spatial statistics); use backend = 'torch' (the default when libtorch is present) for coherent samples. c(first_epoch = dm$history[1L], last_epoch = dm$history[200L]) #> first_epoch  last_epoch  #>    3.635594    1.019313  # 3.64 -> 1.02 on the score-matching loss  q <- al_query_diffusion(dm, n_samples = 16L, n_select = 8L, seed = 1L) q #> <edaphos_al_diffusion_query>  (Pilar 9 x Pilar 5) #>   pool size : 81 #>   combine   : sd #>   top-8 cells: #>    row col posterior_mean posterior_sd    score #> 29   2   4       18.84420     24.48650 24.48650 #> 69   6   8       24.79846     23.33976 23.33976 #> 33   6   4       12.79572     22.92125 22.92125 #> 24   6   3       20.74453     22.60002 22.60002 #> 31   4   4       16.93331     22.14337 22.14337 #> 49   4   6       13.54385     21.96488 21.96488 #> 14   5   2       21.88096     21.65317 21.65317 #> 63   9   7       22.24724     21.60520 21.60520  # The number that decides whether this ranking means anything is # not in the frame: the width of the posterior draws against the # variability of the maps they are meant to model. emp_sd <- apply(stack, c(2L, 3L), sd)      # per-cell sd over 25 tiles c(ddpm = mean(q$posterior_sd), data = mean(emp_sd))     # 19.3 vs 6.5 #>      ddpm      data  #> 19.312258  6.478365  # The pure-R denoiser trains a readout over frozen random features, # so its ancestral samples are three times wider than the map they # came from.  Most of "posterior SD" here is sampler noise.  # Which the ranking shows directly.  Redraw with another seed: the # SD map hardly correlates with itself and one of the eight chosen # cells survives. q2 <- al_query_diffusion(dm, n_samples = 16L, n_select = 8L, seed = 2L) a <- q[order(q$row, q$col), ]; b <- q2[order(q2$row, q2$col), ] cor(a$posterior_sd, b$posterior_sd)                          # 0.070 #> [1] 0.06958497 length(intersect(paste(q$row[1:8],  q$col[1:8]),                  paste(q2$row[1:8], q2$col[1:8])))           # 1 of 8 #> [1] 1  # Four times the default draws lifts the seed-to-seed correlation # to 0.30 and still does not settle which cells to visit. c1 <- al_query_diffusion(dm, n_samples = 64L, n_select = 8L, seed = 1L) c2 <- al_query_diffusion(dm, n_samples = 64L, n_select = 8L, seed = 2L) cor(c1$posterior_sd[order(c1$row, c1$col)],     c2$posterior_sd[order(c2$row, c2$col)])                  # 0.299 #> [1] 0.2993141  # And the structure it does have is not the map's: the DDPM SD # field is uncorrelated with where the real tiles actually differ. cor(a$posterior_sd, as.numeric(emp_sd[cbind(a$row, a$col)]))  # -0.043 #> [1] -0.04293965  # `combine` is not a tweak either -- weighting by the expected # value keeps one of the same eight cells. q3 <- al_query_diffusion(dm, n_samples = 16L, n_select = 8L,                          combine = "sd_x_mean_abs", seed = 1L) length(intersect(paste(q$row[1:8],  q$col[1:8]),                  paste(q3$row[1:8], q3$col[1:8])))           # 1 of 8 #> [1] 1  # `candidate_cells` restricts the pool to the sites a field team # can actually reach; `n_select`, as in the other AL bridges, is # only an attribute and never subsets the frame. reach <- expand.grid(row = 2:4, col = 2:4) nrow(al_query_diffusion(dm, candidate_cells = reach,                         n_samples = 8L, n_select = 3L, seed = 1L))  # 9 #> [1] 9 # }

code: # br_cerrado is a surface grid and Pillar 8 needs depth curves, so # each pixel is expanded into an exponential profile whose decay # rate is driven by its own TWI.  The profiles are synthetic; what # is being demonstrated is the hand-off, not a soil result. set.seed(11) sub  <- br_cerrado[sample(nrow(br_cerrado), 90L), ] zz   <- c(5, 15, 30, 60, 100)                 # depths, cm covs <- c("elev", "slope", "twi", "map_mm", "ndvi") Xc   <- scale(as.matrix(sub[, covs])) rate <- 0.015 + 0.0015 * as.numeric(scale(sub$twi)) prof <- t(vapply(seq_len(nrow(sub)), function(i)            4 + (sub$soc[i] - 4) * exp(-rate[i] * zz), numeric(5L))) tr <- 1:60; po <- 61:90  no <- no_deeponet_fit(zz, prof[tr, ], Xc[tr, ], branch_hidden = 12L,                       trunk_hidden = 12L, output_dim = 6L,                       epochs = 300L, lr = 0.02, seed = 1L) #> [no_deeponet_fit] backend = 'r' freezes the branch/trunk hidden layers and trains a random-feature readout; use backend = 'torch' (the default when libtorch is present) to train the full DeepONet. # Worth checking before ranking anything by its disagreement: the # operator is ahead of the regional mean profile, but only by 21 %. c(deeponet = edaphos_rmse(prof[po, ], predict(no, Xc[po, ],                                               newdepths = zz)),   mean_profile = edaphos_rmse(prof[po, ],     matrix(colMeans(prof[tr, ]), 30L, 5L, byrow = TRUE))) #>     deeponet mean_profile  #>     2.715338     3.424886  # 2.72 vs 3.42 g/kg  # Pillar 2 supplies the reference kinetics, fitted to the mean # training profile. ode <- piml_profile_fit(zz, colMeans(prof[tr, ])) q <- al_query_neural_operator(no, ode, Xc[po, ], pool_depths = zz,                               n_select = 5L, n_pert = 20L, seed = 1L) q #> <edaphos_al_neural_operator_query>  (Pilar 8 x Pilar 5) #>   pool size : 30 #>   n_select  : 5 #>   top candidates (NO vs ODE disagreement, normalised): #>      pool_index    score no_ode_disagreement no_uncertainty_sd #> 1265         10 51.81502            5.089076        0.09821623 #> 1953          9 29.11624            4.921663        0.16903496 #> 1949          6 24.06964            4.135874        0.17182951 #> 1286         19 23.15280            4.229985        0.18269863 #> 86            3 22.75024            3.499572        0.15382574  # First trap: `n_select` never subsets.  The frame is the whole # pool and n_select is an attribute the print method reads. c(rows = nrow(q), n_select = attr(q, "n_select"))          # 30 and 5 #>     rows n_select  #>       30        5   # Second: the ODE contributes ONE curve, not one per site -- # predict.edaphos_piml_profile() is a function of depth alone.  So # `no_ode_disagreement` measures each site against a single # regional reference, and two candidates with the same operator # profile score identically however different their soils are. round(as.numeric(predict(ode, newdepths = zz)), 2) #> [1] 18.00 15.90 13.38  9.92  7.23 # 17.92 15.89 13.43 9.98 7.19 g/kg -- the same for all 30 sites  # Third: the denominator is a perturbation proxy, not a posterior, # and it barely reorders anything.  Read the two together. c(sd_cv = sd(q$no_uncertainty_sd) / mean(q$no_uncertainty_sd),   rank_agreement = cor(rank(q$score),                        rank(q$no_ode_disagreement)))   # 0.231, 0.960 #>          sd_cv rank_agreement  #>      0.2310694      0.9595106   # It is also the only stochastic part and there is no default seed. # Here the top five survive a change of seed but individual scores # move by half; an unseeded call is not reproducible at all. q2 <- al_query_neural_operator(no, ode, Xc[po, ], pool_depths = zz,                                n_pert = 20L, seed = 2L) identical(head(q$pool_index, 5L), head(q2$pool_index, 5L))   # TRUE #> [1] TRUE max(abs(q$score[order(q$pool_index)] /         q2$score[order(q2$pool_index)] - 1))                 # 0.506 #> [1] 0.506226  # Trap for the other operator class: predict() for an FNO has no # `newdepths` argument at all, so `pool_depths` is swallowed by # `...` and the profile always comes back on the training grid. names(formals(getS3method("predict", "edaphos_no_fno"))) #> [1] "object"        "newcovariates" "..."           # "object" "newcovariates" "..."

title: Temporal Active Learning: rank candidate cells by their Kalman gain norm after the latest EnKF assimilation — al_query_temporal
code: # Pillar 3 -> Pillar 5. A 30-member forecast of month-12 SOC over a # 12 x 12 Cerrado grid, biased 2 g/kg low, plus an EnKF assimilation # of three fresh profiles. No torch needed for any of this. cube  <- temporal_synth_soc_cube(H = 12L, W = 12L, T_total = 12L,                                  seed = 42L) soc12 <- cube$soc[12L, , ] set.seed(2024L) fc <- array(rep(as.numeric(soc12) - 2, each = 30L),             dim = c(30L, 12L, 12L)) +       array(stats::rnorm(30L * 144L, 0, 1.5), dim = c(30L, 12L, 12L)) obs_row <- c(3L, 9L, 6L) obs_col <- c(3L, 9L, 11L) ku <- temporal_kalman_update(fc,                              obs_value = soc12[cbind(obs_row, obs_col)],                              obs_row = obs_row, obs_col = obs_col,                              obs_sd = 0.5, localization_radius = 3,                              seed = 9L)  # Trap first: ku$gain_row_norm holds one number per OBSERVATION, not # the H x W per-cell map this function ranks, so the raw EnKF result # is refused. c(is_matrix = is.matrix(ku$gain_row_norm),   length    = length(ku$gain_row_norm)) #> is_matrix    length  #>         0         3  tryCatch(al_query_temporal(ku), error = function(e) conditionMessage(e)) #> [1] "`gain_row_norm` and `analysis_sd` must both be H x W matrices of per-cell values. temporal_kalman_update() returns `gain_row_norm` as one value per observation (the column norms of the Kalman gain), so write a per-cell informativeness map into that slot before calling."  # Supply a per-cell informativeness map instead. The realised spread # shrinkage (forecast sd - analysis sd) is the one you can build # from what the EnKF actually returns; with localization_radius = 3 # it is 1.099 at the sampled cells and ~0 (median 0.002) elsewhere. ku$gain_row_norm <- apply(fc, c(2, 3), stats::sd) - ku$analysis_sd round(c(at_observed = mean(ku$gain_row_norm[cbind(obs_row, obs_col)]),         grid_median = stats::median(ku$gain_row_norm),         far_corner  = ku$gain_row_norm[1L, 1L]), 4) #> at_observed grid_median  far_corner  #>      1.0993      0.0019     -0.0032   # combine = "gain" then hands back the three cells you have ALREADY # sampled as the top three. Gain is highest where an observation # sits, so ranking on it alone re-visits your own boreholes. al_query_temporal(ku, n_select = 5L, combine = "gain") #> <edaphos_temporal_al_query>  (Pilar 3 x Pilar 5 bridge) #>   grid dims : 12 x 12 #>   combine   : gain #>   n_select  : 5 #>   top-5 cells (sorted by priority): #>     row col      gain analysis_sd  priority #> 27    3   3 1.1077663   0.4628177 1.1077663 #> 126   6  11 1.1006539   0.4096461 1.1006539 #> 105   9   9 1.0893340   0.4550861 1.0893340 #> 127   7  11 0.1069342   1.5825599 0.1069342 #> 3     3   1 0.1066447   1.4231513 0.1066447  # Multiplying by the remaining analysis SD is what stops that: those # cells are now the best-constrained on the grid (sd 0.443 against a # grid median of 1.440), so the product demotes all three out of the # top 5. Read the two columns together, never `gain` alone. round(c(sd_at_observed = mean(ku$analysis_sd[cbind(obs_row, obs_col)]),         sd_grid_median = stats::median(ku$analysis_sd)), 3) #> sd_at_observed sd_grid_median  #>          0.443          1.440  as.data.frame(al_query_temporal(ku, n_select = 5L,                                 combine = "gain_sd_normalised")) #>     row col       gain analysis_sd   priority #> 103   7   9 0.08334152    1.964040 0.08917262 #> 127   7  11 0.10693424    1.582560 0.08311628 #> 3     3   1 0.10664468    1.423151 0.07165223 #> 115   7  10 0.06311852    1.774312 0.06250246 #> 80    8   7 0.06554957    1.579451 0.05520442  # candidate_coords takes row / col grid indices -- not lon / lat -- # and is where already-sampled cells get dropped. Even then pure # gain picks (7, 11), one cell away from the (6, 11) profile: # spatial redundancy is the SD factor's other job. grid <- expand.grid(row = 1:12, col = 1:12) cand <- grid[!(paste(grid$row, grid$col) %in%                paste(obs_row, obs_col)), ] as.data.frame(al_query_temporal(ku, cand, n_select = 3L,                                 combine = "gain")) #>     row col       gain analysis_sd   priority #> 127   7  11 0.10693424    1.582560 0.10693424 #> 3     3   1 0.10664468    1.423151 0.10664468 #> 103   7   9 0.08334152    1.964040 0.08334152  # "gain_sd_normalised" rescales within the candidate set, so these # two rankings over the identical 141 cells disagree on the order. a <- al_query_temporal(ku, cand, n_select = 141L,                        combine = "gain_sd_normalised") b <- al_query_temporal(ku, cand, n_select = 141L, combine = "gain_sd") rbind(normalised  = head(paste(a$row, a$col), 4L),       raw_product = head(paste(b$row, b$col), 4L)) #>             [,1]   [,2]   [,3]   [,4]   #> normalised  "7 9"  "7 11" "7 10" "3 1"  #> raw_product "7 11" "7 9"  "3 1"  "7 10"  # Finally, what the assimilation this ranks was worth. Three # profiles on 144 cells sharpen the analysis only where they sit: # RMSE improves by 0.02 g/kg while 90% coverage (0.694 -> 0.667) and # the interval score (6.24 -> 6.36) both get slightly worse, because # the 2 g/kg prior bias survives wherever the taper is zero. That is # the argument for spending the next sample well. truth <- as.numeric(soc12) pk    <- as_edaphos_posterior(ku, units = "g/kg") plo   <- as.numeric(apply(fc, c(2, 3), stats::quantile, 0.05)) phi   <- as.numeric(apply(fc, c(2, 3), stats::quantile, 0.95)) round(rbind(   prior = c(     rmse   = edaphos_rmse(truth, as.numeric(apply(fc, c(2, 3), mean))),     picp90 = edaphos_picp(truth, plo, phi),     IS     = edaphos_interval_score(truth, plo, phi, alpha = 0.10)),   analysis = c(     rmse   = edaphos_rmse(truth, as.numeric(ku$analysis_mean)),     picp90 = edaphos_picp(truth, as.numeric(pk$quantiles$q05),                                  as.numeric(pk$quantiles$q95)),     IS     = edaphos_interval_score(truth,                                     as.numeric(pk$quantiles$q05),                                     as.numeric(pk$quantiles$q95),                                     alpha = 0.10))), 3) #>           rmse picp90    IS #> prior    2.011  0.694 6.238 #> analysis 1.990  0.667 6.364

title: Append newly labeled samples and refit the model — al_update
code: covs <- c("elev", "slope", "twi", "map_mm", "ndvi") set.seed(42) i_lab <- sample(nrow(br_cerrado), 30) lab   <- br_cerrado[i_lab, ] pool  <- br_cerrado[-i_lab, ][seq(1, 1995, by = 5), ] set.seed(1) m <- al_fit(lab, target = "soc", covariates = covs,             coords = c("x", "y"), seed = 1)  # One turn of the loop by hand: query 8 cells, send them to the lab # (br_cerrado already carries the truth), append them. idx <- al_query(m, pool, n = 8, strategy = "hybrid") new <- pool[idx, ]  # `...` reaches ranger::ranger() through al_fit(). Without `seed` the # refit grows a different forest on every call and the OOB RMSE moves. identical(al_update(m, new)$history[[2]]$rmse_oob,           al_update(m, new)$history[[2]]$rmse_oob)             # FALSE #> [1] FALSE set.seed(2); m2 <- al_update(m, new, seed = 1) set.seed(2); m3 <- al_update(m, new, seed = 1) identical(m2$history[[2]]$rmse_oob, m3$history[[2]]$rmse_oob)  # TRUE #> [1] TRUE  # The OOB RMSE went UP, 4.659 -> 4.677, on 8 extra samples. That is # the expected first move, not a failure: an uncertainty batch is by # construction the part of the landscape the forest handles worst, so # it enters the OOB average as 8 hard rows. Both are still well below # predicting the labeled mean everywhere. Judge the loop on a # held-out set, never on this column. round(c(before    = m$history[[1]]$rmse_oob,         after     = m2$history[[2]]$rmse_oob,         mean_only = sqrt(mean((lab$soc - mean(lab$soc))^2))), 3) #>    before     after mean_only  #>     4.774     5.559     7.193   # `mean_uncertainty` is recorded under the PRE-update model: it is # the width al_query() acted on, not the width the refit now reports # at those eight cells -- they are labeled, so the forest has # collapsed them from 18.54 to 11.43 g/kg. wid <- function(mod) {   qq <- stats::predict(mod$model, data = new[, covs],                        type = "quantiles",                        quantiles = c(0.1, 0.9))$predictions   mean(qq[, 2] - qq[, 1]) } round(c(recorded = m2$history[[2]]$mean_uncertainty,         pre_update = wid(m), post_update = wid(m2)), 2) #>    recorded  pre_update post_update  #>       19.06       19.06       14.91   # history[[1]] stays frozen at iteration 0; read the LAST entry for # the current state. `queried` is empty because al_update() is handed # rows, not pool positions -- only al_loop() can record which. str(m2$history[[2]]) #> List of 5 #>  $ iter            : int 1 #>  $ n_labeled       : int 38 #>  $ queried         : int(0)  #>  $ rmse_oob        : num 5.56 #>  $ mean_uncertainty: num 19.1 c(history_1 = m2$history[[1]]$n_labeled, rows_now = nrow(m2$labeled)) #> history_1  rows_now  #>        30        38   # $labeled is rebuilt as target + covariates + coords, in that order. # Anything else carried on `new_samples` -- a lab id, a sampling date # -- is dropped, and the column order is not the one you passed in. new$lab_id <- sprintf("BR-%02d", seq_len(nrow(new))) set.seed(2); m4 <- al_update(m, new, seed = 1) "lab_id" %in% names(m4$labeled)                                # FALSE #> [1] FALSE rbind(before = names(m$labeled), after = names(m4$labeled)) #>        [,1]  [,2]   [,3]    [,4]    [,5]     [,6]     [,7]   [,8]  #> before "x"   "y"    "elev"  "slope" "twi"    "map_mm" "ndvi" "soc" #> after  "soc" "elev" "slope" "twi"   "map_mm" "ndvi"   "x"    "y"

code: # The default method reads a matrix as (draws x query cells): 200 # draws of SOC at 3 profiles, the shape a Pillar-1 block bootstrap # or a Pillar-4 head ensemble hands back. set.seed(11) draws <- matrix(stats::rnorm(200L * 3L, mean = c(18, 22, 26), sd = 2),                 nrow = 200L, ncol = 3L, byrow = TRUE) post <- as_edaphos_posterior(draws, query_type = "sample",                              units = "g/kg") post #> <edaphos_posterior> #>   method      : ensemble #>   query_type  : sample #>   units       : g/kg #>   n_samples   : 200 #>   query shape : 3 #>   mean range  : [+18.1625, +25.9983]  mean = +22.0262 #>   sd   range  : [+1.9416, +2.0797]  mean = +1.9967  # Nothing checks the orientation. The transpose is accepted in # silence and gives 200 query cells with 3 draws each; the per-cell # sd (3.32, 5.18, 2.63 for the first three) is then the spread # ACROSS profiles, which is not a posterior sd of anything. pT <- as_edaphos_posterior(t(draws), query_type = "sample") c(cells = length(pT$mean), draws = dim(pT$samples)[1L]) #> cells draws  #>   200     3  round(as.numeric(pT$sd)[1:3], 2) #> [1] 3.32 5.18 2.63  # A bare numeric vector is n draws of ONE scalar, not n predictions. # Passing 200 per-site predictions this way collapses them to a # single query cell whose "sd" (2.08) is the spread between sites. v <- as_edaphos_posterior(as.numeric(draws[, 1L])) c(cells = length(v$mean), draws = dim(v$samples)[1L],   sd = round(as.numeric(v$sd), 3)) #>  cells  draws     sd  #>   1.00 200.00   2.08   # `method` defaults to "ensemble" whatever produced the draws, so a # bootstrap posterior mislabels its own provenance unless you say so. c(default = as_edaphos_posterior(draws)$method,   tagged  = as_edaphos_posterior(draws, method = "bootstrap")$method) #>     default      tagged  #>  "ensemble" "bootstrap"   # The identity method returns `x` and drops every extra argument, so # an existing posterior cannot be re-tagged through the adapter: # `units` stays "g/kg" and the object comes back untouched. identical(as_edaphos_posterior(post, units = "kg/m2"), post) #> [1] TRUE  # The adapter is narrower than the constructor it wraps: a # (draws x H x W) map ensemble has no default method and must go # through edaphos_posterior(samples = ) directly. arr <- array(stats::rnorm(50L * 4L * 5L), dim = c(50L, 4L, 5L)) try(as_edaphos_posterior(arr)) #> Error : No `as_edaphos_posterior` method for class <array>. dim(edaphos_posterior(samples = arr, query_type = "map")$mean) #> [1] 4 5

title: Benchmark wrapper: Pilar 10 – GAT seed-ensemble on k-NN graph — benchmark_fit_p10_gat
code: data(br_cerrado) set.seed(3) sub <- br_cerrado[sample(nrow(br_cerrado), 160L), ] names(sub)[names(sub) == "x"] <- "lon" names(sub)[names(sub) == "y"] <- "lat" covs  <- c("elev", "slope", "twi", "map_mm", "ndvi") train <- sub[1:120, ]; test <- sub[121:160, ]  # The k-NN graph spans train AND test, but only the training nodes carry # an observed target, so `test` never needs a `soc` column: the wrapper # fills the held-out targets with NA and masks them out of the loss. post <- benchmark_fit_p10_gat(train, test[, c("lon", "lat", covs)], covs,                               k = 6L, hidden = 8L, n_heads = 2L,                               n_layers = 2L, epochs = 40L, lr = 0.05,                               n_ensemble = 4L, seed = 1L) #> Warning: P10: inner blocked CV could not run on this training partition; the residual scale falls back to training residuals and the interval is expected to undercover. dim(post$samples)                 # 4 seed-distinct members x 40 sites #> [1]  4 40  # Two baselines, both computed here: the training mean and OLS on the # same five covariates.  5.090 / 7.289 / 4.679 -- on 120 training nodes # the attention over the co-location graph beats the mean by 30% and # still loses to the linear model by 9%.  A GAT row in a benchmark # table means nothing without that middle column. cal <- uncertainty_calibrate(post, truth = test$soc) ols <- lm(soc ~ elev + slope + twi + map_mm + ndvi, data = train) round(c(gat  = cal$point_rmse,         null = sqrt(mean((mean(train$soc) - test$soc)^2)),         ols  = sqrt(mean((predict(ols, test) - test$soc)^2))), 3) #>   gat  null   ols  #> 4.930 7.289 4.679   # `n_ensemble` is not only how precisely the point prediction is # averaged: the posterior IS the ensemble, so a 90% interval read off # four draws cannot be wider than their range.  Going to eight members # widens it from 7.75 to 9.62 g/kg and lifts coverage from 0.50 to # 0.60 -- closer to nominal, still well short of it. big <- benchmark_fit_p10_gat(train, test, covs, k = 6L, hidden = 8L,                              n_heads = 2L, n_layers = 2L, epochs = 40L,                              lr = 0.05, n_ensemble = 8L, seed = 1L) #> Warning: P10: inner blocked CV could not run on this training partition; the residual scale falls back to training residuals and the interval is expected to undercover. cal_big <- uncertainty_calibrate(big, truth = test$soc) round(c(picp90_4 = cal$picp[["0.90"]], picp90_8 = cal_big$picp[["0.90"]],         mpiw90_4 = cal$mpiw[["0.90"]], mpiw90_8 = cal_big$mpiw[["0.90"]]), 3) #> picp90_4 picp90_8 mpiw90_4 mpiw90_8  #>    0.525    0.550    7.832    9.086   # Where that width comes from matters.  `calibrate = FALSE` leaves only # the seed-to-seed spread of the fitted means -- 1.10 g/kg, and 20% # coverage -- against a residual sd of 3.79.  The members disagree far # less with each other than any of them disagrees with the truth, which # is the usual state of a deep ensemble and the reason the aleatoric # term is added by default. epi <- benchmark_fit_p10_gat(train, test, covs, k = 6L, hidden = 8L,                              n_heads = 2L, n_layers = 2L, epochs = 40L,                              lr = 0.05, n_ensemble = 4L, seed = 1L,                              calibrate = FALSE) round(c(sd_epistemic = mean(apply(epi$samples, 2L, sd)),         sd_calibrated = mean(apply(post$samples, 2L, sd)),         sigma_resid = post$metadata$sigma_resid,         picp90_epistemic =           uncertainty_calibrate(epi, truth = test$soc)$picp[["0.90"]]), 3) #>     sd_epistemic    sd_calibrated      sigma_resid picp90_epistemic  #>            1.054            3.957            3.681            0.175   # Member-by-member RMSE, for scale: the four seeds score 4.98 to 5.46 # and their average scores 5.09 -- inside that range, not below it.  On # this problem the ensemble is buying an interval, not accuracy. round(apply(epi$samples, 1L, function(p) sqrt(mean((p - test$soc)^2))), 3) #> [1] 5.138 5.133 4.764 5.087  # Each member is one gnn_fit() on a single transductive graph: train # and test nodes together, held-out targets NA, loss on the training # mask.  Rebuilding member 1 by hand reproduces it exactly -- and shows # what `epochs` actually did.  gnn_fit() keeps a validation slice and # restores its best epoch, which here is epoch 2 of the 40 asked for; # it stops at 22 and discards the rest.  Nothing above is a training # curve, which is the other half of why this loses to lm(). df_all <- rbind(cbind(train[, c("lon", "lat", covs)], soc = train$soc),                 cbind(test[,  c("lon", "lat", covs)], soc = NA_real_)) g1 <- gnn_build_graph(df_all, k = 6L, feature_cols = covs) f1 <- gnn_fit(g1, df_all$soc, train_mask = !is.na(df_all$soc),               hidden = 8L, n_heads = 2L, n_layers = 2L, epochs = 40L,               lr = 0.05, seed = 2L)          # member b uses seed + b c(best_epoch = f1$best_epoch, epochs_run = length(f1$history)) #> best_epoch epochs_run  #>          2         22  isTRUE(all.equal(predict(f1)[121:160], epi$samples[1, ])) #> [1] TRUE

title: Benchmark wrapper: Pilar 1 – DAG-adjusted OLS + parametric bootstrap — benchmark_fit_p1_causal
code: data(br_cerrado)  # The wrapper checks for the response `soc` and the named covariates # and nothing else -- it never reads a coordinate column, and its # bootstrap is a plain row resample. So the split below is RANDOM, not # spatial, and the interval it produces does not account for spatial # dependence between train and test. For a spatially blocked # comparison see `data-raw/benchmark_wosis_6pilar.R`, which is what # the published six-pillar figures use. set.seed(1) sub <- br_cerrado[sample(nrow(br_cerrado), 300L), ] covs  <- c("elev", "slope", "twi", "map_mm", "ndvi") train <- sub[1:240, ]; test <- sub[241:300, ]  post <- benchmark_fit_p1_causal(train, test, covs, n_boot = 300L, seed = 1L) dim(post$samples)          # 300 bootstrap draws x 60 held-out sites #> [1] 300  60  # Score it against the baseline any soil map has to beat -- predicting # the training mean everywhere.  3.680 g/kg against 6.173. cal <- uncertainty_calibrate(post, truth = test$soc) round(c(rmse = cal$point_rmse,         null = sqrt(mean((mean(train$soc) - test$soc)^2))), 3) #>  rmse  null  #> 3.680 6.173   # `calibrate = TRUE` (the default) convolves the in-sample residual sd # into every draw.  The noise is centred within each test column, so the # point prediction survives untouched -- colMeans() moves by ~3e-14 -- # and only the interval changes. raw <- benchmark_fit_p1_causal(train, test, covs, n_boot = 300L,                                seed = 1L, calibrate = FALSE) max(abs(colMeans(post$samples) - colMeans(raw$samples))) #> [1] 0  # Read that next to the coverage, which is the whole point of the term. # Bootstrap spread alone is the uncertainty of the FITTED MEAN, not of a # new profile: its 90% intervals are 1.99 g/kg wide and hold 22% of the # held-out truth.  With the aleatoric term they are 13.46 wide and hold # 93%, which on 60 sites is 0.9 binomial standard errors off nominal -- # calibrated, as far as this test set can tell. cal_raw <- uncertainty_calibrate(raw, truth = test$soc) round(c(picp90_raw = cal_raw$picp[["0.90"]],         picp90_cal = cal$picp[["0.90"]],         mpiw90_raw = cal_raw$mpiw[["0.90"]],         mpiw90_cal = cal$mpiw[["0.90"]],         se90 = sqrt(0.9 * 0.1 / nrow(test))), 3) #> picp90_raw picp90_cal mpiw90_raw mpiw90_cal       se90  #>      0.217      0.933      1.989     13.461      0.039   # TRAP: the DAG filter asks for the parents of a hard-coded outcome node # named "soc_topsoil_gkg".  A DAG that calls its outcome anything else # raises inside dagitty::parents(), and the fallback keeps every node # NAME in the graph -- so `elev` and `slope`, parents of nothing but # `ndvi` and `twi`, survive a selection advertised as causal. if (requireNamespace("dagitty", quietly = TRUE)) {   d_wrong <- dagitty::dagitty(     "dag { elev -> ndvi ; ndvi -> soc ; map_mm -> soc ; slope -> twi }")   print(dagitty::parents(d_wrong, "soc"))     # map_mm, ndvi   print(benchmark_fit_p1_causal(train, test, covs, dag = d_wrong,                                 n_boot = 50L,                                 seed = 1L)$metadata$adjusted_features)    # Name the outcome the way the wrapper expects and the parent set is   # honoured: three covariates instead of five.   d_ok <- dagitty::dagitty(     "dag { map_mm -> soc_topsoil_gkg ; ndvi -> soc_topsoil_gkg ;            twi -> soc_topsoil_gkg ; elev -> map_mm ; slope -> twi }")   print(benchmark_fit_p1_causal(train, test, covs, dag = d_ok,                                 n_boot = 50L,                                 seed = 1L)$metadata$adjusted_features)    # And a DAG leaving fewer than two covariates reverts to the full set   # rather than fitting a one-covariate model -- also silently.   # `metadata$adjusted_features` is the only place any of this shows.   d_one <- dagitty::dagitty("dag { ndvi -> soc_topsoil_gkg }")   print(benchmark_fit_p1_causal(train, test, covs, dag = d_one,                                 n_boot = 50L,                                 seed = 1L)$metadata$adjusted_features) } #> [1] "map_mm" "ndvi"   #> [1] "elev"   "slope"  "twi"    "map_mm" "ndvi"   #> [1] "twi"    "map_mm" "ndvi"   #> [1] "elev"   "slope"  "twi"    "map_mm" "ndvi"

text: train, test Data frames soc + cov_cols. cov_cols Character vector covariate column names. n_pcs Integer; number PCs (= qubits).  Default 6L. reps Integer; ZZFeatureMap repetitions.  Default 2L. lambda Ridge regulariser.  Default 0.5. n_boot Integer; number bootstrap KRR fits.  Default 20L. seed Optional RNG seed. calibrate Logical (default TRUE). title: Benchmark wrapper: Pilar 6 – bootstrap-ensembled quantum KRR — benchmark_fit_p6_quantum
code: data(br_cerrado) set.seed(2) sub <- br_cerrado[sample(nrow(br_cerrado), 120L), ] names(sub)[names(sub) == "x"] <- "lon" names(sub)[names(sub) == "y"] <- "lat" covs  <- c("elev", "slope", "twi", "map_mm", "ndvi") train <- sub[1:90, ]; test <- sub[91:120, ]  # `n_pcs` IS the qubit count: the simulator carries a 2^n_pcs state # vector per site and the Gram matrix needs O(n^2) of them, so keep it # small.  It also cannot exceed the number of non-constant covariates -- # with these five columns the package default of 6 stops the fit. try(benchmark_fit_p6_quantum(train, test, covs, n_pcs = 6L, n_boot = 2L)) #> Error : Only 5 non-constant embedding columns; n_pcs=6 requested.  post <- benchmark_fit_p6_quantum(train, test, covs, n_pcs = 4L, reps = 1L,                                  n_boot = 5L, lambda = 0.5, seed = 1L) dim(post$samples)                  # 5 bootstrap members x 30 sites #> [1]  5 30  # Do not read this as a working model.  Against the training mean and # against OLS on the same five covariates: 7.047 / 7.048 / 4.361. cal <- uncertainty_calibrate(post, truth = test$soc) ols <- lm(soc ~ elev + slope + twi + map_mm + ndvi, data = train) round(c(qkrr = cal$point_rmse,         null = sqrt(mean((mean(train$soc) - test$soc)^2)),         ols  = sqrt(mean((predict(ols, test) - test$soc)^2))), 3) #>  qkrr  null   ols  #> 7.047 7.048 4.361   # It ties the null because it has collapsed onto it.  At 4 qubits the # ZZFeatureMap Gram matrix is nearly the identity (mean off-diagonal # 0.063), the dual weights explain almost nothing, and predictions fall # back on the offset that quantum_krr_fit() centres the response with -- # i.e. mean(train$soc).  The predictions vary by 1.75 g/kg where the # truth varies by 7.13. pt <- colMeans(post$samples) red <- qf_embed_reduce(as.matrix(rbind(train[, covs], test[, covs])),                        n_pcs = 4L) K <- quantum_kernel(red$X_q[1:90, ], reps = 1L) round(c(sd_pred = sd(pt), sd_truth = sd(test$soc),         mean_pred = mean(pt), train_mean = mean(train$soc),         gram_offdiag = mean(K[upper.tri(K)])), 3) #>      sd_pred     sd_truth    mean_pred   train_mean gram_offdiag  #>        1.754        7.130       20.420       19.938        0.063   # Note which rows went into that PCA: the wrapper reduces # rbind(train, test) jointly, so the rotation and the [-pi, pi] rescale # have seen the test covariates.  Fine for a benchmark of the kernel, # not a clean out-of-sample protocol -- PC1 takes 0.489 of the variance # jointly against 0.477 on the training rows alone. round(rbind(joint = red$variance_explained,             train_only = qf_embed_reduce(as.matrix(train[, covs]),                                          n_pcs = 4L)$variance_explained), 3) #>              PC1   PC2   PC3   PC4 #> joint      0.489 0.275 0.169 0.051 #> train_only 0.477 0.276 0.171 0.055  # The interval story is separate, and n_boot bounds it: a 90% interval # read off 5 members cannot be wider than their range.  More members # widen it, but they cannot rescue a posterior centred in the wrong # place -- coverage is still 0.467 at n_boot = 50. picp <- vapply(c(5L, 20L, 50L), function(nb) {   p <- benchmark_fit_p6_quantum(train, test, covs, n_pcs = 4L, reps = 1L,                                 n_boot = nb, lambda = 0.5, seed = 1L)   uncertainty_calibrate(p, truth = test$soc)$picp[["0.90"]] }, numeric(1)) round(picp, 3) #> [1] 0.500 0.533 0.667

title: Fit a Bayesian hierarchical spatial linear model (Pilar 7) — bhs_fit
code: data(br_cerrado)  # A contiguous 13 x 13 block of the Cerrado grid: 169 sites, 0.0080 deg # apart in longitude and 0.0068 in latitude.  bhs_fit() wants the # coordinates under lon / lat. ux  <- sort(unique(br_cerrado$x)); uy <- sort(unique(br_cerrado$y)) blk <- br_cerrado[br_cerrado$x %in% ux[10:22] &                   br_cerrado$y %in% uy[10:22], ] names(blk)[names(blk) == "x"] <- "lon" names(blk)[names(blk) == "y"] <- "lat"  # phi is a RATE: it enters the correlation as exp(-phi * d), so 3 / phi is # a practical correlation range in the units of `coords` -- degrees here. # # The likelihood on this block keeps improving as the range shrinks, so # whatever you cap phi at is what you get back. That is why a CONSTANT # bracket cannot be a sensible default: it decides the answer. The default # is now derived from the data, and its upper end is the closest pair of # observations -- the point past which the correlation has decayed to # nothing between any two of them, so there is nothing left to estimate. fit_auto  <- bhs_fit(blk, soc ~ elev + slope, nmcmc = 600L, seed = 1L) #> Warning: bhs_fit(): the profile-MLE of phi (440) is at the upper end of phi_range = c(23.86, 440), derived from the data. The bracket is derived from the data, and its upper end is the closest pair of sites: a practical range shorter than that has decayed to nothing between any two observations, so this survey cannot distinguish the field from a nugget. Widening the bracket would not help; a denser survey would. phi is a rate (1/distance) in the units of `coords`. fit_wide  <- bhs_fit(blk, soc ~ elev + slope, nmcmc = 600L, seed = 1L,                      phi_range = c(0.1, 2000)) #> Warning: bhs_fit(): the profile-MLE of phi (2000) is at the upper end of phi_range = c(0.1, 2000), supplied. Widen phi_range and refit; the spatial variance fraction is not trustworthy until phi is interior. phi is a rate (1/distance) in the units of `coords`. fit_huge  <- bhs_fit(blk, soc ~ elev + slope, nmcmc = 600L, seed = 1L,                      phi_range = c(0.1, 1e5)) #> Warning: bhs_fit(): the profile-MLE of phi (1e+05) is at the upper end of phi_range = c(0.1, 1e+05), supplied. Widen phi_range and refit; the spatial variance fraction is not trustworthy until phi is interior. phi is a rate (1/distance) in the units of `coords`. fit_auto #> <edaphos_bhs>  (Pilar 7 -- Bayesian Hierarchical Spatial) #>   backend : gibbs #>   n_obs   : 169 #>   p (covariates + intercept) : 3 #>   MCMC draws kept : 300 #>   phi (profile-MLE) : 439.9999 #>   beta posterior means: #>     (Intercept)          52.1543 (sd 5.3841) #>     elev                 -0.0263 (sd 0.0063) #>     slope                -0.5666 (sd 0.0722) #>   sigma^2 posterior mean : 0.7577 #>   tau^2   posterior mean : 20.2302 #>   spatial share sigma^2/(sigma^2 + tau^2) : 0.036 #>   practical range 3/phi : 0.006818 (nearest-neighbour spacing 0.006818, same units as coords) #>   <-- phi railed at the upper end of its bracket; the bracket, not #>       the data, set the correlation rate  # That is not a cosmetic complaint.  Under the two hand-picked brackets the # spatial share of the residual variance, sigma^2 / (sigma^2 + tau^2), # comes out around 0.89 -- the same data and formula reporting a strong # latent field, on a correlation range far shorter than the grid spacing. # The derived bracket stops at the spacing and the share falls to about # 0.04, which is the honest reading: this block is nearly all nugget. round(c(phi_auto = fit_auto$phi_hat, phi_wide = fit_wide$phi_hat,         phi_huge = fit_huge$phi_hat,         share_auto = fit_auto$spatial$spatial_share,         share_wide = fit_wide$spatial$spatial_share,         share_huge = fit_huge$spatial$spatial_share), 4) #>    phi_auto    phi_wide    phi_huge  share_auto  share_wide  share_huge  #>    439.9999   1999.9999  99999.9970      0.0361      0.8862      0.8862   # All three still rail, and that is now informative rather than arbitrary: # `$phi_range_source` says whether the bracket was derived or supplied, and # `$range_below_spacing` says whether the fitted range survived to the # closest pair. Only the hand-picked ones fail that test. vapply(list(fit_auto, fit_wide, fit_huge),        function(f) f$spatial$range_below_spacing, logical(1)) #> [1] FALSE  TRUE  TRUE  # The tie-breaker is not the likelihood, it is the geometry.  At # phi = 2000 the correlation between the two CLOSEST sites in the block # is 1e-06: exp(-phi * d) has decayed to nothing well inside one grid # cell, so w and eps are the same white noise and their split is # arbitrary.  An "89% spatial" fit whose correlation range is 55 m on a # 750 m grid is reporting a nugget under another name. d <- as.matrix(dist(as.matrix(blk[, c("lon", "lat")]))) round(c(range_deg = 1 / fit_wide$phi_hat, min_spacing = min(d[d > 0]),         corr_at_min_spacing = exp(-fit_wide$phi_hat * min(d[d > 0]))), 6) #>           range_deg         min_spacing corr_at_min_spacing  #>            0.000500            0.006818            0.000001   # Which is also why the beta posterior sits on top of OLS: with the # correlation matrix effectively the identity, generalised least squares # has nothing to weight.  Both slopes agree to well under a third of a # posterior sd. o <- lm(soc ~ elev + slope, data = blk) round(rbind(bhs = colMeans(fit_wide$beta_draws), ols = coef(o),             post_sd = apply(fit_wide$beta_draws, 2L, sd)), 4) #>         (Intercept)    elev   slope #> bhs         52.6592 -0.0265 -0.5879 #> ols         53.6279 -0.0279 -0.5701 #> post_sd      5.0989  0.0056  0.0698  # `nmcmc` is the raw chain; `burn` (half of it by default) and `thin` # decide how much survives, and every downstream interval -- including # predict()'s -- is built from those kept draws alone. c(nmcmc = fit_wide$nmcmc, burn = fit_wide$burn,   kept = nrow(fit_wide$beta_draws)) #> nmcmc  burn  kept  #>   600   300   300

code: if (requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)) {   # Synthetic panel whose MAP -> SOC effect decays over 36 slices,   # with elevation as the confounder that must be adjusted away.   set.seed(11)   panel <- expand.grid(site = 1:10, t = 1:36)   elev  <- runif(10, 400, 1100)   panel$elev     <- elev[panel$site]   panel$map_anom <- -0.10 * (panel$elev - 750) + rnorm(nrow(panel), 0, 60)   panel$soc      <- 22 + 0.006 * panel$elev +     (0.022 - 0.0006 * panel$t) * panel$map_anom + rnorm(nrow(panel), 0, 0.8)    boot <- causal_effect_time_varying(panel, NULL, "map_anom", "soc",                                      window = 12L, step = 3L,                                      adjustment = "elev", B = 100L,                                      seed = 42)   g <- causal_4d_plot(boot)   print(inherits(g, "ggplot"))   # print(g) draws it on the device    # The subtitle is a live Mann-Kendall test on exactly the windows   # being drawn, so it inherits their overlap.  Read it as a label   # for the curve, not as an independent significance test.   print(g$labels$subtitle)    # The ribbon is simply ci_lo/ci_hi.  With B = 0 those are the OLS   # normal limits rather than a bootstrap, and the ribbon looks no   # different: here the bootstrap band is in fact the narrower of   # the two (mean width 0.00485 against 0.00515).   norm <- causal_effect_time_varying(panel, NULL, "map_anom", "soc",                                      window = 12L, step = 3L,                                      adjustment = "elev", B = 0L)   print(round(c(bootstrap = mean(boot$ci_hi - boot$ci_lo),                 normal    = mean(norm$ci_hi - norm$ci_lo)), 5))    # No autoplot() method is registered for this class, despite the   # wording of the error raised when ggplot2 is missing.   inherits(try(ggplot2::autoplot(boot), silent = TRUE), "try-error") } #> [1] TRUE #> [1] "Mann-Kendall: S=-36, tau=-1, p=0.000263 (decreasing)" #> bootstrap    normal  #>   0.00485   0.00515  #> [1] TRUE

code: if (requireNamespace("dagitty", quietly = TRUE)) {   dag <- causal_clorpt_dag()    # `effect` decides WHICH estimand you are adjusting for, and the   # default is "direct". That distinction is not cosmetic.   #   # Climate is exogenous in this DAG -- it has no parents at all --   # so the TOTAL effect of Climate on SOC is not confounded by   # anything, and the adjustment set is empty:   dagitty::parents(dag, "Climate")   causal_adjustment_set(dag, "Climate", "SOC", effect = "total")    # The default asks a different question. Climate reaches SOC both   # directly and through Organisms, so isolating the DIRECT effect   # means blocking the indirect path:   causal_adjustment_set(dag, "Climate", "SOC")   # effect = "direct"    # Organisms is a CHILD of Climate, not a common cause of both.   dagitty::children(dag, "Climate")    # So do not read a non-empty adjustment set as "these are the   # confounders". Conditioning on a mediator does not remove bias --   # it changes the estimand from total to direct, and conditioning   # on one when you wanted the total effect introduces bias rather   # than removing it. } #> [1] "Organisms"  "SOC"        "Weathering"

title: Augment a base DAG with edges from a Knowledge Graph — causal_augment_dag
code: if (requireNamespace("dagitty", quietly = TRUE) &&     requireNamespace("igraph", quietly = TRUE)) {    base <- causal_cerrado_dag()   # 13 edges over the br_cerrado columns    # Three claims of the shape an LLM extractor returns: one   # plausible, one read backwards, one weakly supported.   kg <- causal_kg_new()   kg <- causal_kg_add_edge(kg, "elev", "ndvi",                            source = "altitudinal zonation",                            confidence = 0.92)   kg <- causal_kg_add_edge(kg, "soc", "map_mm",                            source = "mis-extracted direction",                            confidence = 0.99)   kg <- causal_kg_add_edge(kg, "fire_frequency", "soc",                            source = "single-site study",                            confidence = 0.45)    # At the default threshold the 0.45 fire claim is never   # considered. The 0.99 reversed claim is, and is then thrown out   # by the acyclicity guard (with a warning) because base already   # has map_mm -> soc. Only elev -> ndvi is actually added.   aug <- causal_augment_dag(base, kg)   print(unlist(attributes(aug)[c("n_base_edges", "n_added_edges",                                  "n_rejected")]))    # Note what that implies: confidence 0.99 bought nothing and   # confidence 0.92 bought an edge. `min_confidence` ranks claims,   # it never weighs them -- an edge is either in or out.    # Lowering the threshold buys the fire claim, and with it a node   # that no column of br_cerrado measures.   loose <- causal_augment_dag(base, kg, min_confidence = 0.4)   print(setdiff(names(loose), names(base)))    # allow_new_nodes = FALSE locks the structural vocabulary, so   # that edge is dropped again even though it cleared the   # threshold.   locked <- causal_augment_dag(base, kg, min_confidence = 0.4,                                allow_new_nodes = FALSE)   print(setdiff(names(locked), names(base))) } #> Warning: Rejected 1 edge(s) that would have introduced a directed cycle: soc -> map_mm #>  n_base_edges n_added_edges    n_rejected  #>            13             1             1  #> Warning: Rejected 1 edge(s) that would have introduced a directed cycle: soc -> map_mm #> [1] "fire_frequency" #> Warning: Rejected 1 edge(s) that would have introduced a directed cycle: soc -> map_mm #> character(0)

code: if (requireNamespace("dagitty", quietly = TRUE) &&     requireNamespace("igraph", quietly = TRUE)) {    base <- causal_cerrado_dag()    # Two mined claims. The first is sound -- clay protects organic   # carbon. The second is a pedogenetic relation read backwards:   # rainfall drives weathering drives clay, not clay drives   # rainfall. The extractor was equally confident about both.   kg <- causal_kg_new()   kg <- causal_kg_add_edge(kg, "clay", "soc",    confidence = 0.95)   kg <- causal_kg_add_edge(kg, "clay", "map_mm", confidence = 0.95)    aug   <- causal_augment_dag(base, kg)   diffs <- causal_augment_diff(base, aug)   print(diffs[diffs$origin == "kg", ])    # The wrong edge is not inert. Together the two claims make   # `clay` a confounder of map_mm -> soc, so the minimal adjustment   # set grows by a variable br_cerrado does not contain.   print(causal_adjustment_set(base, "map_mm", "soc"))   adj <- causal_adjustment_set(aug, "map_mm", "soc")   print(setdiff(adj, names(br_cerrado)))    # So read `origin == "kg"` as "asserted by the extractor", never   # as "validated". The only filters causal_augment_dag() applies   # are the confidence threshold and acyclicity.    # The diff also sees only edges that survived, so a KG edge   # rejected as cycle-forming appears nowhere in it; its count   # lives on the augmented DAG. Nothing cycled here, hence 0.   print(attr(aug, "n_rejected")) } #>   cause effect origin #> 1  clay map_mm     kg #> 2  clay    soc     kg #> [1] "elev"  "ndvi"  "slope" "twi"   #> [1] "clay" #> [1] 0

This one is nearly   # saturated: it implies only two conditional independencies, so   # passing them is weak evidence for the structure, not proof.   print(dagitty::impliedConditionalIndependencies(dag))    # Both do hold in br_cerrado -- the partial correlations come out   # under 0.03 in absolute value, and neither confidence interval   # excludes zero.   print(dagitty::localTests(dag, br_cerrado)) } #> [1] TRUE #> elev _||_ ndvi | mp_m, slop, twi #> mp_m _||_ slop | elev #>                                    estimate   p.value        2.5%      97.5% #> elev _||_ ndvi | mp_m, slop, twi 0.02075439 0.3509765 -0.02285807 0.06428808 #> mp_m _||_ slop | elev            0.01331066 0.5495577 -0.03027714 0.05684796

title: Real-data Cerrado pedogenetic DAG — causal_cerrado_real_dag
text: edges encode six classes Cerrado pedogenetic relations: Relief -> climate Elevation modulates temperature (adiabatic lapse) precipitation (orographic forcing) via elev -> bio1, elev -> bio12, elev -> slope. Climate -> vegetation / land cover Bio1 (mean annual temperature) bio12 (mean annual precipitation) drive fraction land covered trees, grassland cropland. Relief -> texture Steep slopes export fine fractions (slope -> soilgrids_clay) accumulate coarse fractions downslope (slope -> soilgrids_sand). Texture -> bulk density Fine-textured soils compact differently (soilgrids_clay -> soilgrids_bdod). Climate + texture -> SOC (direct) sides drive decomposition vs mineral protection. Land cover -> SOC Native savanna vs. pasture vs. cropland produce 3-4x SOC differences Cerrado topsoil; land-cover fractions dominant single factor.

title: Real-data Cerrado pedogenetic DAG — causal_cerrado_real_dag
code: if (requireNamespace("dagitty", quietly = TRUE)) {   dag  <- causal_cerrado_real_dag()   prof <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "case_cerrado_results.rds",                               package = "edaphos"))$profiles    # The whole point of this DAG: all of its nodes are real columns   # of the WoSIS case-study table, whereas the schematic   # causal_cerrado_dag() shares only two names with it.   print(all(names(dag) %in% names(prof)))   print(intersect(names(causal_cerrado_dag()), names(prof)))    # Total vs direct effect of clay on topsoil SOC. The total effect   # only needs slope; the direct effect must additionally block bulk   # density (a mediator) and then sand as well, because bdod is a   # collider of clay and sand.   print(causal_adjustment_set(dag, "soilgrids_clay",                               "soc_topsoil_gkg", effect = "total"))   print(causal_adjustment_set(dag, "soilgrids_clay",                               "soc_topsoil_gkg", effect = "direct"))    # Roughly two thirds of the clay effect is mediated: the total   # slope is about 0.54 g/kg SOC per unit of soilgrids_clay, the   # direct one about 0.19 with an interval that only just clears   # zero. Report which one you mean.   print(causal_estimate_effect(prof, dag, "soilgrids_clay",                                "soc_topsoil_gkg", effect = "total"))   print(causal_estimate_effect(prof, dag, "soilgrids_clay",                                "soc_topsoil_gkg", effect = "direct")) } #> [1] TRUE #> [1] "elev"  "slope" #> [1] "slope" #> [1] "slope"          "soilgrids_bdod" "soilgrids_sand" #> <edaphos_causal_effect> #>   soilgrids_clay -> soc_topsoil_gkg   (estimator: lm) #>   adjustment set : {slope} #>   total effect   : 0.5371   (95% CI: 0.4239, 0.6504) #>   naive effect   : 0.5257   (un-adjusted, likely confounded) #> <edaphos_causal_effect> #>   soilgrids_clay -> soc_topsoil_gkg   (estimator: lm) #>   adjustment set : {slope, soilgrids_bdod, soilgrids_sand} #>   direct effect  : 0.1949   (95% CI: 0.009367, 0.3804) #>   naive effect   : 0.5257   (un-adjusted, likely confounded)

code: if (requireNamespace("dagitty", quietly = TRUE)) {   dag <- causal_clorpt_dag()   print(names(dag))    # Only four of the five CLORPT factors come out exogenous:   # Organisms does not, because the graph asserts Climate ->   # Organisms.   print(dagitty::exogenousVariables(dag))    # Trap: these are conceptual labels, not column names. The DAG   # shares no node at all with the bundled br_cerrado grid, so the   # two cannot be handed to causal_estimate_effect() together.   print(intersect(names(dag), names(br_cerrado)))    # CEC is a common effect of Clay and SOC, i.e. a collider. Given   # the shared causes Climate and Time the two are d-separated ...   print(dagitty::dconnected(dag, "SOC", "Clay", c("Climate", "Time")))   # ... and adding CEC to the conditioning set re-opens the path,   # manufacturing a clay-carbon association that is not causal.   # This is what "control for every covariate we measured" buys you.   print(dagitty::dconnected(dag, "SOC", "Clay",                             c("Climate", "Time", "CEC"))) } #>  [1] "CEC"            "Clay"           "Climate"        "Erosion"        #>  [5] "Organisms"      "ParentMaterial" "Relief"         "SOC"            #>  [9] "TWI"            "Time"           "Weathering"     "pH"             #> [1] "Climate"        "ParentMaterial" "Relief"         "Time"           #> character(0) #> [1] FALSE #> [1] TRUE

code: # A merged SciELO + OpenAlex pull on Cerrado pedology: the same # paper arrives twice, once per source, with the DOI cased # differently. corpus <- data.frame(   source = c("scielo", "openalex", "openalex", "scielo"),   title  = c("Soil organic carbon under Cerrado pasture",              "soil organic  carbon under cerrado pasture",              "Termite mounds and phosphorus availability",              "Soil organic carbon under Cerrado pasture"),   doi    = c("10.1590/S0100-06832011000100001",              "10.1590/s0100-06832011000100001",              "10.1016/j.geoderma.2019.05.001",              NA_character_),   stringsAsFactors = FALSE )  dedup <- causal_corpus_deduplicate(corpus) dedup[, c("source", "doi")] #>     source                             doi #> 1   scielo 10.1590/S0100-06832011000100001 #> 2 openalex  10.1016/j.geoderma.2019.05.001 #> 3   scielo                            <NA>  # Rows 1 and 2 collapse on the case-folded DOI and the FIRST # occurrence survives, so which record wins is decided by row # order, not by record quality -- stack the feed you trust on top. dedup$source[1]  # "scielo" #> [1] "scielo"  # The trap: row 4 is that paper a third time but with no DOI, so # it is keyed on its title while row 1 is keyed on its DOI. Keys # drawn from different columns never match, and the duplicate # survives. nrow(dedup)  # 3, not 2 #> [1] 3  # Forcing a single key space fixes it; title matching also folds # case and collapses runs of whitespace. nrow(causal_corpus_deduplicate(corpus, by = "title"))  # 2 #> [1] 2  # Records with neither a DOI nor a title get an NA key and are all # kept -- "unknown" is not treated as "the same". blank <- data.frame(doi   = c(NA_character_, NA_character_),                     title = c(NA_character_, NA_character_)) nrow(causal_corpus_deduplicate(blank))  # 2 #> [1] 2

code: if (requireNamespace("dagitty", quietly = TRUE)) {   dag <- causal_cerrado_dag()   d   <- br_cerrado    # The bootstrap resamples CLUSTERS, not rows, so `data` must carry   # a cluster column -- `br_cerrado` does not ship one. Nine spatial   # blocks from k-means on the coordinates, as in the Cerrado   # pipeline.   set.seed(42)   d$kmeans_cluster <- stats::kmeans(d[, c("x", "y")], centers = 9L)$cluster    # B = 50 keeps this example fast; a real analysis wants several   # hundred. At B = 50 the tail quantiles are themselves noisy: the   # 95% width wandered between 0.23 and 0.37 across five seeds here,   # against 0.35 at B = 500.   boot <- causal_effect_bootstrap(d, dag, "twi", "soc", B = 50L, seed = 1L)   quantile(boot, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))    # Block resampling does not automatically widen the interval: here   # it lands on the asymptotic confint(lm) width, which says these   # (synthetic) residuals carry little block-level dependence. Check   # that before calling the clustered interval the conservative one.   fit <- causal_estimate_effect(d, dag, "twi", "soc")   c(block_boot = unname(diff(quantile(boot, c(0.025, 0.975)))),     asymptotic = unname(diff(fit$effect_ci)))    # What resampling cannot check is the graph. Same rows, same seed,   # one edge-level decision -- "direct" blocks the twi -> ndvi -> soc   # mediator, "total" leaves it open -- and the target moves from   # 1.51 to 1.80, with the two 95% intervals overlapping by 0.02.   tot <- causal_effect_bootstrap(d, dag, "twi", "soc", B = 50L,                                  seed = 1L, effect = "total")   c(direct = mean(boot), total = mean(tot)) } #>   direct    total  #> 1.512274 1.800608

B = 50 keeps   # the example fast; use several hundred for anything you report.   post <- causal_effect_posterior(d, dag, "twi", "soc", B = 50L,                                   seed = 1L, units = "g/kg per TWI unit")   post    # `post$quantiles` holds q05/q50/q95 -- a 90% interval, not the   # 95% one most papers quote. Take that from the draws directly.   quantile(post$samples[, 1], c(0.025, 0.975))    # When the adjustment set is derived from the DAG rather than   # passed in, the LM path records `metadata$adjustment` as NULL.   # Recover the set from the graph for your provenance record.   post$metadata$adjustment   causal_adjustment_set(dag, "twi", "soc", effect = "direct")    # The posterior is conditional on the DAG *and* on the estimator.   # BART on the same graph and the same rows returns about 1.20,   # outside the LM bootstrap interval of roughly [1.36, 1.69]. No   # number of resamples exposes that -- it is a functional-form   # disagreement, not sampling noise.   if (requireNamespace("dbarts", quietly = TRUE)) {     pb <- causal_effect_posterior(       d, dag, "twi", "soc", estimator = "bart",       bart_kwargs = list(ntree = 50L, ndpost = 200L, nskip = 100L,                          seed = 1L)     )     c(lm = post$mean, bart = pb$mean)   } } #>       lm     bart  #> 1.512274 1.197336

title: Time-varying causal effect beta(t) over a sliding window — causal_effect_time_varying
code: # A synthetic 36-slice soil panel: 10 sites, an annual-rainfall # anomaly (mm from the long-term normal) driving topsoil SOC, and # elevation confounding both (orographic rain, cooler moister # soils).  The MAP -> SOC slope is built to decay over the record. set.seed(11) panel <- expand.grid(site = 1:10, t = 1:36) elev  <- runif(10, 400, 1100) panel$elev     <- elev[panel$site] panel$map_anom <- -0.10 * (panel$elev - 750) + rnorm(nrow(panel), 0, 60) panel$soc      <- 22 + 0.006 * panel$elev +   (0.022 - 0.0006 * panel$t) * panel$map_anom + rnorm(nrow(panel), 0, 0.8)  # `dag` is consulted only when `adjustment = NULL`, so an explicit # adjustment set lets you pass `dag = NULL`.  Only `t`, the exposure, # the outcome and the adjustment columns are ever read -- the panel # here carries no `lon`/`lat` at all. bt <- causal_effect_time_varying(panel, dag = NULL,                                  exposure = "map_anom", outcome = "soc",                                  window = 12L, step = 3L,                                  adjustment = "elev", B = 0L) bt #> <edaphos_causal_4d>  (Pilar 1 x Pilar 3 bridge) #>   target effect : map_anom -> soc #>   adjustment    : elev #>   window / step : 12 / 3 #>   n windows     : 9 #>   beta_hat mean : 0.0103 (range [0.0046, 0.0154]) #>   Mann-Kendall  : S=-36, tau=-1, p=0.000263, trend=decreasing  # Dropping the confounder does not merely add noise: it collapses # the level of the whole trajectory while leaving the downward shape # intact.  A convincing-looking beta(t) decline is therefore no # evidence at all that the backdoor was closed. naive <- causal_effect_time_varying(panel, NULL, "map_anom", "soc",                                     window = 12L, step = 3L,                                     adjustment = character(0), B = 0L) round(rbind(adjusted = bt$beta_hat, naive = naive$beta_hat), 4) #>            [,1]   [,2]   [,3]   [,4]   [,5]   [,6]   [,7]    [,8]    [,9] #> adjusted 0.0154 0.0149 0.0139 0.0122 0.0104 0.0088 0.0069  0.0056  0.0046 #> naive    0.0066 0.0059 0.0053 0.0033 0.0031 0.0035 0.0018 -0.0012 -0.0046 round(c(adjusted = mean(bt$beta_hat), naive = mean(naive$beta_hat)), 4) #> adjusted    naive  #>   0.0103   0.0026   # With B = 0 the interval is exactly beta_hat +/- 1.96 * se, not a # bootstrap.  Note also how the metadata attributes survive # subsetting: `[` KEEPS them when you subset rows (R >= 4.0), but # drops them the moment you subset columns, after which print() # reports "adjustment : <none>".  as.data.frame() is the safe route # when you only want the numbers. isTRUE(all.equal(bt$ci_lo, bt$beta_hat - qnorm(0.975) * bt$se)) #> [1] TRUE head(as.data.frame(bt)[, c("t_centre", "n", "beta_hat", "ci_lo")], 3) #>   t_centre   n   beta_hat      ci_lo #> 1        7 120 0.01537246 0.01275146 #> 2       10 120 0.01489947 0.01232345 #> 3       13 120 0.01392307 0.01137323  # dagitty can derive the same adjustment set from the graph instead. if (requireNamespace("dagitty", quietly = TRUE)) {   dag <- dagitty::dagitty(     "dag { elev -> map_anom  elev -> soc  map_anom -> soc }")   bt2 <- causal_effect_time_varying(panel, dag, "map_anom", "soc",                                     window = 12L, step = 3L, B = 0L)   identical(attr(bt2, "adjustment"), "elev") } #> [1] TRUE

title: Mann-Kendall trend test on a beta(t) trajectory — causal_effect_trend_test
code: # One synthetic soil panel per seed: elevation confounds a rainfall # anomaly and topsoil SOC, and `drift` fixes how fast the causal # MAP -> SOC slope decays across the 36 time slices. sim_beta <- function(seed, drift) {   set.seed(seed)   d <- expand.grid(site = 1:10, t = 1:36)   e <- runif(10, 400, 1100)   d$elev     <- e[d$site]   d$map_anom <- -0.10 * (d$elev - 750) + rnorm(nrow(d), 0, 60)   d$soc      <- 22 + 0.006 * d$elev +     (0.022 - drift * d$t) * d$map_anom + rnorm(nrow(d), 0, 0.8)   causal_effect_time_varying(d, NULL, "map_anom", "soc", window = 12L,                              step = 3L, adjustment = "elev", B = 0L) }  # A genuine decay is picked up: tau = -1, p = 0.000263, "decreasing". bt <- sim_beta(11, drift = 0.0006) causal_effect_trend_test(bt) #> $S #> [1] -36 #>  #> $tau #> [1] -1 #>  #> $p_value #> [1] 0.0002632608 #>  #> $trend_direction #> [1] "decreasing" #>  #> $z #> [1] -3.649002 #>  #> $n #> [1] 9 #>   # The test reads `beta_hat` and nothing else.  Inflating every # standard error a thousandfold leaves the verdict untouched, so a # window fitted on 30 points votes as loudly as one fitted on 3000. loose <- bt loose$se <- loose$se * 1000 identical(causal_effect_trend_test(loose), causal_effect_trend_test(bt)) #> [1] TRUE  # "none" can also mean "not enough windows": with fewer than four # finite beta_hat values the test returns p_value = NA and direction # "none".  That is silence, not evidence of a stable effect. causal_effect_trend_test(bt[1:3, ]) #> $S #> [1] NA #>  #> $tau #> [1] NA #>  #> $p_value #> [1] NA #>  #> $trend_direction #> [1] "none" #>   # The normal approximation assumes independent windows.  At step = 3 # and window = 12 neighbouring windows share 9 of their 12 slices, so # the p-value is badly anti-conservative: under a constant effect # (drift = 0) it still flags a trend in 0.3 of 60 replicates, six # times the nominal 0.05.  Use step >= window before quoting p. p_null <- vapply(1:60, function(s) {   causal_effect_trend_test(sim_beta(s, drift = 0))$p_value }, numeric(1)) mean(p_null < 0.05) #> [1] 0.3
