title: Deep-ensemble fine-tune of a Pillar 4 foundation encoder — foundation_finetune_ensemble
code: if (requireNamespace("torch", quietly = TRUE) &&     isTRUE(torch::torch_is_installed())) {   # 8 x 8 covariate patches cut on a stride-6 grid over the 45 x 45   # br_cerrado raster; the label is mean SOC inside the patch.   g <- 45L; p <- 8L   cov4 <- lapply(br_cerrado[c("elev", "slope", "twi", "ndvi")],                  function(v) matrix(scale(v)[, 1L], g, g))   soc_m <- matrix(br_cerrado$soc, g, g)   ij <- expand.grid(i = seq(1L, g - p + 1L, by = 6L),                     j = seq(1L, g - p + 1L, by = 6L))   x <- array(0, dim = c(nrow(ij), 4L, p, p))   y <- numeric(nrow(ij))   for (k in seq_len(nrow(ij))) {     rr <- ij$i[k] + 0:(p - 1L); cc <- ij$j[k] + 0:(p - 1L)     for (ch in 1:4) x[k, ch, , ] <- cov4[[ch]][rr, cc]     y[k] <- mean(soc_m[rr, cc])   }   set.seed(2024)   test  <- sample(nrow(ij), 12L)   train <- setdiff(seq_len(nrow(ij)), test)    # A MoCo fit exposes backbone_features(), which is what the   # fine-tune heads read. A SimCLR fit does not: its heads are fed   # the projection output instead, so there proj_dim must equal   # feature_dim or the head is built at the wrong width.   enc <- foundation_moco_pretrain(     x[train, , , , drop = FALSE], feature_dim = 16L, proj_dim = 8L,     queue_size = 16L, batch_size = 8L, epochs = 5L, seed = 42L)    # READ THIS BEFORE READING ANY NUMBER BELOW. In   # foundation_moco_pretrain(), `epochs` counts optimiser steps and   # not passes over the data: one mini-batch is drawn per epoch. So   # `enc` above is five gradient steps on batches of 8 -- 40 patch   # presentations drawn from 37 patches. Its own diagnostic says   # what that buys: the InfoNCE loss of an encoder whose logits are   # all equal, i.e. one that cannot pick the positive key out of its   # queue_size negatives, is log1p(queue_size). The trace below is   # noise around that line rather than a descent: it is not   # monotone, and which side of the baseline its last value lands on   # is not stable.   print(round(enc$loss_history, 3))   print(round(c(final_infonce    = enc$final_loss,                 all_logits_equal = log1p(enc$queue_size),                 patch_draws      = length(enc$loss_history) *                                      enc$batch_size), 3))   print(c(monotone = all(diff(enc$loss_history) < 0)))   # Do not read the exact figures as a property of `seed = 42L`   # either: that argument fixes only the torch RNG, while the batch   # draw and the augmentations come from R's RNG, so the whole trace   # -- final value included -- moves with the ambient R seed.    # `enc` is therefore, for practical purposes, a random   # convolutional feature map -- and the fine-tune keeps it that   # way, because freeze_backbone defaults to TRUE and only the head   # is trained. Everything below is a demonstration of the ENSEMBLE   # MACHINERY -- the fitting loop, the (K_ens, N) predict contract,   # how to aggregate it, how to score it -- and none of it is   # evidence about soil carbon. A representation worth fine-tuning   # needs patches by the 1e4-1e6 and thousands of steps;   # foundation_moco_pretrain_tiles() is the entry point that   # streams a corpus that size.    # K_ens = 3 and 20 epochs keep this example short; an ensemble you   # would report wants 5-10 members. With K = 3 the member sd below   # has two degrees of freedom.   ens <- foundation_finetune_ensemble(     enc, x = x[train, , , , drop = FALSE], y = y[train],     task = "regression", K_ens = 3L, base_seed = 301L,     head = "mlp", hidden = 8L, dropout = 0.2,     epochs = 20L, batch_size = 16L, lr = 0.01, device = "cpu")   print(ens)    # Member k is fit with seed = base_seed + k - 1, and that seed   # drives the head initialisation, the mini-batch order AND the   # internal val_split holdout -- so no two members train on exactly   # the same patches, and they do not converge to the same loss.   print(round(ens$final_losses, 3))    # predict() returns the raw (K_ens, N) member stack, never a   # summary; aggregating it is the caller's job.   newx  <- x[test, , , , drop = FALSE]   preds <- predict(ens, x = newx)   print(dim(preds))   mu   <- colMeans(preds)   sd_k <- apply(preds, 2L, stats::sd)   print(round(rbind(mean = mu, sd = sd_k)[, 1:4], 2))    # Averaging is not cosmetic, and this part survives the useless   # backbone: in squared error the ensemble mean is at least as good   # as the average member for ANY collection of members, good or   # garbage (the ambiguity decomposition). It is not guaranteed to   # beat the best member, and it still has to beat an achievable   # null -- the training mean.   sq_err <- function(z) mean((y[test] - z)^2)   print(round(c(member         = apply(preds, 1L, sq_err),                 ensemble_mean  = sq_err(mu),                 average_member = mean(apply(preds, 1L, sq_err)),                 train_mean     = sq_err(rep(mean(y[train]),                                             length(test)))), 3))    # Beating that null is no verdict on the pretraining either. With   # the backbone frozen this is random-feature regression, and a   # trained head on random features is already a real (weak)   # predictor. The matched control: same head, same seed 301, on an   # encoder given ONE gradient step instead of five.   enc1 <- foundation_moco_pretrain(     x[train, , , , drop = FALSE], feature_dim = 16L, proj_dim = 8L,     queue_size = 16L, batch_size = 8L, epochs = 1L, seed = 42L)   fit1 <- foundation_fit_regressor(     enc1, x = x[train, , , , drop = FALSE], y = y[train],     head = "mlp", hidden = 8L, dropout = 0.2, epochs = 20L,     batch_size = 16L, lr = 0.01, device = "cpu", seed = 301L)   print(round(c(     member1_enc_5ep   = sq_err(preds[1L, ]),     same_head_enc_1ep = sq_err(as.numeric(predict(fit1, x = newx))),     member_spread     = diff(range(apply(preds, 1L, sq_err)))), 3))   # That contrast would have to come out decisively for the 5-step   # encoder before any accuracy above could be credited to the   # pretraining, and 12 test patches cannot settle it whichever way   # it lands on your machine -- compare the gap between the two   # against member_spread, which is pure head-seed noise.    # The member spread is not a posterior: it covers initialisation   # and optimisation, not the noise in y. Score the band rather than   # trust it -- PICP against the nominal 0.95, read next to the   # interval score, which also charges for width.   lo <- mu - 1.96 * sd_k; up <- mu + 1.96 * sd_k   print(round(c(picp           = edaphos_picp(y[test], lo, up),                 mean_width     = mean(up - lo),                 interval_score = edaphos_interval_score(y[test],                                                          lo, up)), 3))   # With length(test) = 12, PICP moves in steps of 1/12 and carries   # a standard error near 0.1: a smoke test that the plumbing runs,   # not a calibration result for this or any encoder. }

code: if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{   # The loaded object carries the shapes the encoder was trained   # with: 31 standardised channels of 16 x 16 patches for v1.   moco <- foundation_weights_load("edaphos-cerrado-moco-v1")   n_ch <- moco$n_channels    # SYNTHETIC PATCHES, NOT A SOIL SURVEY. The patches below are   # standard normal noise, so the signal has to be planted by hand:   # each soil order gets a different mean level in channel 1. The   # label then genuinely depends on the patch it is paired with and   # the probe has something real to find -- but what it finds is the   # offset planted three lines down, not pedology.   set.seed(1)   soil_order <- factor(rep(c("Oxisol", "Ultisol", "Inceptisol"),                             each = 70L))   patches <- array(rnorm(210 * n_ch * 16 * 16),                    dim = c(210, n_ch, 16, 16))   patches[, 1, , ] <- patches[, 1, , ] +     c(Oxisol = -1.5, Ultisol = 0,       Inceptisol = 1.5)[as.character(soil_order)]    fit <- foundation_fit_classifier(     moco, patches, soil_order,     freeze_backbone = TRUE, head = "linear",     epochs = 40L, device = "mps", seed = 1L   )    # Read the accuracy against what a constant predictor would score,   # which is the majority-class rate -- 1/3 for these balanced   # labels. The planted offset is 1.5 sd wide, so a linear probe   # should land far above it (a local encoder of the same   # architecture separates the three groups completely).   print(c(best_val_acc  = max(fit$val_accuracy_history, na.rm = TRUE),           final_val_acc = utils::tail(fit$val_accuracy_history, 1L),           majority_rate = max(table(soil_order)) / length(soil_order)))    pred <- predict(fit, patches, type = "class")   # in-sample labels   prob <- predict(fit, patches[1:5, , , , drop = FALSE], type = "prob")    # Delete the two lines that add the offset into `patches` -- i.e.   # draw the labels independently of the patches, as an earlier   # version of this example did -- and `final_val_acc` falls back   # onto the majority rate: there is then nothing to learn, and any   # apparent skill is memorisation of 210 noise vectors. Note that   # `best_val_acc` stays visibly above the baseline even in that   # no-signal case; a maximum over 40 noisy epochs is an optimistic   # statistic, so quote the final epoch, not the best one.    # None of this is a soil-order model. That needs patches cut from   # real covariate rasters (foundation_tile_align() ->   # foundation_tile_dataset()), standardised over your own area of   # interest, and soil orders observed at those same locations. } # }

code: if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{   moco <- foundation_weights_load("edaphos-cerrado-moco-v1")   n_ch <- moco$n_channels    # SYNTHETIC PATCHES, NOT A SOIL SURVEY -- as in   # foundation_fit_classifier(), the signal is planted by hand.   # Each patch gets its own offset in channel 1 and `soc` is a   # linear function of that offset plus noise, so the target really   # does depend on the patch it is paired with.   set.seed(2)   level   <- rnorm(300)   patches <- array(rnorm(300 * n_ch * 16 * 16),                    dim = c(300, n_ch, 16, 16))   patches[, 1, , ] <- patches[, 1, , ] + level   soc <- 15 + 6 * level + rnorm(300, sd = 2)   # stands in for g/kg    fit <- foundation_fit_regressor(     moco, patches, soc,     freeze_backbone = TRUE, head = "linear",     epochs = 40L, device = "mps", seed = 1L   )    # An RMSE means nothing on its own: compare it with the RMSE of   # predicting mean(soc) for every patch, which is sd(soc). A local   # encoder of the same architecture cuts it to about two fifths of   # that -- and that ratio is a property of the planted signal, not   # evidence that the encoder knows anything about carbon.   print(c(best_val_rmse       = min(fit$val_rmse_history, na.rm = TRUE),           intercept_only_rmse = stats::sd(soc)))    pred <- predict(fit, patches)   print(c(cor_pred_soc = stats::cor(pred, soc)))   print(round(utils::head(pred, 10), 2))    # Delete the line that adds `level` into `patches` -- i.e. make   # `soc` independent of the input, as an earlier version of this   # example did -- and the only attainable model is the intercept:   # `cor_pred_soc` goes to ~0, the ten printed predictions bunch up   # near mean(soc) instead of tracking it, and the held-out RMSE   # stops beating sd(soc) (it lands slightly worse, since the head   # still fits the training noise). Printing predictions from that   # fit, as the earlier example did, shows an intercept dressed up   # as a soil map.    # Nothing here maps SOC. That needs patches cut from real   # covariate rasters (foundation_tile_align() ->   # foundation_tile_dataset()), standardised over your own area of   # interest, and measured SOC at those same locations. } # }

title: MC-dropout predictive draws from a fine-tuned Pillar 4 fit — foundation_mcdropout_predict
code: if (requireNamespace("torch", quietly = TRUE) &&     isTRUE(torch::torch_is_installed())) {   # Same 8 x 8 br_cerrado patches as foundation_finetune_ensemble().   g <- 45L; p <- 8L   cov4 <- lapply(br_cerrado[c("elev", "slope", "twi", "ndvi")],                  function(v) matrix(scale(v)[, 1L], g, g))   soc_m <- matrix(br_cerrado$soc, g, g)   ij <- expand.grid(i = seq(1L, g - p + 1L, by = 6L),                     j = seq(1L, g - p + 1L, by = 6L))   x <- array(0, dim = c(nrow(ij), 4L, p, p))   y <- numeric(nrow(ij))   for (k in seq_len(nrow(ij))) {     rr <- ij$i[k] + 0:(p - 1L); cc <- ij$j[k] + 0:(p - 1L)     for (ch in 1:4) x[k, ch, , ] <- cov4[[ch]][rr, cc]     y[k] <- mean(soc_m[rr, cc])   }   set.seed(2024)   test  <- sample(nrow(ij), 12L)   train <- setdiff(seq_len(nrow(ij)), test)   enc <- foundation_moco_pretrain(     x[train, , , , drop = FALSE], feature_dim = 16L, proj_dim = 8L,     queue_size = 16L, batch_size = 8L, epochs = 5L, seed = 42L)    # Same warning as in foundation_finetune_ensemble(). `epochs`   # counts optimiser steps, not passes over the data, so `enc` is   # five gradient steps on batches of 8. Read its final InfoNCE loss   # against log1p(queue_size), the loss of an encoder whose logits   # are all equal -- one that cannot pick the positive key out of   # its queue_size negatives. The trace is noise around that line   # rather than a descent, and it moves with the ambient R seed:   # `seed=` fixes only the torch RNG.   print(round(enc$loss_history, 3))   print(round(c(final_infonce    = enc$final_loss,                 all_logits_equal = log1p(enc$queue_size),                 patch_draws      = length(enc$loss_history) *                                      enc$batch_size), 3))    # freeze_backbone defaults to TRUE, so the head below is fit on   # that frozen, effectively random feature map. Read the rest as a   # demonstration of the MC-DROPOUT MACHINERY -- what `seed`   # controls, how the draws differ from predict(), and when the   # "posterior" is secretly a point mass -- not as an uncertainty   # statement about soil carbon.    # MC-dropout can only sample if the head carries a stochastic   # layer: head = "mlp" with dropout > 0. See the trap below.   fit <- foundation_fit_regressor(     enc, x = x[train, , , , drop = FALSE], y = y[train],     head = "mlp", hidden = 8L, dropout = 0.2,     epochs = 20L, batch_size = 16L, lr = 0.01,     device = "cpu", seed = 301L)    # n_draws = 20 is small for speed; a draw sd you report wants 100+.   newx  <- x[test, , , , drop = FALSE]   draws <- foundation_mcdropout_predict(fit, x = newx, n_draws = 20L,                                         seed = 7L)   print(dim(draws))    # The dropout masks are resampled on every call, so `seed` is what   # makes a reported posterior reproducible.   print(c(seeded_same = isTRUE(all.equal(             draws, foundation_mcdropout_predict(fit, x = newx,                                                 n_draws = 20L,                                                 seed = 7L))),           unseeded_differs = !isTRUE(all.equal(             draws, foundation_mcdropout_predict(fit, x = newx,                                                 n_draws = 20L)))))    # The MC mean is not predict(): predict() switches dropout off and   # runs the whole head, while the draws average thinned copies.   point <- as.numeric(predict(fit, x = newx))   print(round(c(predict_1    = point[1L],                 mc_mean_1    = colMeans(draws)[1L],                 mean_abs_gap = mean(abs(point - colMeans(draws)))), 3))    # TRAP: with no dropout layer the "posterior" silently collapses   # to a point. A linear head -- and equally head = "mlp" with   # dropout = 0 -- still returns n_draws rows, but they are   # identical and their sd is exactly 0.   fit_lin <- foundation_fit_regressor(     enc, x = x[train, , , , drop = FALSE], y = y[train],     head = "linear", epochs = 20L, batch_size = 16L, lr = 0.01,     device = "cpu", seed = 301L)   print(max(apply(foundation_mcdropout_predict(fit_lin, x = newx,                                                n_draws = 5L, seed = 7L),                   2L, stats::sd)))    # What the spread does not contain: it is the variation of ONE   # network's units, conditional on the single optimisation run that   # produced `fit`. Refit under another seed and it moves. That   # second source of variance is what foundation_finetune_ensemble()   # covers instead -- the two are not estimates of the same thing.   # This point does not depend on the backbone being any good: it is   # a statement about which sources of variation each estimator   # integrates over, and it would hold identically for an encoder   # pretrained on a million patches.   fit2 <- foundation_fit_regressor(     enc, x = x[train, , , , drop = FALSE], y = y[train],     head = "mlp", hidden = 8L, dropout = 0.2,     epochs = 20L, batch_size = 16L, lr = 0.01,     device = "cpu", seed = 302L)   draws2 <- foundation_mcdropout_predict(fit2, x = newx,                                          n_draws = 20L, seed = 7L)   print(round(c(     median_sd_seed301 = stats::median(apply(draws,  2L, stats::sd)),     median_sd_seed302 = stats::median(apply(draws2, 2L, stats::sd))), 3))    # And neither route is calibrated by construction: score the band   # before reporting it. Nominal coverage here is 0.95. Print the   # mean half-width next to the RMSE the band would have to span.   # The dropout masks are the only thing that varies across draws,   # so the interval is centred on a point estimate whose own error   # it cannot see. Read the three numbers together: the mean   # half-width (1.53) is WIDER than the RMSE (1.29), and coverage is   # still only 0.58 against a nominal 0.95. A wide interval that   # under-covers is the signature of a centre that is off, not of a   # spread that is too small -- widening it further would not fix   # the problem, because MC-dropout never samples the bias of the   # frozen backbone it sits on. At length(test) = 12, and on a   # backbone this untrained, read the direction and not the digits.   mu <- colMeans(draws); s <- apply(draws, 2L, stats::sd)   print(round(c(     picp = edaphos_picp(y[test], mu - 1.96 * s, mu + 1.96 * s),     mean_half_width = mean(1.96 * s),     rmse            = sqrt(mean((y[test] - point)^2)),     interval_score = edaphos_interval_score(y[test], mu - 1.96 * s,                                             mu + 1.96 * s)), 3)) }

title: Extract backbone embeddings from a fitted MoCo v2 encoder — foundation_moco_embed
code: # The installed-package check is not enough on its own: libtorch / # lantern is a separate binary download, and torch_is_installed() is # what tells you it is actually there. if (requireNamespace("torch", quietly = TRUE) &&     isTRUE(torch::torch_is_installed())) {  # The same 8 x 8 Cerrado patch corpus used by # foundation_moco_pretrain(). g <- 45L cube <- vapply(c("elev", "slope", "twi", "map_mm", "ndvi"),                function(v) {                  m <- matrix(br_cerrado[[v]], g, g)                  (m - mean(m)) / stats::sd(m)                }, matrix(0, g, g)) set.seed(42) top  <- sample(g - 7L, 24L, replace = TRUE) left <- sample(g - 7L, 24L, replace = TRUE) patches <- array(0, dim = c(24L, 5L, 8L, 8L)) for (i in 1:24) {   patches[i, , , ] <- aperm(cube[top[i]:(top[i] + 7L),                                  left[i]:(left[i] + 7L), ], c(3, 1, 2)) } set.seed(1) fit <- foundation_moco_pretrain(patches, feature_dim = 16L,                                 proj_dim = 8L, batch_size = 8L,                                 epochs = 8L, seed = 1L)  # Default: the reusable backbone representation, feature_dim wide. emb <- foundation_moco_embed(fit, patches) print(dim(emb))  # The two outputs live in different spaces and must never be mixed # in one distance calculation. Backbone features leave a ReLU, so # they are non-negative and of arbitrary length; the projection head # L2-normalises, so its rows sit on the unit sphere and may be # negative. Regress on the backbone, do cosine geometry on the # projection. z <- foundation_moco_embed(fit, patches, projection = TRUE) print(c(backbone_cols = ncol(emb), proj_cols = ncol(z),         backbone_min = min(emb), proj_min = min(z))) print(range(round(sqrt(rowSums(z^2)), 6)))  # The encoder is switched to eval() inside, so BatchNorm uses its # stored running statistics rather than the statistics of whatever # you happened to pass. That is what makes an embedding a property # of the patch instead of a property of the batch: encoding three # patches alone reproduces the corresponding rows of the full run # (to float32 precision), and a repeated call is bit-identical. chunk <- foundation_moco_embed(fit, patches[1:3, , , , drop = FALSE]) print(c(chunked  = isTRUE(all.equal(chunk, emb[1:3, , drop = FALSE],                                     tolerance = 1e-4)),         repeated = identical(foundation_moco_embed(fit, patches),                              emb)))  # Only the query encoder is read here. `fit$encoder_k` is the # momentum copy that built the dictionary during training and is # never consulted by this function. }

title: Apply a fitted MoCo v2 encoder over a full raster mosaic — foundation_moco_embed_raster
code: # Guard on the libtorch binaries as well as on the R package -- # requireNamespace() alone is TRUE on machines that cannot run a # single tensor operation. if (requireNamespace("torch", quietly = TRUE) &&     isTRUE(torch::torch_is_installed()) &&     requireNamespace("terra", quietly = TRUE)) {  covs <- terra::rast(br_cerrado[, c("x", "y", "elev", "slope", "twi",                                    "map_mm", "ndvi")], type = "xyz") ds <- foundation_tile_dataset(covs, patch_size = 8L, n_patches = 64L,                               seed = 7L) set.seed(11) moco <- foundation_moco_pretrain_tiles(ds, feature_dim = 8L,                                        proj_dim = 4L, queue_size = 32L,                                        batch_size = 8L, epochs = 6L,                                        seed = 11L)  # One output layer per backbone feature, on a grid coarsened by # `stride`. Pass the same `dataset` you trained on: its per-channel # means and sds are the normalisation, and a different dataset would # feed the encoder a differently-scaled raster. emb <- foundation_moco_embed_raster(moco, covs, ds, stride = 8L) print(c(layers = terra::nlyr(emb), feature_dim = moco$feature_dim)) print(terra::res(emb) / terra::res(covs))  # TRAP: the output is not co-registered with the input. The grid is # anchored at the input's top-left corner and is ncol(emb) * stride # input columns wide, so with 45 columns and stride 8 the last five # columns -- and the last five rows -- of `covs` are not covered. print(terra::ncol(covs) - 8L * terra::ncol(emb)) print(rbind(covs = as.vector(terra::ext(covs)),             emb  = as.vector(terra::ext(emb))))  # It overshoots just as happily in the other direction: stride 24 # gives two columns of 24 cells, i.e. 48 > 45, and the embedding # raster sticks out past the input. Always crop or resample to a # reference grid before overlaying anything on it. emb24 <- foundation_moco_embed_raster(moco, covs, ds, stride = 24L) print(c(covered = 24L * terra::ncol(emb24),         input = terra::ncol(covs),         overshoots = terra::xmax(emb24) > terra::xmax(covs)))  # TRAP: missing data is imputed, not propagated. NA cells are set to # the channel mean before encoding, so a patch that is entirely # no-data -- all five channels blank, below -- still gets a finite # embedding. The output cannot be used to find gaps: carry a separate # mask. blank <- terra::cellFromRowCol(covs, rep(1:8, each = 8), rep(1:8, 8)) gap <- terra::deepcopy(covs) for (k in 1:5) gap[[k]][blank] <- NA emb_gap <- foundation_moco_embed_raster(moco, gap, ds, stride = 24L) print(colSums(is.na(terra::values(gap)))) print(c(na_in_output = sum(is.na(terra::values(emb_gap)))))  # Rows 1:8 / columns 1:8 are exactly the window of the first stride-24 # patch, so row 1 of the gapped output is the all-NA patch. Finite it # is; "close to an average patch" it is not, and nothing in the # encoder pulls it there. The line below prints its distance to the # mean of the four real embeddings, then how far the real patches # themselves sit from that same mean, on average and at worst. The # blank patch comes out FARTHER from the average than the average # real patch is -- the opposite of reassuring. Read the printed # values, do not quote a number from this comment: they move with the # fit, and this one is 6 optimiser steps on 64 patches. Nor is the # gap recoverable this way in general; the load-bearing number is the # NA count above -- zero NA reaches the output, so carry a mask. real <- terra::values(emb24) ctr  <- colMeans(real) print(round(c(blank_to_mean = sqrt(sum((terra::values(emb_gap)[1, ] -                                           ctr)^2)),               real_to_mean_mean = mean(sqrt(rowSums(sweep(real, 2,                                                           ctr)^2))),               real_to_mean_max  = max(sqrt(rowSums(sweep(real, 2,                                                          ctr)^2)))), 3))  # `projection = TRUE` swaps in the L2-normalised head, so each cell # of the output has unit length across layers: a ready-made cosine # similarity space, and a useless magnitude map. embp <- foundation_moco_embed_raster(moco, covs, ds, stride = 24L,                                      projection = TRUE) print(c(layers = terra::nlyr(embp), proj_dim = moco$proj_dim)) print(range(round(sqrt(rowSums(terra::values(embp)^2)), 6))) }

title: Pillar 4 – MoCo v2 pre-training on raster covariate patches — foundation_moco_pretrain
code: # `requireNamespace("torch")` is TRUE as soon as the R package is # installed, but the libtorch/lantern shared libraries are a separate # separate binary download that CI and CRAN machines routinely lack # (about 0.45 GB installed here). Both halves # of the guard are needed. if (requireNamespace("torch", quietly = TRUE) &&     isTRUE(torch::torch_is_installed())) {  # MoCo v2 consumes (N, C, H, W). `br_cerrado` is a complete 45 x 45 # grid, so every covariate reshapes into a surface and the 8 x 8 # windows cut out of it are genuine soil-landscape patches. # Standardise the surfaces first: the augmentation stack adds noise # of a fixed sd and jitters brightness multiplicatively, so map_mm # (millimetres) and ndvi (a unitless index) would otherwise be # perturbed by wildly different relative amounts. g <- 45L cube <- vapply(c("elev", "slope", "twi", "map_mm", "ndvi"),                function(v) {                  m <- matrix(br_cerrado[[v]], g, g)                  (m - mean(m)) / stats::sd(m)                }, matrix(0, g, g)) set.seed(42) top  <- sample(g - 7L, 24L, replace = TRUE) left <- sample(g - 7L, 24L, replace = TRUE) patches <- array(0, dim = c(24L, 5L, 8L, 8L)) for (i in 1:24) {   patches[i, , , ] <- aperm(cube[top[i]:(top[i] + 7L),                                  left[i]:(left[i] + 7L), ], c(3, 1, 2)) }  set.seed(1) fit <- foundation_moco_pretrain(patches, feature_dim = 16L,                                 proj_dim = 8L, queue_size = 1024L,                                 batch_size = 8L, epochs = 8L,                                 seed = 1L) print(fit)  # `queue_size` is a request, not a setting: it is silently clamped # to N - batch_size, so the 1024-key dictionary asked for above is # 16 keys wide over 24 patches. Always read it back off the object. print(c(requested = 1024, actual = fit$queue_size))  # Worse, the loss at step t is computed against the queue as it stood # at the END of step t - 1, and the FIFO first drops the oldest # batch_size rows, then appends the current keys. Halve the corpus and # the clamp leaves queue_size equal to batch_size, so the drop empties # the queue and the append refills it: the dictionary in force at step # t is exactly the keys of step t - 1. Every negative is then a key of # the PREVIOUS mini-batch under the previous momentum encoder, none # come from the current one (the current batch supplies only the # positive), and no key older than a single step ever survives -- # which is MoCo's whole advantage over SimCLR. `retained` is how many # pre-existing keys outlive a step; keep N well above 2 * batch_size # to make it positive. tiny <- foundation_moco_pretrain(patches[1:16, , , , drop = FALSE],                                  feature_dim = 8L, proj_dim = 4L,                                  batch_size = 8L, epochs = 2L,                                  seed = 1L) print(c(queue = tiny$queue_size, batch = tiny$batch_size,         retained = tiny$queue_size - tiny$batch_size))  # `epochs` counts optimiser steps, not passes over `patches`: one # mini-batch is drawn per epoch, so a short trace reports which # patches were sampled at least as much as it reports learning. # Read its tail next to log1p(queue_size) -- the InfoNCE value of a # model whose logits are all equal -- before concluding anything. print(round(fit$loss_history, 3)) print(c(final = fit$final_loss,         all_logits_equal = log1p(fit$queue_size)))  # Reproducibility needs BOTH generators. `seed=` only sets the torch # RNG (weight init, additive sensor noise); the mini-batch draw and # the crop / flip / rotation / channel-drop / cutout / brightness # augmentations are all drawn from R's RNG. The same `seed=` under a # different R seed is a different run. set.seed(99) a <- foundation_moco_pretrain(patches, feature_dim = 8L, proj_dim = 4L,                               batch_size = 8L, epochs = 3L, seed = 1L) set.seed(123) b <- foundation_moco_pretrain(patches, feature_dim = 8L, proj_dim = 4L,                               batch_size = 8L, epochs = 3L, seed = 1L) set.seed(99) d <- foundation_moco_pretrain(patches, feature_dim = 8L, proj_dim = 4L,                               batch_size = 8L, epochs = 3L, seed = 1L) print(c(other_R_seed = identical(a$loss_history, b$loss_history),         same_R_seed  = identical(a$loss_history, d$loss_history))) }

code: # torch_is_installed() is the half of the guard that matters on a # fresh machine: the R package installs in seconds, the libtorch / # lantern binaries behind it are a separate download. if (requireNamespace("torch", quietly = TRUE) &&     isTRUE(torch::torch_is_installed()) &&     requireNamespace("terra", quietly = TRUE)) {  # A tile dataset streams patches out of a raster instead of holding # an (N, C, H, W) array in RAM. The mosaic here is small enough to # build in memory from `br_cerrado`, but the call sequence is the # one you use for a SoilGrids + WorldClim + SRTM stack that is not. covs <- terra::rast(br_cerrado[, c("x", "y", "elev", "slope", "twi",                                    "map_mm", "ndvi")], type = "xyz") ds <- foundation_tile_dataset(covs, patch_size = 8L, n_patches = 64L,                               seed = 7L)  set.seed(11) mt <- foundation_moco_pretrain_tiles(ds, feature_dim = 16L,                                      proj_dim = 8L, queue_size = 32L,                                      batch_size = 8L, epochs = 6L,                                      seed = 11L, device = "cpu") print(mt)  # Unlike foundation_moco_pretrain(), `queue_size` is honoured here # rather than clamped to the corpus size. The FIFO still only # retains queue_size - batch_size old keys per step, so this is the # knob that decides how much of a dictionary you actually have. print(c(queue = mt$queue_size, batch = mt$batch_size,         retained = mt$queue_size - mt$batch_size))  # The queue is warmed by drawing min(queue_size, 4 * batch_size) # patches in a single call, and foundation_tile_dataset() refuses a # draw larger than `n_patches`. So the dataset must satisfy # n_patches >= min(queue_size, 4 * batch_size); below, min(256, 32) # is 32 and the dataset only holds 20. small <- foundation_tile_dataset(covs, patch_size = 8L,                                  n_patches = 20L, seed = 3L) try(foundation_moco_pretrain_tiles(small, feature_dim = 8L,                                    proj_dim = 4L, queue_size = 256L,                                    batch_size = 8L, epochs = 2L,                                    seed = 3L))  # `device` is resolved, not obeyed: an unavailable backend prints a # note and the run silently continues on CPU. Read the resolved # value back rather than trusting the argument you passed -- a # "GPU run" that took CPU wall-clock is usually this. set.seed(11) gpu <- foundation_moco_pretrain_tiles(ds, feature_dim = 8L,                                       proj_dim = 4L, queue_size = 32L,                                       batch_size = 8L, epochs = 2L,                                       seed = 11L, device = "cuda") print(identical(gpu$device,                 if (torch::cuda_is_available()) "cuda" else "cpu"))  # Checkpointing is what makes a multi-day run restartable. Four # epochs at checkpoint_every = 2 leave both encoders, the dictionary # queue and the loss history on disk; `resume=` restores them and # carries on at the stored next_epoch, so run2 holds run1's four # losses verbatim plus the two new ones. ck <- file.path(tempdir(), "moco_ck") set.seed(21) run1 <- foundation_moco_pretrain_tiles(ds, feature_dim = 8L,                                        proj_dim = 4L, queue_size = 32L,                                        batch_size = 8L, epochs = 4L,                                        seed = 21L, checkpoint_dir = ck,                                        checkpoint_every = 2L) print(list.files(ck)) set.seed(22) run2 <- foundation_moco_pretrain_tiles(ds, feature_dim = 8L,                                        proj_dim = 4L, queue_size = 32L,                                        batch_size = 8L, epochs = 6L,                                        seed = 22L, resume = ck) print(length(run2$loss_history)) print(identical(run2$loss_history[1:4], run1$loss_history)) unlink(ck, recursive = TRUE) }  if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{ # The real target: a multi-source mosaic that does not fit in RAM. # Every source below downloads, so this block is never run by # examples -- but it is the working pipeline. aoi  <- c(-48.5, -47.0, -16.5, -15.0)   # xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax srtm <- foundation_tile_source_srtm(aoi, derive = c("slope", "TPI"),                                     country = "BRA") clim <- foundation_tile_source_worldclim(c("prec", "tavg"),                                          country = "BRA", aoi = aoi) soil <- foundation_tile_source_soilgrids(c("soc", "clay"),                                          depth = "0-5cm", aoi = aoi) mosaic <- foundation_tile_align(   list(srtm = srtm, clim = clim, soil = soil),   target_res = 0.005, aoi = aoi) ds_big <- foundation_tile_dataset(mosaic, patch_size = 32L,                                   n_patches = 20000L, seed = 1L) moco <- foundation_moco_pretrain_tiles(   ds_big, queue_size = 4096L, batch_size = 64L, epochs = 20000L,   device = "mps", checkpoint_dir = "moco_ck", checkpoint_every = 500L,   verbose = TRUE) } # }

title: Extract embeddings from a pretrained SimCLR encoder — foundation_simclr_embed
code: if (requireNamespace("torch", quietly = TRUE) &&     isTRUE(torch::torch_is_installed())) {   data(br_cerrado)    # Twelve 8 x 8 tiles, three standardised covariate channels.   grids <- lapply(c("elev", "twi", "ndvi"), function(v) {     m <- matrix(br_cerrado[[v]], nrow = 45, ncol = 45)     (m - mean(m)) / sd(m)   })   patches <- array(0, dim = c(12L, 3L, 8L, 8L))   k <- 0L   for (r0 in c(0L, 8L, 16L)) for (c0 in c(0L, 8L, 16L, 24L)) {     k <- k + 1L     for (j in seq_along(grids)) {       patches[k, j, , ] <- grids[[j]][r0 + 1:8, c0 + 1:8]     }   }    # Warm torch up first, else `seed` misses the lazily-loaded   # backend (see `foundation_simclr_pretrain()`).   invisible(torch::torch_manual_seed(11L))   set.seed(1)   fit <- foundation_simclr_pretrain(patches, epochs = 30L,                                     batch_size = 6L, seed = 11L)    # The default is the backbone feature, `feature_dim` wide. The   # projection head, `proj_dim` wide, exists only to shape the   # contrastive loss; Chen et al. (2020) throw it away and reuse   # the feature, which is why `projection = FALSE` is the default.   feat <- foundation_simclr_embed(fit, patches)   proj <- foundation_simclr_embed(fit, patches, projection = TRUE)   print(c(feature = ncol(feat), projection = ncol(proj)))    # They differ in geometry, not merely in width. Projection rows   # are unit-norm by construction. Backbone features are pooled   # ReLU activations: never negative, and with row norms spread   # over nearly an order of magnitude -- scale them before handing   # them to a distance-based or penalised downstream model.   print(round(c(feat_min  = min(feat),                 feat_norm = range(sqrt(rowSums(feat^2))),                 proj_norm = range(sqrt(rowSums(proj^2)))), 4))    # Embedding applies no augmentation, so it is deterministic.   print(identical(feat, foundation_simclr_embed(fit, patches)))    # Adaptive average pooling makes the encoder size-agnostic: a   # 16 x 16 patch still yields `feature_dim` columns. The channel   # count and order, though, must match pre-training exactly.   print(dim(foundation_simclr_embed(     fit, array(0, dim = c(2L, 3L, 16L, 16L)))))    # How much has it actually learned? Compare two retrieval probes   # against a barely-trained encoder.   set.seed(1)   raw <- foundation_simclr_pretrain(patches, epochs = 1L,                                     batch_size = 6L, seed = 11L)   unit <- function(m) m / sqrt(rowSums(m^2))   top1 <- function(f, query) {     s <- tcrossprod(unit(foundation_simclr_embed(f, query)),                     unit(foundation_simclr_embed(f, patches)))     mean(apply(s, 1, which.max) == seq_len(nrow(s)))   }   set.seed(2)   noisy <- patches + array(rnorm(length(patches), sd = 0.25),                            dim(patches))    # `noise` retrieves each patch from a noisy copy; `flip` from a   # vertically flipped one, the invariance the augmentation asks   # the encoder to acquire.   print(rbind(     untrained = c(noise = top1(raw, noisy),                   flip  = top1(raw, patches[, , 8:1, ])),     trained   = c(noise = top1(fit, noisy),                   flip  = top1(fit, patches[, , 8:1, ])),     chance    = c(1 / 12, 1 / 12)))    # The noise probe is saturated before training starts, so it   # cannot tell the two encoders apart; only the flip probe moves.   # Treat even that as an interface check: an encoder pre-trained   # on twelve tiles for thirty epochs has memorised twelve tiles,   # not learned a transferable covariate representation. }

title: SimCLR pre-training on raster covariate patches (Pillar 4 scaffold) — foundation_simclr_pretrain
code: if (requireNamespace("torch", quietly = TRUE) &&     isTRUE(torch::torch_is_installed())) {   data(br_cerrado)    # `noise_sd` is additive in the units of `patches`, so standardise   # every channel first. The default noise is a fixed 0.1 while the   # raw covariates are on wildly different scales; take the ratio of   # the two and the augmentation turns out to be about a thousandth   # of elevation's spread, yet 1.19 times the whole spread of NDVI.   chan <- c("elev", "twi", "ndvi")   nsd  <- formals(foundation_simclr_pretrain)$noise_sd   sds  <- sapply(br_cerrado[chan], sd)   print(round(c(noise_sd = nsd, sds), 3))   # noise_sd     elev      twi     ndvi   #    0.100  109.380    2.862    0.084   print(round(nsd / sds, 4))   #   elev    twi   ndvi   # 0.0009 0.0349 1.1871    # br_cerrado is a complete 45 x 45 grid with x cycling fastest, so   # each covariate reshapes straight into an image.   grids <- lapply(chan, function(v) {     m <- matrix(br_cerrado[[v]], nrow = 45, ncol = 45)     (m - mean(m)) / sd(m)   })    # `patches` must be 4-D, (N, C, H, W): twelve 8 x 8 tiles here. A   # 3-D (N, H, W) array is rejected even for a single covariate --   # the channel axis is never inferred for you.   patches <- array(0, dim = c(12L, 3L, 8L, 8L))   k <- 0L   for (r0 in c(0L, 8L, 16L)) for (c0 in c(0L, 8L, 16L, 24L)) {     k <- k + 1L     for (j in seq_along(grids)) {       patches[k, j, , ] <- grids[[j]][r0 + 1:8, c0 + 1:8]     }   }   print(dim(patches))    # The first torch call of a session is what loads the libtorch   # backend, and a `seed` handed to that same call does not stick.   # Touch torch once before you rely on `seed`.   invisible(torch::torch_manual_seed(11L))    set.seed(1)   fit <- foundation_simclr_pretrain(patches, epochs = 40L,                                     batch_size = 6L, seed = 11L)   print(fit)    # One mini-batch per epoch, so `loss_history` is a noisy trace and   # `final_loss` is its last draw rather than its best. Read both   # against the NT-Xent chance level log(2 * batch_size - 1) -- the   # loss of an encoder that cannot pick the matching view at all.   print(round(c(first  = fit$loss_history[1],                 min    = min(fit$loss_history),                 final  = fit$final_loss,                 chance = log(2 * fit$batch_size - 1)), 3))    # `batch_size` is silently clamped to the number of patches, and   # the chance level moves with it: losses obtained under different   # batch sizes are not comparable numbers.   set.seed(2)   wide <- foundation_simclr_pretrain(patches, epochs = 10L,                                      batch_size = 64L, seed = 11L)   print(c(requested = 64, used = wide$batch_size,           chance = round(log(2 * wide$batch_size - 1), 3)))    # Reproducibility needs BOTH seeds: `seed` reaches only torch   # (weight init, Gaussian noise), while the mini-batch draw, the   # flips and the channel dropout come from R's own RNG.   set.seed(1)   a <- foundation_simclr_pretrain(patches, epochs = 3L,                                   batch_size = 6L, seed = 11L)   set.seed(1)   b <- foundation_simclr_pretrain(patches, epochs = 3L,                                   batch_size = 6L, seed = 11L)   print(identical(a$loss_history, b$loss_history))    # Drop the set.seed() and the run drifts, `seed` notwithstanding.   c1 <- foundation_simclr_pretrain(patches, epochs = 3L,                                    batch_size = 6L, seed = 11L)   c2 <- foundation_simclr_pretrain(patches, epochs = 3L,                                    batch_size = 6L, seed = 11L)   print(identical(c1$loss_history, c2$loss_history)) }

title: Align multiple raster sources onto a common analysis grid — foundation_tile_align
code: if (requireNamespace("terra", quietly = TRUE)) {   # Two Cerrado covariates on deliberately mismatched grids: soil at   # 0.05 degrees, terrain at 0.10, on extents that only partly   # overlap.   set.seed(1)   soc <- terra::rast(nrows = 40, ncols = 40,                      xmin = -50, xmax = -48, ymin = -16, ymax = -14,                      crs = "EPSG:4326")   terra::values(soc) <- stats::rnorm(terra::ncell(soc), 22, 4)   names(soc) <- "soc"    elev <- terra::rast(nrows = 20, ncols = 20,                       xmin = -49.5, xmax = -47.5,                       ymin = -15.5, ymax = -13.5, crs = "EPSG:4326")   terra::values(elev) <- stats::rnorm(terra::ncell(elev), 900, 80)   names(elev) <- "elev"    fused <- foundation_tile_align(list(soil = soc, topo = elev),                                    target_res = 0.05)   print(terra::res(fused))    # both sources now on the 0.05 grid   print(names(fused))         # names come from the rasters, not from                               # the names of `sources`    # The template is the UNION of the source extents, not their   # intersection, so each layer is NA wherever its own source did not   # reach -- 36 percent of the grid here, for both layers.   print(terra::global(fused, "isNA") / terra::ncell(fused))    # `aoi` cuts the template back to ground both sources cover, and   # that is what removes the NA frame.   inner <- foundation_tile_align(list(soil = soc, topo = elev),                                    target_res = 0.05,                                    aoi = c(-49.5, -48, -15.5, -14))   print(terra::global(inner, "isNA"))    # Mixed CRS is handled, but the union is taken AFTER reprojection.   # A UTM 23S tile several degrees east of the soil tile produces a   # mosaic that is 73 and 98 percent NA -- and a contrastive encoder   # will train on it perfectly happily.   utm <- terra::rast(nrows = 30, ncols = 30,                      xmin = 700000, xmax = 760000,                      ymin = 8250000, ymax = 8310000,                      crs = "EPSG:31983")   terra::values(utm) <- stats::rnorm(terra::ncell(utm), 14, 3)   names(utm) <- "clay"   far <- foundation_tile_align(list(soil = soc, clay = utm),                                  target_res = 0.05)   print(dim(far))   print(round(terra::global(far, "isNA") / terra::ncell(far), 2))    # `target_res` is in the units of `target_crs`. The 0.005 default is   # degrees; carrying it over to a metre-based CRS asks for 5 mm   # cells. Give metres -- and read the realised resolution off the   # result, because terra fits a whole number of cells into the   # extent instead of honouring `target_res` exactly.   polyconic <- foundation_tile_align(list(soil = soc),                                        target_res = 5000,                                        target_crs = "EPSG:5880")   print(terra::res(polyconic))   # near 5000 m, not exactly 5000    # Two sources that each carry a layer called "soc" give a stack with   # two layers called "soc", and [["soc"]] then returns both of them   # with only a warning. Rename before aligning, not after.   dup <- foundation_tile_align(list(a = soc, b = soc), target_res = 0.05)   print(names(dup))                  # "soc" "soc"   print(terra::nlyr(dup[["soc"]]))   # 2, after a warning that reads                                      # "[subset] using a name that is                                      # not unique"    # method = "bilinear" is for continuous covariates. Use "near" for   # anything categorical -- interpolating soil-class codes invents   # classes that do not exist. } #> [1] 0.05 0.05 #> [1] "soc"  "elev" #>      isNA #> soc  0.36 #> elev 0.36 #>      isNA #> soc     0 #> elev    0 #> [1]  40 149   2 #>      isNA #> soc  0.73 #> clay 0.98 #> [1] 4968.697 4990.300 #> [1] "soc" "soc" #> Warning: [subset] using a name that is not unique #> [1] 2

title: Build a lazy patch dataset over a terra::SpatRaster — foundation_tile_dataset
code: if (requireNamespace("terra", quietly = TRUE)) {   data(br_cerrado, package = "edaphos")   # br_cerrado is a complete 45 x 45 grid, so it converts straight to   # a SpatRaster; x and y have to be the first two columns.   cerr <- terra::rast(br_cerrado[, c("x", "y", "soc", "elev", "twi")],                       type = "xyz", crs = "EPSG:4326")    ds <- foundation_tile_dataset(cerr, patch_size = 8L,                                   n_patches = 200L, seed = 1L)   print(ds)   # (B, C, H, W) -- channel-first, the layout torch conv layers want.   print(dim(ds$sample(batch_size = 4L)))    # Normalisation uses GLOBAL raster statistics computed once at   # construction, never per-batch ones. They are the column statistics   # of the source table -- to floating-point tolerance, not bit for   # bit, because terra accumulates in a different order:   print(c(ds$means[1], mean(br_cerrado$soc)))   print(c(ds$sds[1], stats::sd(br_cerrado$soc)))   print(isTRUE(all.equal(ds$means[1], mean(br_cerrado$soc))))    # TRUE   print(identical(ds$means[1], mean(br_cerrado$soc)))            # FALSE    # `seed` fixes WHICH patches the dataset owns, not which ones a   # call draws. Two datasets built with the same seed agree on   # patch_cells and still disagree on their batches, so seed the RNG   # immediately before sample() when you need a reproducible batch.   d2 <- foundation_tile_dataset(cerr, patch_size = 8L,                                   n_patches = 200L, seed = 1L)   print(identical(ds$patch_cells, d2$patch_cells))   # TRUE   print(identical(ds$sample(4L), d2$sample(4L)))     # FALSE   set.seed(99); b1 <- ds$sample(4L)   set.seed(99); b2 <- d2$sample(4L)   print(identical(b1, b2))                           # TRUE    # normalise = FALSE returns raw units, which is what you want when   # inspecting a patch and not what you want in a contrastive loss:   # elevation in metres would swamp TWI.   raw <- foundation_tile_dataset(cerr, patch_size = 8L,                                    n_patches = 200L, normalise = FALSE,                                    seed = 1L)   set.seed(7); print(round(apply(raw$sample(8L), 2, mean), 2))   set.seed(7); print(round(apply(ds$sample(8L),  2, mean), 2))    # Patch CENTRES must sit at least patch_size %/% 2 cells from every   # edge, so a large patch on a small grid leaves very few of them.   # On 45 x 45 with patch_size = 40 only rows and columns 21 to 25   # qualify -- 25 centres -- and n_patches = 200 is then drawn WITH   # replacement. The dataset reports 200 patches and owns 25 windows.   crowded <- foundation_tile_dataset(cerr, patch_size = 40L,                                        n_patches = 200L, seed = 1L)   print(crowded$n_patches)                          # 200 reported   print(length(unique(crowded$patch_cells)))        # 25 distinct   print(apply(terra::rowColFromCell(cerr,                                     unique(crowded$patch_cells)),               2, range))                            # rows/cols 21..25    # Ask for a patch the grid cannot hold at all and it is an error,   # not a silent shrink.   try(foundation_tile_dataset(cerr, patch_size = 46L, n_patches = 10L))    # A valid_mask restricts eligible centres -- here to the cells above   # mean TWI, which is a bit over half the grid, not exactly half. It   # is resampled onto the stack with method "near", so a coarser mask   # is allowed.   wet <- cerr[["twi"]] > terra::global(cerr[["twi"]], "mean")[1, 1]   print(mean(terra::values(wet)[, 1]))   # fraction of cells kept   dw <- foundation_tile_dataset(cerr, patch_size = 8L, n_patches = 100L,                                   valid_mask = wet, seed = 1L)   print(all(terra::values(wet)[dw$patch_cells, 1] > 0))    # Only the FIRST layer decides eligibility. A gap in any other   # channel is invisible to the sampler; those cells are imputed to   # the channel mean instead, which after normalisation is an exact   # zero. Put the layer with the honest coverage first.   gappy <- cerr   v <- terra::values(gappy[[2]]); v[1:900] <- NA   # the top 20 rows   terra::values(gappy[[2]]) <- v   dg <- foundation_tile_dataset(gappy, patch_size = 8L,                                   n_patches = 200L, seed = 1L)   print(identical(dg$patch_cells, ds$patch_cells))   # TRUE   # Numerator and denominator, plus the gap-free control that shows   # the zeros are imputation and not coincidence:   set.seed(5); print(sum(dg$sample(16L)[, 2, , ] == 0))   # hundreds   print(16L * 8L * 8L)                                    # of 1024   set.seed(5); print(sum(ds$sample(16L)[, 2, , ] == 0))   # 0    # batch_size is capped by n_patches, not by memory.   try(ds$sample(batch_size = 1000L)) } #> <edaphos_tile_dataset> #>   stack       : 45 x 45 x 3 (rows x cols x channels) #>   patch_size  : 8 x 8 #>   n_patches   : 200 #>   channels    : soc, elev, twi #> [1] 4 3 8 8 #> [1] 19.50303 19.50303 #> [1] 6.510679 6.510679 #> [1] TRUE #> [1] FALSE #> [1] TRUE #> [1] FALSE #> [1] TRUE #> [1]  18.61 994.61   8.53 #> [1] -0.14  0.52 -0.49 #> [1] 200 #> [1] 25 #>      [,1] [,2] #> [1,]   21   21 #> [2,]   25   25 #> Error : No valid cells leave enough margin for patch_size = 46. #> [1] 0.517037 #> [1] TRUE #> [1] TRUE #> [1] 448 #> [1] 1024 #> [1] 0 #> Error in ds$sample(batch_size = 1000L) :  #>   batch_size <= n_patches is not TRUE

code: if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{ # The stub always errors; it is a signpost, not an implementation. foundation_tile_source_era5()  # Supported route: register at the Copernicus Climate Data Store, # store the key once, request the NetCDF, then convert. ecmwfr::wf_set_key(key = "your-cds-personal-access-token") req <- list(   dataset_short_name = "reanalysis-era5-land-monthly-means",   product_type       = "monthly_averaged_reanalysis",   variable = c("2m_temperature", "total_evaporation"),   year = "2020", month = sprintf("%02d", 1:12), time = "00:00",   # The CDS bounding box is north, west, south, east -- the reverse   # convention to the c(xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax) that every   # foundation_tile_* function in this package expects.   area = c(-14, -50, -16, -48),   format = "netcdf",   target = "era5_land_cerrado_2020.nc" ) ecmwfr::wf_request(req, path = tempdir()) era5 <- terra::rast(file.path(tempdir(), "era5_land_cerrado_2020.nc"))  aoi  <- c(-50, -48, -16, -14) soil <- foundation_tile_source_soilgrids(variables = "soc", aoi = aoi) stack <- foundation_tile_align(list(soil = soil, era5 = era5),                                  target_res = 0.0025, aoi = aoi)  # ERA5-Land is a 0.1 degree (roughly 9 km) reanalysis -- confirm on # the object you actually downloaded rather than taking it on trust: terra::res(era5) # Projected onto a 250 m grid with the default bilinear method it # becomes a smooth channel carrying no information below 9 km. That # is harmless for a contrastive encoder and misleading in a # covariate-importance table. } # }

code: if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{ # The stub always errors, whatever you pass it. It exists so that # downstream code has one canonical MODIS entry point to name. foundation_tile_source_modis()  # The supported route is to pre-process outside edaphos -- MODIStsp, # rgee or the AppEEARS service all work -- write a GeoTIFF mosaic, # and read it back with terra. Nothing downstream cares where a # raster came from. ndvi <- terra::rast("modis/MOD13Q1_NDVI_2020_cerrado.tif")  # MOD13Q1 stores NDVI as int16 with a 1e-4 scale factor and -3000 as # the fill value, and both survive terra::rast() untouched. Drop the # fill and rescale before stacking, otherwise the "ndvi" channel is a # mixture of index values and sentinels. ndvi[ndvi < -2000] <- NA ndvi <- ndvi * 1e-4 names(ndvi) <- "ndvi"  aoi  <- c(-50, -48, -16, -14) soil <- foundation_tile_source_soilgrids(variables = "soc", aoi = aoi) stack <- foundation_tile_align(list(soil = soil, modis = ndvi),                                  target_res = 0.0025, aoi = aoi) ds <- foundation_tile_dataset(stack, patch_size = 32L,                                 n_patches = 5000L, seed = 1L)  # A 16-day composite is not a snapshot: neighbouring pixels of # MOD13Q1 can come from different days. Treat it as one channel of a # pretraining stack, not as a same-date observation of the soil. } # }

title: Fetch a SoilGrids soil-property stack over an AoI — foundation_tile_source_soilgrids
code: if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{ # A 2 x 2 degree window over the Brazilian Cerrado. The AoI is # c(xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax) in WGS84 degrees -- not the # c(north, west, south, east) that Copernicus and NASA services use. aoi <- c(-50, -48, -16, -14)  soil <- foundation_tile_source_soilgrids(   variables = c("soc", "clay", "phh2o"),   depth = "0-5cm", stat = "mean", aoi = aoi,   path = tools::R_user_dir("edaphos", "cache") ) names(soil)   # one layer per variable, prefixed "soilgrids_"  # `depth` is normalised internally, so the documented string form and # geodata's own integer upper bound in centimetres are one request: by_string  <- foundation_tile_source_soilgrids("soc", depth = "0-5cm",                                                  aoi = aoi) by_integer <- foundation_tile_source_soilgrids("soc", depth = 5,                                                  aoi = aoi)  # Anything outside the six standard intervals is rejected before a # single byte is downloaded, and the message names all six: foundation_tile_source_soilgrids("soc", depth = "0-10cm", aoi = aoi) ## Error: Unknown depth string '0-10cm'. Use one of: 0-5cm, 5-15cm, ##   15-30cm, 30-60cm, 60-100cm, 100-200cm (or an integer in ##   c(5, 15, 30, 60, 100, 200)).  # Two limits this wrapper cannot check for you, because they belong # to geodata::soil_world(): `variables` must be one of bdod, cfvo, # clay, nitrogen, ocd, ocs, phh2o, sand, silt, soc, wrb; and geodata's # own help notes that only stat = "mean" down to 60 cm is currently # served, so the quantile statistics and the two deepest intervals # fail at download time rather than at argument checking.  # geodata serves the 30 arc-second aggregation of SoilGrids, not the # native 250 m grid, so read the realised cell size off the result # rather than trusting the "250 m" in the product's name. Aligning # these layers onto a 250 m grid resamples; it does not restore # detail that was never downloaded. terra::res(soil)   # ~0.008333 degrees = 30 arc-seconds, roughly 1 km  # `path` is geodata's download cache, not scratch space. The default # tempdir() dies with the session, so every new R process re-fetches # the whole global mosaic before cropping to `aoi`. } # }

code: if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{ aoi <- c(-50, -48, -16, -14)  topo <- foundation_tile_source_srtm(   aoi = aoi, derive = c("slope", "TPI"), country = "BRA",   path = tools::R_user_dir("edaphos", "cache") ) names(topo)   # "elev" "slope" "TPI"  # `country` picks which national tile geodata fetches and the crop to # `aoi` happens afterwards, so the default "BRA" is wrong the moment # the AoI leaves Brazil. The failure comes from terra, not from a # helpful check: "[crop] extents do not overlap". foundation_tile_source_srtm(aoi = c(30, 32, -2, 0), country = "KEN")  # geodata::elevation_30s() masks to the country border by default and # this wrapper does not expose that argument, so an AoI straddling a # border comes back NA on the foreign side. terra::global(topo, "isNA")  # Every entry of `derive` goes through terra::terrain(), which needs a # full 3 x 3 neighbourhood, so each derived layer is NA on the outer # ring of the tile even where `elev` is present. # foundation_tile_dataset() imputes those NAs to the layer mean # without warning -- crop with a margin if that matters to you.  # `unit = "degrees"` is passed for every derived layer but only # affects "slope" and "aspect"; TPI, TRI and roughness stay in the # units of `elev`.  # elevation_30s() is the 30 arc-SECOND (roughly 1 km) aggregation of # the 90 m CGIAR-SRTM, not a 30 m product -- the cell size says so: terra::res(topo)   # ~0.008333 degrees = 30 arc-seconds, roughly 1 km # Slope computed from that is a kilometre-scale gradient and will not # match a slope map derived from a fine LiDAR DEM over the same field. } # }

title: Fetch a WorldClim 2.1 climate stack over an AoI — foundation_tile_source_worldclim
code: if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{ aoi <- c(-50, -48, -16, -14)  # Country scope: geodata downloads the whole of Brazil at 30 # arc-seconds and the crop to `aoi` only happens afterwards, so a # small AoI does not buy a small download. clim <- foundation_tile_source_worldclim(   variables = c("prec", "tavg"), country = "BRA", aoi = aoi,   path = tools::R_user_dir("edaphos", "cache") )  # Every monthly WorldClim variable is a 12-layer raster, so the two # variables above give 24 channels, not 2. Check this before the # stack reaches foundation_tile_dataset(): the channel count is what # the encoder's first convolution must match. terra::nlyr(clim)   # 24 names(clim)   # wc_prec_01 ... wc_prec_12, wc_tavg_01 ... wc_tavg_12 terra::res(clim)    # country scope is always 30 arc-seconds,                     # i.e. ~0.008333 degrees; `res` never enters it  # `res` is ignored while `country` is non-NULL. Pass country = NULL # for the global product, which is the right choice when the AoI # crosses a border -- worldclim_country() returns one country only. bio <- foundation_tile_source_worldclim(   variables = "bio", country = NULL, res = 2.5, aoi = aoi )  # `bio` is not monthly, so it does not follow the 12-layer rule -- # print its channel count instead of assuming one: terra::nlyr(bio)    # 19 bioclimatic variables, named wc_bio_01..19  # geodata documents its own `var` argument as one of tmin, tmax, # tavg, prec, wind, vapr, bio. The "elev" and "srad" entries listed # among `variables` above are outside that documented set, although # geodata's stopifnot() does accept them. "elev" in particular is a # single-band product, so it breaks the layer arithmetic above -- # again, count, do not assume: el <- foundation_tile_source_worldclim(variables = "elev",                                        country = "BRA", aoi = aoi) terra::nlyr(el)  # WorldClim 2.1 is a 1970-2000 climate normal, not a time series. # Stacking it beside a 2020 vegetation composite gives channels that # describe different decades: acceptable for self-supervised # pretraining, wrong for any statement about a particular year. } # }

code: # Needs network access to Zenodo, so it is not run here. if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{   loc <- foundation_weights_download("edaphos-cerrado-moco-v1",                                      verbose = TRUE)    # This function only fetches and SHA-256-verifies the file; it   # builds no encoder. `loc$path` is a bare state dict, and loading   # from a *path* cannot infer the encoder geometry, so the three   # shapes are mandatory. They live in the registry row that came   # back alongside the file:   moco <- foundation_weights_load(loc$path,                                   n_channels  = loc$entry$n_channels,                                   feature_dim = loc$entry$feature_dim,                                   proj_dim    = loc$entry$proj_dim)    # Equivalent, and the idiomatic route: pass the registry *name*   # and the download (or cache hit) and the shape lookup both happen   # for you. Call foundation_weights_download() directly only when   # you want the file itself — to stage it on an offline machine, or   # to pre-warm a shared cache_dir.   moco <- foundation_weights_load("edaphos-cerrado-moco-v1")    # Check what you got before you trust it. v1 predates the   # normalisation-statistics field, so its training mean / sd are   # unrecoverable: standardise your own inputs over your AoI and   # report that you did so.   print(loc$entry$norm_stats_status)   # "unrecoverable" } # }

code: # The registry route needs a network download from Zenodo, so it is # not run here. It fills the three shapes from the registry row, so # they are the one thing you do not have to pass. if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{   moco <- foundation_weights_load("edaphos-cerrado-moco-v1")   # v1 expects 31 channels in the registry's band order; `patches`   # must be a numeric (N, 31, 16, 16) array, standardised over your   # own AoI (v1's training mean / sd are unrecoverable — see   # foundation_weights_list()$norm_stats_status).   emb <- foundation_moco_embed(moco, patches) } # }  # The local-path route is offline, and is also how you reload your # own encoders. It is shown here end to end on a throwaway model. if (requireNamespace("torch", quietly = TRUE) &&     isTRUE(torch::torch_is_installed())) {  # A 3-step fit on random noise. This is plumbing, not a model: it # has learned nothing and its embeddings are meaningless. A usable # encoder needs a real tile corpus and thousands of steps — see # foundation_moco_pretrain_tiles(). set.seed(42) patches <- array(stats::rnorm(24L * 5L * 8L * 8L), dim = c(24L, 5L, 8L, 8L)) set.seed(1) fit <- foundation_moco_pretrain(patches, feature_dim = 16L, proj_dim = 8L,                                 batch_size = 8L, epochs = 3L, seed = 1L) pt <- tempfile(fileext = ".pt") torch::torch_save(fit$encoder_q$state_dict(), pt)  # A `.pt` is a bare state dict: it fixes the tensor sizes but records # nothing about what they mean, so all three shapes are mandatory here # and must match what was saved. moco <- foundation_weights_load(pt, n_channels = 5L,                                 feature_dim = 16L, proj_dim = 8L) print(c(n_channels = moco$n_channels, feature_dim = moco$feature_dim,         proj_dim = moco$proj_dim))  # Only encoder_q is restored, and it comes back in eval() mode, so the # reloaded copy reproduces the source object's embeddings exactly. print(all.equal(foundation_moco_embed(moco, patches),                 foundation_moco_embed(fit, patches)))  # Omitting the shapes is a refusal, not a default. Note that this is # what `foundation_weights_load(loc$path)` would hit after a # foundation_weights_download() — pass loc$entry's shapes, or skip # the download and load by name. print(tryCatch(foundation_weights_load(pt), error = conditionMessage)) unlink(pt) }

title: Graph-based causal discovery (Pilar 10 x Pilar 1) — gnn_causal_discovery
code: # `causal_structure_learn()` needs bnlearn AND igraph, both # Suggests, so the whole hand-off is guarded. if (requireNamespace("bnlearn", quietly = TRUE) &&     requireNamespace("igraph", quietly = TRUE)) {    set.seed(1)   sub <- br_cerrado[sample(nrow(br_cerrado), 150L), ]   names(sub)[names(sub) == "x"] <- "lon"   names(sub)[names(sub) == "y"] <- "lat"    # Pillar 10 side: a k-NN co-location graph over the pixels, then   # a GAT whose node embeddings have already absorbed each pixel's   # spatial neighbourhood.   g <- gnn_build_graph(sub, k = 6L,                        feature_cols = c("elev", "slope", "twi",                                         "map_mm", "ndvi"))   gat <- gnn_fit(g, sub$soc, hidden = 8L, n_heads = 2L,                  n_layers = 1L, epochs = 40L, seed = 1L)    # Pillar 1 side: hill-climbing over the six covariates PLUS four   # embedding dimensions carried along as conditioners.   feats <- sub[, c("elev", "slope", "twi", "map_mm", "ndvi", "soc")]   kg <- gnn_causal_discovery(gat, feats, method = "hc",                              n_emb_cols = 4L, seed = 1L)    # The restriction the name promises lives in one extra field.   # `kg$graph` is still the augmented DAG -- 10 vertices, 25 arcs,   # 17 of them touching a conditioner.  Anything that reads   # `kg$graph` gets the nuisance nodes too.   print(c(vertices     = igraph::vcount(kg$graph),           arcs         = igraph::ecount(kg$graph),           feature_only = nrow(kg$edges_feature_only)))   e <- causal_kg_edges(kg)   print(sum(grepl("^z_emb_", e$cause) | grepl("^z_emb_", e$effect)))    # What the conditioning bought, read against the same search with   # no embeddings at all: eight arcs over the six covariates   # against seven, four of them shared.   plain <- causal_structure_learn(feats, variables = names(feats),                                   method = "hc")   p <- causal_kg_edges(plain)   a_arcs <- paste(kg$edges_feature_only[, 1L], "->",                   kg$edges_feature_only[, 2L])   p_arcs <- paste(p$cause, "->", p$effect)   print(setdiff(a_arcs, p_arcs))   # "elev -> map_mm" "map_mm -> ndvi" "slope -> soc" "twi -> soc"   print(setdiff(p_arcs, a_arcs))   # "soc -> map_mm" "slope -> map_mm" "twi -> map_mm"    # Read those two lines together before believing either DAG.   # Without the embeddings three arrows run INTO mean annual   # rainfall, from carbon and from terrain; conditioning on four   # GAT dimensions removes all three, puts elevation upstream of   # rainfall instead, and sends slope and TWI straight to SOC.   # Encouraging -- but a BIC score is identical across a Markov   # equivalence class, so arc DIRECTION out of `hc` is a search   # artefact and not evidence.  Pin the arrows you already know   # with `whitelist` / `blacklist` before reading any of it   # causally. } #>     vertices         arcs feature_only  #>           10           22            5  #> [1] 17 #> [1] "elev -> map_mm" #> [1] "soc -> map_mm"   "slope -> map_mm" "twi -> map_mm"

title: Node-level embeddings from a fitted GAT — gnn_embed
code: data(br_cerrado) set.seed(10)  sub <- br_cerrado[sample(nrow(br_cerrado), 150L), ] names(sub)[names(sub) == "x"] <- "lon" names(sub)[names(sub) == "y"] <- "lat" g <- gnn_build_graph(sub, k = 6L,                      feature_cols = c("elev", "slope", "twi", "map_mm"))  test  <- rep(c(FALSE, FALSE, TRUE), length.out = nrow(sub)) y_obs <- sub$soc; y_obs[test] <- NA fit <- gnn_fit(g, y_obs, hidden = 8L, n_heads = 2L, n_layers = 2L,                epochs = 60L, seed = 1L) emb <- gnn_embed(fit)  # One row per NODE, not per training node: message passing ran over # the whole graph, so the 50 held-out profiles carry embeddings too. c(rows = nrow(emb), cols = ncol(emb),   nodes = g$n, trained_on = fit$n_train) #>       rows       cols      nodes trained_on  #>        150          8        150        100   # The embedding is NOT the design the head was fitted on.  With # `readout_skip` (the default) the head also saw the raw features # un-smoothed, so a downstream model fed `emb` alone is missing # four columns -- and the readout_skip comparison in [gnn_fit()] # shows how much of the score lives in them. c(emb = ncol(emb), design = ncol(fit$head_design),   raw_features = ncol(g$features)) #>          emb       design raw_features  #>            8           12            4  isTRUE(all.equal(fit$head_design, cbind(emb, g$features),                  check.attributes = FALSE)) #> [1] TRUE  # The column count follows `average_heads`: averaged (the default) # gives `hidden`, concatenated gives hidden * n_heads. fit_cat <- gnn_fit(g, y_obs, hidden = 8L, n_heads = 2L, n_layers = 2L,                    epochs = 60L, seed = 1L, average_heads = FALSE) c(averaged = ncol(emb), concatenated = ncol(gnn_embed(fit_cat))) #>     averaged concatenated  #>            8           16

title: Fit a Graph Attention Network on a WoSIS-style co-location graph — gnn_fit
code: data(br_cerrado) set.seed(10)  # gnn_build_graph() wants the coordinates under `lon` / `lat`. sub <- br_cerrado[sample(nrow(br_cerrado), 150L), ] names(sub)[names(sub) == "x"] <- "lon" names(sub)[names(sub) == "y"] <- "lat" g <- gnn_build_graph(sub, k = 6L,                      feature_cols = c("elev", "slope", "twi", "map_mm"))  # Hold every third profile out by setting its target to NA: the # default train_mask is !is.na(targets), so those nodes still pass # messages to their neighbours but never enter the loss. test  <- rep(c(FALSE, FALSE, TRUE), length.out = nrow(sub)) y     <- sub$soc y_obs <- y; y_obs[test] <- NA  fit <- gnn_fit(g, y_obs, hidden = 8L, n_heads = 2L, n_layers = 2L,                epochs = 60L, seed = 1L) c(n_train = fit$n_train, n_val = fit$n_val,   epochs_run = length(fit$history), best_epoch = fit$best_epoch) #>    n_train      n_val epochs_run best_epoch  #>        100         20         21          1   # Score the held-out nodes against an achievable null -- the # TRAINING mean -- and against OLS on the same four covariates. null_mean <- mean(y[!test]) nse <- function(pred)   1 - sum((pred - y[test])^2) / sum((y[test] - null_mean)^2) ols <- lm(soc ~ elev + slope + twi + map_mm, data = sub[!test, ]) round(c(gat = nse(predict(fit)[test]),         ols = nse(predict(ols, sub[test, ]))), 4) #>    gat    ols  #> 0.6259 0.5974   # Before crediting the graph, read `best_epoch`.  It is 1 here: no # epoch of attention training beat the initialisation on the # internal validation split, so what came back is the random-init # encoder plus the closed-form ridge head -- and the four raw # covariates the readout skip hands that head do nearly all of it. fit_ns <- gnn_fit(g, y_obs, hidden = 8L, n_heads = 2L, n_layers = 2L,                   epochs = 60L, seed = 1L, readout_skip = FALSE) round(c(with_skip = nse(predict(fit)[test]),         without   = nse(predict(fit_ns)[test])), 4) #> with_skip   without  #>    0.6259    0.3806   # Inventing a target for the held-out nodes instead of masking them # -- the training mean is the usual choice -- fits the head to # reproduce that invented value and drags the test set towards it. y_imp <- y; y_imp[test] <- null_mean fit_imp <- gnn_fit(g, y_imp, hidden = 8L, n_heads = 2L, n_layers = 2L,                    epochs = 60L, seed = 1L) round(c(masked = nse(predict(fit)[test]),         invented = nse(predict(fit_imp)[test])), 4) #>   masked invented  #>   0.6259   0.4186   # `history` is the TRAINING loss and the printed "final MSE" is its # last entry.  Neither describes the parameters you got back, which # come from `best_epoch` on the validation split. round(c(train_at_best = fit$history[fit$best_epoch],         train_min     = min(fit$history),         train_at_end  = fit$history[length(fit$history)]), 4) #> train_at_best     train_min  train_at_end  #>        0.5043        0.4820        0.8000

title: Seed ensemble of GAT fits — gnn_fit_ensemble
code: data(br_cerrado) set.seed(10)  sub <- br_cerrado[sample(nrow(br_cerrado), 150L), ] names(sub)[names(sub) == "x"] <- "lon" names(sub)[names(sub) == "y"] <- "lat" g <- gnn_build_graph(sub, k = 6L,                      feature_cols = c("elev", "slope", "twi", "map_mm"))  test  <- rep(c(FALSE, FALSE, TRUE), length.out = nrow(sub)) y     <- sub$soc y_obs <- y; y_obs[test] <- NA  ens <- gnn_fit_ensemble(g, y_obs, n_ensemble = 4L, seed = 1L,                         hidden = 8L, n_heads = 2L, n_layers = 2L,                         epochs = 60L) ens #> <edaphos_gnn_ensemble> #>   members = 4   nodes = 150   trained on = 100 #>   mean between-member sd = 0.6984  # Members differ only in their seed.  That alone moves the held-out # score by more than most modelling choices do, which is the whole # argument for reporting an ensemble instead of one lucky fit. null_mean <- mean(y[!test]) nse <- function(pred)   1 - sum((pred - y[test])^2) / sum((y[test] - null_mean)^2) member <- vapply(ens$members, function(m) nse(predict(m)[test]),                  numeric(1)) round(c(worst = min(member), mean = mean(member), best = max(member),         ensemble = nse(predict(ens)[test])), 4) #>    worst     mean     best ensemble  #>   0.4799   0.5138   0.5507   0.5262   # Note what averaging does and does not buy: it beats the AVERAGE # member, not the best one -- and which seed was best is knowable # only from the held-out labels you are not supposed to have.  # `member_sd` is the spread BETWEEN seeds, not a predictive # interval.  It is under a fifth of the actual error here, so a # +-1.96 sd band covers a quarter of the profiles, not 95 percent. round(c(rmse       = sqrt(mean((predict(ens)[test] - y[test])^2)),         mean_sd    = mean(ens$member_sd[test]),         coverage95 = mean(abs(y[test] - predict(ens)[test]) <=                           1.96 * ens$member_sd[test])), 3) #>       rmse    mean_sd coverage95  #>      4.339      0.746      0.240

code: n_claims <- function(recs) sum(vapply(recs, function(r)   if (is.data.frame(r$claims)) nrow(r$claims) else 0L, integer(1)))  draft <- system.file("extdata", "cerrado_gold_standard_v1_draft.jsonl",                      package = "edaphos")  # The bundled draft holds 93 machine claims, every one still at # status = "draft".  Export keeps NONE of them, and says so: 30 # abstracts, 0 claims.  "draft" means no human ever looked, and an # unreviewed claim is not gold-standard evidence. kept <- llm_annotation_export(draft, file.path(tempdir(), "hollow.jsonl")) #> === Exported gold standard: /tmp/RtmpNvtEGq/hollow.jsonl (30 abstracts, 0 claims) === n_claims(kept) #> [1] 0  # Accept the first claim of each abstract and re-export.  Only the # `status` string decides -- nothing else in the record matters. reviewed <- file.path(tempdir(), "reviewed.jsonl") writeLines(sub('"status":"draft"', '"status":"accepted"',                readLines(draft, warn = FALSE), fixed = TRUE), reviewed) n_claims(llm_annotation_export(reviewed, file.path(tempdir(), "g2.jsonl"))) #> === Exported gold standard: /tmp/RtmpNvtEGq/g2.jsonl (30 abstracts, 30 claims) === #> [1] 30  # Back-compat trap in the other direction: the hand-annotated v1 # seed has no `status` column at all, and those claims are treated # as already accepted, so all 72 survive.  A file with no statuses # keeps everything; a file with only draft statuses keeps nothing. gs <- system.file("extdata", "cerrado_gold_standard_v1.jsonl",                   package = "edaphos") once <- file.path(tempdir(), "once.jsonl") c(once  = n_claims(llm_annotation_export(gs, once)),   twice = n_claims(llm_annotation_export(             once, file.path(tempdir(), "twice.jsonl")))) #> === Exported gold standard: /tmp/RtmpNvtEGq/once.jsonl (30 abstracts, 72 claims) === #> === Exported gold standard: /tmp/RtmpNvtEGq/twice.jsonl (30 abstracts, 72 claims) === #>  once twice  #>    72    72   # Idempotent because `status` is stripped on the way out -- which # also means you cannot re-review an exported file.  Keep the # reviewed JSONL; the export is a derived artefact.  # `include_rationale = FALSE` drops the free-text justification, # leaving the four fields llm_annotation_validate() requires. names(llm_annotation_export(gs, file.path(tempdir(), "no_rat.jsonl"),                             include_rationale = FALSE)[[1]]$claims) #> === Exported gold standard: /tmp/RtmpNvtEGq/no_rat.jsonl (30 abstracts, 72 claims) === #> [1] "cause"      "effect"     "polarity"   "confidence"

code: if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{ # Phase 2.  This blocks until the browser tab is closed, so it only # makes sense from an interactive session, and it needs shiny, DT, # bslib and shinyjs installed. corpus <- list(   list(abstract_id   = "CER_A",        abstract_text = "Rainfall raised topsoil SOC on 520 Oxisols.") ) draft <- file.path(tempdir(), "cerrado_draft.jsonl") llm_preannotate(corpus, backend = "simulator", output_path = draft)  # In-place review: `output_path` defaults to `draft_path`, and the # app rewrites the file after every abstract, so an interrupted # session loses at most the abstract you were on. llm_annotation_launch(draft)  # Better for anything you will publish: keep the machine draft # pristine and write the human verdicts elsewhere.  In-place review # destroys the LLM-vs-human comparison you need to report the # extractor's precision and recall. reviewed <- file.path(tempdir(), "cerrado_reviewed.jsonl") llm_annotation_launch(draft, output_path = reviewed)  # `port` only matters when the app must be reachable from outside # the R process (container, remote annotator); leave it NULL and # shiny picks a free port. llm_annotation_launch(draft, output_path = reviewed, port = 8080)  # Claims the reviewer never touched are still status = "draft" and # are discarded here -- check the claim count in the message before # treating the result as a finished gold standard. llm_annotation_export(reviewed, file.path(tempdir(), "cerrado_gold.jsonl")) llm_annotation_validate(file.path(tempdir(), "cerrado_gold.jsonl")) } # }
