title: Package a reviewed gold-standard into a Zenodo-ready deposit bundle — llm_annotation_to_zenodo
code: gs <- system.file("extdata", "cerrado_gold_standard_v1.jsonl",                   package = "edaphos") bundle <- file.path(tempdir(), "cerrado_kg_deposit")  # `zip = FALSE` because utils::zip() shells out to an external # `zip` executable that is not present everywhere.  Pass `version` # explicitly too: it defaults to Sys.Date(), so metadata.json and # README.md otherwise differ on every run and the bundle is not # reproducible. llm_annotation_to_zenodo(gs, bundle,                          title = "Cerrado gold-standard KG (v1)",                          version = "1.0.0", zip = FALSE) #> === Exported gold standard: /tmp/RtmpNvtEGq/cerrado_kg_deposit/gold_standard.jsonl (30 abstracts, 72 claims) === #> === Zenodo bundle ready: /tmp/RtmpNvtEGq/cerrado_kg_deposit === sort(list.files(bundle)) #> [1] "README.md"           "gold_standard.jsonl" "kg.ttl"              #> [4] "metadata.json"        # The 72 accepted claims become 72 reified rdf:Statement blocks, # plus 30 eda:Abstract provenance nodes carrying title and year. ttl <- readLines(file.path(bundle, "kg.ttl"), warn = FALSE) c(statements = sum(grepl("a rdf:Statement", ttl, fixed = TRUE)),   abstracts  = sum(grepl("a eda:Abstract", ttl, fixed = TRUE))) #> statements  abstracts  #>         72         30   # The licence is lower-cased into metadata.json on purpose: that is # the identifier the Zenodo REST API expects, not the SPDX spelling # you passed in. md <- jsonlite::fromJSON(file.path(bundle, "metadata.json")) c(license = md$metadata$license, version = md$metadata$version) #>     license     version  #> "cc-by-4.0"     "1.0.0"   # Trap: this runs llm_annotation_export() internally, so a reviewed # file whose claims are all still "draft" produces a bundle that # SUCCEEDS, prints its usual banner, and contains zero statements. # Check the count before you mint a DOI, not the exit status. draft <- system.file("extdata", "cerrado_gold_standard_v1_draft.jsonl",                      package = "edaphos") hollow <- file.path(tempdir(), "hollow_deposit") llm_annotation_to_zenodo(draft, hollow, version = "1.0.0", zip = FALSE) #> === Exported gold standard: /tmp/RtmpNvtEGq/hollow_deposit/gold_standard.jsonl (30 abstracts, 0 claims) === #> === Zenodo bundle ready: /tmp/RtmpNvtEGq/hollow_deposit === sum(grepl("a rdf:Statement",           readLines(file.path(hollow, "kg.ttl"), warn = FALSE), fixed = TRUE)) #> [1] 0  # `authors` must carry all four columns.  NA values are fine and # omit that field from the creator, but a missing COLUMN aborts # part-way through, leaving a half-written directory behind. who <- data.frame(family_name = c("Silva", "Costa"),                   given_name  = c("Ana", "Bruno"),                   orcid       = c("0000-0001-2345-6789", NA),                   affiliation = c("Embrapa Cerrados", NA),                   stringsAsFactors = FALSE) authored <- file.path(tempdir(), "authored_deposit") llm_annotation_to_zenodo(gs, authored, authors = who,                          version = "1.0.0", zip = FALSE) #> === Exported gold standard: /tmp/RtmpNvtEGq/authored_deposit/gold_standard.jsonl (30 abstracts, 72 claims) === #> === Zenodo bundle ready: /tmp/RtmpNvtEGq/authored_deposit === jsonlite::fromJSON(file.path(authored, "metadata.json"),                    simplifyVector = FALSE)$metadata$creators #> [[1]] #> [[1]]$name #> [1] "Silva, Ana" #>  #> [[1]]$orcid #> [1] "0000-0001-2345-6789" #>  #> [[1]]$affiliation #> [1] "Embrapa Cerrados" #>  #>  #> [[2]] #> [[2]]$name #> [1] "Costa, Bruno" #>  #>

code: gs <- system.file("extdata", "cerrado_gold_standard_v1.jsonl",                   package = "edaphos") v <- llm_annotation_validate(gs) v$ok #> [1] TRUE  # The v1 seed: 30 abstracts, 72 claims, 1 to 5 claims each, clean # under the strict vocabulary. c(records = nrow(v$summary), claims = sum(v$summary$n_claims)) #> records  claims  #>      30      72  range(v$summary$n_claims) #> [1] 1 5  # A file with one of each failure mode.  The second record has no # `claims` key at all. bad <- file.path(tempdir(), "bad.jsonl") writeLines(c(   paste0('{"abstract_id":"BAD_01","abstract_text":"Tree cover raised SOC.",',          '"claims":[{"cause":"tree_cover","effect":"soc",',          '"polarity":"positive","confidence":0.8},',          '{"cause":"clay","effect":"soc","polarity":"+",',          '"confidence":1.4}]}'),   '{"abstract_id":"BAD_02","abstract_text":"No claims field at all."}' ), bad) llm_annotation_validate(bad)$errors #> [1] "BAD_01: 1 claim(s) with invalid polarity"         #> [2] "BAD_01: 1 claim(s) with confidence outside [0,1]" #> [3] "BAD_01: 1 claim(s) with non-canonical vocabulary" #> [4] "BAD_02: missing required field(s) claims"          # `strict_vocab = FALSE` retires the vocabulary error only -- the # polarity and confidence checks always run.  Use it while a new # term like "tree_cover" is still being argued about, not to make a # file pass. llm_annotation_validate(bad, strict_vocab = FALSE)$errors #> [1] "BAD_01: 1 claim(s) with invalid polarity"         #> [2] "BAD_01: 1 claim(s) with confidence outside [0,1]" #> [3] "BAD_02: missing required field(s) claims"          # Read `summary` next to `errors`, never alone: a record that fails # the required-field check is skipped before it is counted, so # BAD_02 has no row and nrow(summary) is not the file's length. c(rows_in_summary = nrow(llm_annotation_validate(bad)$summary),   lines_in_file   = length(readLines(bad, warn = FALSE))) #> rows_in_summary   lines_in_file  #>               1               2   # And `ok` is a schema verdict, not a coverage one.  An export that # dropped every claim validates perfectly, so gate a deposit on the # claim count as well. empty <- file.path(tempdir(), "empty.jsonl") writeLines('{"abstract_id":"E_01","abstract_text":"x","claims":[]}', empty) e <- llm_annotation_validate(empty) e$ok #> [1] TRUE sum(e$summary$n_claims) #> [1] 0

title: Estimate per-1 000-claim extraction cost — llm_benchmark_cost
code: # List prices, not invoices: published per-token rates times assumed # token counts (700 in / 110 out).  Nothing is measured. str(llm_benchmark_cost("anthropic", model = "claude-sonnet-4-5",                        n_abstracts = 30L, claims_per_abstract = 2.4)) #> List of 6 #>  $ backend               : chr "anthropic" #>  $ model                 : chr "claude-sonnet-4-5" #>  $ n_abstracts           : int 30 #>  $ n_claims              : num 72 #>  $ cost_total_usd        : num 0.113 #>  $ cost_per_1k_claims_usd: num 1.56  # Scaling a Cerrado systematic review to 10 000 abstracts.  The # local model reads $0 because list price is all this function # knows -- it is blind to the GPU, and to the 15.9 s/abstract that # the shipped latency summary records for Gemma 4 against 3.0 s for # GPT-4o-mini. round(c(   ollama    = llm_benchmark_cost("ollama",                                  n_abstracts = 10000L)$cost_total_usd,   openai    = llm_benchmark_cost("openai",                                  n_abstracts = 10000L)$cost_total_usd,   anthropic = llm_benchmark_cost("anthropic",                                  n_abstracts = 10000L)$cost_total_usd), 2) #>    ollama    openai anthropic  #>      0.00      1.71     37.50   # Trap 1: `n_abstracts` cancels out of `cost_per_1k_claims_usd`. # That headline is a function of the token assumptions and # `claims_per_abstract` alone and says nothing about your corpus. c(n30 = llm_benchmark_cost("openai", n_abstracts = 30L,          claims_per_abstract = 2.4)$cost_per_1k_claims_usd,   n10k = llm_benchmark_cost("openai", n_abstracts = 10000L,           claims_per_abstract = 2.4)$cost_per_1k_claims_usd) #>     n30    n10k  #> 0.07125 0.07125   # Trap 2: an unrecognised backend returns NA prices rather than # erroring, so a typo quietly turns a paid model into a free one. llm_benchmark_cost("gemini", n_abstracts = 30L)$cost_total_usd #> [1] NA  # Trap 3: the denominator is claims EXTRACTED, not claims CORRECT, # so over-extraction buys a cheaper headline.  Re-normalise on the # true positives from the shipped benchmark and both backends get # dearer -- GPT by 1.43x, Claude by 1.22x -- and the advertised 22x # price gap between them narrows to 19x. res_path <- system.file("extdata", "llm_benchmark_results.rds",                         package = "edaphos") if (nzchar(res_path)) {   mt <- readRDS(res_path)$metrics_table   # rows: Gemma, GPT, Claude   per1k <- function(bk, claims) llm_benchmark_cost(     bk, n_abstracts = 30L,     claims_per_abstract = claims / 30)$cost_per_1k_claims_usd   print(round(rbind(     openai    = c(all = per1k("openai",    mt$n_claims[2]),                   tp  = per1k("openai",    mt$tp[2])),     anthropic = c(all = per1k("anthropic", mt$n_claims[3]),                   tp  = per1k("anthropic", mt$tp[3]))), 4)) } #>              all     tp #> openai    0.0703 0.1006 #> anthropic 1.5625 1.9068

title: Pairwise Cohen's kappa between backends on edge presence — llm_benchmark_kappa

title: Pairwise Cohen's kappa between backends on edge presence — llm_benchmark_kappa
text: claims_by_backend Named list data frames, abstract_id, cause, effect. gold Optional gold-standard frame include rater.

title: Pairwise Cohen's kappa between backends on edge presence — llm_benchmark_kappa
code: res_path <- system.file("extdata", "llm_benchmark_results.rds",                         package = "edaphos") if (nzchar(res_path)) {   B <- readRDS(res_path)   print(round(llm_benchmark_kappa(B$backend_claims, gold = B$gold_df), 3))    # Read the `gold` column first: 0.342 / 0.256 / 0.567 against the   # pedologist -- "fair" to "moderate", nowhere near the 0.80 you   # would demand of a second human coder before trusting a KG.   #   # Then read the off-diagonals: two backends that each agree with   # gold can still land at -0.081 with EACH OTHER.  Agreement with a   # reference does not transfer between raters, because they miss   # and invent different edges.    # Trap: the rating universe is the union of edges over whatever   # raters you hand in, so kappa is a property of the CALL, not of   # the pair.  Adding one sloppy fourth rater contributes 169 new   # edges that Gemma and GPT both (correctly) decline, and their   # kappa jumps from -0.081 to 0.385 without either changing a   # single extraction.   set.seed(1)   junk <- data.frame(     abstract_id = sample(unique(B$gold_df$abstract_id), 200,                          replace = TRUE),     cause  = sample(c("clay", "sand", "silt", "ph", "cec"), 200,                     replace = TRUE),     effect = sample(c("erosion", "ndvi", "slope", "land_use"), 200,                     replace = TRUE), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)   print(round(llm_benchmark_kappa(c(B$backend_claims, list(junk = junk)),                                   gold = B$gold_df)[1:2, 1:2], 3))    # Honest caveat on the first matrix: these three "backends" were   # drawn from the gold set by llm_benchmark_simulate() with an   # independent keep-mask per backend, so near-zero pairwise kappa is   # arithmetic from the generator, not evidence about Gemma, GPT or   # Claude.   print(B$mode) } #>                   Gemma 4 GPT-4o-mini Claude Sonnet-4.5  gold #> Gemma 4             1.000      -0.081             0.122 0.342 #> GPT-4o-mini        -0.081       1.000            -0.076 0.256 #> Claude Sonnet-4.5   0.122      -0.076             1.000 0.567 #> gold                0.342       0.256             0.567 1.000 #>             Gemma 4 GPT-4o-mini #> Gemma 4       1.000       0.385 #> GPT-4o-mini   0.385       1.000 #> [1] "simulated"

title: Match extracted LLM claims against a gold-standard set — llm_benchmark_match
code: # The package ships a 30-abstract Cerrado gold standard.  Flatten # its nested `claims` arrays into the one-row-per-edge frame the # matcher expects. gold_path <- system.file("extdata", "cerrado_gold_standard_v1.jsonl",                          package = "edaphos") if (nzchar(gold_path)) {   recs <- lapply(readLines(gold_path), jsonlite::fromJSON)   gold <- do.call(rbind, lapply(recs, function(r) data.frame(     abstract_id = r$abstract_id, cause = r$claims$cause,     effect      = r$claims$effect, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)))   print(c(abstracts = length(recs), claims = nrow(gold)))    # CER_01 is a rainfall / temperature / SOC abstract with five gold   # claims.  Below is an extraction a pedologist would call four out   # of four correct -- only the surface strings differ from the   # annotator's.  Three score TP, one scores FP.   cer1 <- gold[gold$abstract_id == "CER_01", ]   pred <- data.frame(     abstract_id = "CER_01",     cause  = c("Rainfall", "MAP",        "mean annual temperature",                "tree cover"),     effect = c("TOC",      "tree cover", "Corg", "organic carbon"),     stringsAsFactors = FALSE)   print(llm_benchmark_match(pred, cer1))    # P = 0.75, R = 0.60, and BOTH losses are the matching rule rather   # than the model:   #  * "Rainfall" canonicalises to `precipitation`, the annotator   #    wrote `mean_annual_precipitation`, and the normaliser keeps   #    those deliberately apart -- so the same claim is scored as a   #    false positive AND leaves the gold edge as a false negative.   #  * gold lists `mean_annual_temperature -> soc` TWICE for CER_01,   #    and matching is one-to-one, so one predicted edge clears only   #    one of the pair.   print(round(unlist(llm_benchmark_metrics(     llm_benchmark_match(pred, cer1))[       c("tp", "fp", "fn", "precision", "recall")]), 3))    # That duplicate caps the whole benchmark.  Feed gold back as its   # own prediction, deduplicated the way any extractor would emit it,   # and recall stops at 71/72 -- no model can score 1.   ded <- gold[!duplicated(paste(gold$abstract_id, gold$cause,                                 gold$effect)), ]   print(round(unlist(llm_benchmark_metrics(     llm_benchmark_match(ded, gold))[c("tp", "fn", "recall")]), 4))    # Trap: `fuzzy = TRUE` is the default, but it changes nothing here.   # The threshold is the SUM over both endpoints, and no   # predicted/gold pair in this vocabulary sits within 2 edits   # without already matching exactly.  Report the threshold you used   # next to F1 -- see llm_benchmark_simulate() for what raising it   # does.   print(identical(llm_benchmark_match(ded, gold, fuzzy = TRUE),                   llm_benchmark_match(ded, gold, fuzzy = FALSE))) } #> abstracts    claims  #>        30        72  #>            abstract_id                     cause     effect status    source #> CER_01_p.1      CER_01             precipitation        soc     fp predicted #> CER_01_p.2      CER_01 mean_annual_precipitation vegetation     tp predicted #> CER_01_p.3      CER_01   mean_annual_temperature        soc     tp predicted #> CER_01_p.4      CER_01                vegetation        soc     tp predicted #> CER_01_g.1      CER_01 mean_annual_precipitation        soc     fn      gold #> CER_01_g.2      CER_01   mean_annual_temperature        soc     fn      gold #>        tp        fp        fn precision    recall  #>      3.00      1.00      2.00      0.75      0.60  #>      tp      fn  recall  #> 71.0000  1.0000  0.9861  #> [1] TRUE

title: Compute precision / recall / F1 from a match table — llm_benchmark_metrics
code: res_path <- system.file("extdata", "llm_benchmark_results.rds",                         package = "edaphos") if (nzchar(res_path)) {   B <- readRDS(res_path)    # Read this before quoting any number below: the shipped bundle is   # simulator output, not measured API calls.   print(B$mode)    m <- llm_benchmark_metrics(     llm_benchmark_match(B$backend_claims[["Gemma 4"]], B$gold_df))   print(round(unlist(     m[c("tp", "fp", "fn", "precision", "recall", "f1")]), 4))    # Every row of the match table lands in exactly one cell, so the   # three counts reconstruct its length -- a cheap audit that no   # abstract was dropped by the join.   mt <- llm_benchmark_match(B$backend_claims[["Gemma 4"]], B$gold_df)   print(c(counts = m$tp + m$fp + m$fn, rows = nrow(mt)))    # Trap: `per_abstract` returns NA, not 0, whenever a denominator is   # empty.  Precision is NA for the 2 abstracts where this backend   # predicted nothing at all, and F1 is NA for all 5 where it got   # nothing right (precision + recall == 0).   pa <- m$per_abstract   print(c(abstracts = nrow(pa), na_precision = sum(is.na(pa$precision)),           na_f1 = sum(is.na(pa$f1))))    # So the obvious macro average deletes exactly the abstracts the   # backend failed on and reports 0.794; scoring those failures as 0   # gives 0.662; the pooled (micro) F1 is 0.706.  Quote the micro   # figure -- `mean(f1, na.rm = TRUE)` is the flattering one.   print(round(c(macro_narm = mean(pa$f1, na.rm = TRUE),                 macro_zero = mean(ifelse(is.na(pa$f1), 0, pa$f1)),                 micro      = m$f1), 4))    # And read the spread next to the headline: this backend is not   # uniformly mediocre, it is bimodal -- 10 of 30 abstracts perfect,   # 5 a complete miss.   print(c(perfect = sum(pa$f1 == 1, na.rm = TRUE),           total_miss = sum(is.na(pa$f1)))) } #> [1] "simulated" #>        tp        fp        fn precision    recall        f1  #>   48.0000   16.0000   24.0000    0.7500    0.6667    0.7059  #> counts   rows  #>     88     88  #>    abstracts na_precision        na_f1  #>           30            2            5  #> macro_narm macro_zero      micro  #>     0.7941     0.6617     0.7059  #>    perfect total_miss  #>         10          5

title: Simulate backend extractions from a gold-standard set — llm_benchmark_simulate
code: res_path <- system.file("extdata", "llm_benchmark_results.rds",                         package = "edaphos") if (nzchar(res_path)) {   B <- readRDS(res_path)    # Always pass `seed`.  Without one even the row count moves.   print(identical(llm_benchmark_simulate(B$gold_df, seed = 42L),                   llm_benchmark_simulate(B$gold_df, seed = 42L)))    # The shipped benchmark bundle IS this function, not an API call:   # replaying the Gemma 4 profile from data-raw/llm_benchmark_run.R   # reproduces its row of `metrics_table` to the digit.   sim <- llm_benchmark_simulate(B$gold_df, recall = 0.80,                                 precision_target = 0.85,                                 mutate_rate = 0.06, seed = 101L)   m <- llm_benchmark_metrics(llm_benchmark_match(sim, B$gold_df))   print(rbind(     replayed = round(unlist(m[c("precision", "recall", "f1")]), 4),     shipped  = round(unlist(       B$metrics_table[1, c("precision", "recall", "f1")]), 4)))    # `recall` and `precision_target` are knobs on the sampler, not   # properties of the output: 0.80 and 0.85 in give 0.667 and 0.750   # out.  `mutate_rate` is why -- it corrupts endpoint labels AFTER   # sampling, so each mutation costs one TP and adds one FP, pushing   # both metrics down at once.   for (mr in c(0, 0.05, 0.20)) {     s <- llm_benchmark_simulate(B$gold_df, recall = 0.82,                                 precision_target = 0.90,                                 mutate_rate = mr, seed = 7L)     mm <- llm_benchmark_metrics(llm_benchmark_match(s, B$gold_df))     cat(sprintf("mutate_rate %.2f -> precision %.4f (target 0.90)\n",                 mr, mm$precision))   }    # The mutation writes "<label>_alt", four edits away, so the   # default fuzzy_threshold of 2 recovers none of it and a threshold   # of 4 recovers all of it: F1 0.706 -> 0.824.  That single line of   # the scoring rule moves F1 further (+0.118) than the whole spread   # between the three simulated backends (0.116).  Fix the rule   # before you compare models.   if (requireNamespace("stringdist", quietly = TRUE)) {     print(round(vapply(c(2L, 4L), function(th)       llm_benchmark_metrics(llm_benchmark_match(         sim, B$gold_df, fuzzy_threshold = th))$f1, numeric(1)), 4))   }    # `polarity` does not survive, although it is right there in the   # gold frame -- so a downstream KG built from simulated claims   # cannot be scored on the sign of the effect, only on its   # existence.   print(names(sim)) } #> [1] TRUE #>          precision recall     f1 #> replayed      0.75 0.6667 0.7059 #> shipped       0.75 0.6667 0.7059 #> mutate_rate 0.00 -> precision 0.8696 (target 0.90) #> mutate_rate 0.05 -> precision 0.8261 (target 0.90) #> mutate_rate 0.20 -> precision 0.6377 (target 0.90) #> [1] 0.7059 0.8235 #> [1] "abstract_id" "cause"       "effect"      "confidence"

title: Check whether a local Ollama server is reachable — llm_kg_ollama_check
code: # The gate is deliberately cheap and never throws: a refused # connection comes back as a plain FALSE, so a batch script can # branch on it.  Port 1 is always closed. llm_kg_ollama_check(host = "http://127.0.0.1:1", timeout_sec = 0.5) #> $reachable #> [1] FALSE #>   # `reachable` is not "the port is open".  httr2 raises on 4xx/5xx, # so the `status < 400` test in the body is never reached and a # host that answers 404 on /api/tags is indistinguishable from a # refused connection.  In the other direction, anything that # answers 200 counts as reachable -- which is why the model check # below, not `reachable`, is what tells you it is really Ollama.  # Read `model_present` next to `reachable`, never on its own: when # the server is down the element is ABSENT, not FALSE. chk <- llm_kg_ollama_check(host = "http://127.0.0.1:1",                            model = "gemma4:latest", timeout_sec = 0.5) names(chk)                              # "reachable" alone #> [1] "reachable" try(if (!chk$model_present) "missing")  # error: invalid argument type #> Error in !chk$model_present : invalid argument type isFALSE(chk$model_present)              # FALSE -- the safe idiom, #> [1] FALSE                                         # and the one the pipeline uses if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{ # Against a live `ollama serve` the result gains the two extra # elements; `models_available` is what you print when the model # check fails, so the user knows what was actually pulled. chk <- llm_kg_ollama_check(model = "gemma4:latest") chk$model_present chk$models_available } # }

title: Run the Pilar 1 LLM-KG pipeline on a (potentially large) corpus — llm_kg_pipeline_run
code: # Everything outside \dontrun{} below runs offline: the corpus is # arranged so that no record ever reaches an LLM.  The pipeline # opens an `edaphos_causal_kg` on every path, so it needs igraph # (a Suggests) even when it extracts nothing -- and R CMD check # --as-cran does execute this block. if (requireNamespace("igraph", quietly = TRUE)) {    corpus <- tempfile(fileext = ".jsonl")   out    <- tempfile(fileext = ".jsonl")   writeLines(c(     '{"source":"silva2021","abstract":"MAP raised topsoil SOC."}',     '{"source":"reis2019","abstract":""}',     '{"source":"castro2020","abstract":"Clay content'  # truncated   ), corpus)    # What a run killed half way through leaves behind: two claims in   # the output file and one source logged in the `.done` sidecar.   claim <- function(cause, conf)     jsonlite::toJSON(list(cause = cause, effect = "soil organic carbon",                           evidence = "quoted from the abstract",                           confidence = conf, source = "silva2021"),                      auto_unbox = TRUE)   writeLines(c(claim("mean annual precipitation", 0.9),                claim("clay content", 0.7)), out)   writeLines("silva2021", paste0(out, ".done"))    # `backend = "openai"` skips the Ollama pre-flight, and the   # hosted backends have no pre-flight of their own: the API key is   # read only once an abstract is actually sent.  Here none is.   res <- llm_kg_pipeline_run(corpus, out, backend = "openai",                              verbose = FALSE)   print(c(res$n_processed, res$n_skipped, res$n_errors))   # 0 1 1    # Read those three next to the corpus size: they account for 2 of   # 3 lines.  The truncated JSON is dropped at parse time and is   # invisible -- not an error, not a skip, never in `.errors`.   print(length(readLines(corpus)))                         # 3    # An EMPTY abstract, by contrast, is charged as an error and   # logged.  Errors are logged and stepped over, never fatal.   print(readLines(paste0(out, ".errors")))  # "[reis2019]\tempty abstract"    # The trap: `res$kg` holds only the edges extracted in THIS call.   # Resumed sources are skipped and their claims are never read   # back from `output_path`, so the returned graph is empty while   # the claims file has two rows.  Never treat `res$kg` as the   # accumulated graph of a resumed job.   print(nrow(causal_kg_edges(res$kg)))      # 0   print(length(readLines(out)))             # 2    # The claims file is the durable artefact; rebuild the graph from   # it.  Node labels are normalised on insertion, so the two rows   # become mean_annual_precipitation -> soil_organic_carbon and   # clay_content -> soil_organic_carbon.   prev <- jsonlite::stream_in(file(out), verbose = FALSE)   kg <- causal_kg_new()   for (i in seq_len(nrow(prev)))     kg <- causal_kg_add_edge(kg, prev$cause[i], prev$effect[i],                              source     = prev$source[i],                              evidence   = prev$evidence[i],                              confidence = prev$confidence[i])   print(causal_kg_edges(kg)[, c("cause", "effect", "confidence")])    unlink(c(corpus, out, paste0(out, c(".done", ".errors")))) } #> [1] 0 1 1 #> [1] 3 #> [1] "[reis2019]\tempty abstract" #> [1] 0 #> [1] 2 #>                       cause              effect confidence #> 1 mean_annual_precipitation soil_organic_carbon        0.9 #> 2              clay_content soil_organic_carbon        0.7  # A missing credential is treated as a TRANSIENT failure: it is put # on the back-off ladder and then written off, instead of failing # fast.  Guarded on the key so that a reader who has one is not # billed for a live call by running this example. if (requireNamespace("igraph", quietly = TRUE) &&     !nzchar(Sys.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY"))) {   corpus <- tempfile(fileext = ".jsonl")   out    <- tempfile(fileext = ".jsonl")   writeLines('{"source":"silva2021","abstract":"MAP raised SOC."}', corpus)    res <- llm_kg_pipeline_run(corpus, out, backend = "openai",                              max_retries = 0L, verbose = FALSE)   print(res$n_errors)                       # 1   print(readLines(paste0(out, ".errors")))  # "Set OPENAI_API_KEY ..."   print(file.exists(out))                   # FALSE -- an all-error                                             # run never creates                                             # output_path at all    # `max_retries = 0L` is what makes that instant.  At the default   # 3L the very same missing key costs the full back-off ladder,   # 1 + 2 + 4 = 7 s, per abstract before it is written off -- so on   # the 10 000-abstract corpus this function exists for, about 20 h   # of sleeping and not one claim.  Check credentials yourself   # before the run; the pipeline will not do it for you.   unlink(c(corpus, paste0(out, ".errors"))) } #> [1] 1 #> [1] "[silva2021]\tSet OPENAI_API_KEY or pass `api_key`." #> [1] FALSE  if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{ # The networked path.  No key is ever passed as an argument: each # backend reads its own environment variable, and `host` reaches # exactly one of them. #   "ollama"    -- no key; POSTs to <host>/api/chat #   "openai"    -- OPENAI_API_KEY;    `host` ignored #   "anthropic" -- ANTHROPIC_API_KEY; `host` ignored  # Pass `model` explicitly.  The pre-flight only checks the model # when it is non-NULL, so leaving it NULL starts the run happily # and then fails on every single abstract if the default # "gemma4:latest" was never pulled. res <- llm_kg_pipeline_run(   corpus_path    = "cerrado_10k.jsonl",   # {source, abstract} per line   output_path    = "cerrado_claims.jsonl",   backend        = "ollama",   model          = "gemma4:latest",   min_confidence = 0.6,   max_abstracts  = 250L ) res$n_processed  # `min_confidence` is applied before anything is written, and the # source is marked done even when the filter left nothing.  So # raising the threshold on a resumed run is a no-op, and lowering # it does not revisit what is already in `.done`: delete # <output_path>.done to re-extract a corpus at a new threshold. causal_kg_edges(res$kg)[, c("cause", "effect", "confidence")] } # }

title: Pre-annotate a corpus with an LLM to produce draft claims — llm_preannotate
code: # Two abstracts in memory.  `abstract_id` and `abstract_text` are # the only required fields; anything else the record carries (year, # doi, topic) is passed straight through into the draft. corpus <- list(   list(abstract_id   = "CER_A",        abstract_text = "Rainfall raised topsoil SOC on 520 Oxisols.",        year = 2021),   list(abstract_id   = "CER_B",        abstract_text = "Fire frequency cut vegetation cover on sands.",        year = 2019) ) draft <- file.path(tempdir(), "cerrado_draft.jsonl") d <- llm_preannotate(corpus, backend = "simulator",                      output_path = draft, verbose = FALSE) vapply(d, function(r) nrow(r$claims), integer(1)) #> [1] 5 2  # Every drafted claim is stamped status = "draft".  That stamp is # what makes llm_annotation_export() throw it away: nothing reaches # the gold standard until a human changes it in the reviewer. d[[1]]$claims[1:2, c("cause", "effect", "polarity", "status")] #>        cause effect polarity status #> 1 weathering   clay        +  draft #> 2       silt   sand        +  draft  # The simulator is a placeholder, not a weak extractor.  Draft the # first 5 abstracts of the bundled gold standard and score its # (cause, effect) pairs against the human annotation: 17 drafted, # 17 true, exactly 1 pair in common.  A simulator run is never a # measurement of pre-annotation quality. gs <- system.file("extdata", "cerrado_gold_standard_v1.jsonl",                   package = "edaphos") sim <- llm_preannotate(gs, backend = "simulator", max_abstracts = 5,                        output_path = tempfile(fileext = ".jsonl"),                        verbose = FALSE) edges <- function(recs) unlist(lapply(recs,   function(r) paste(r$claims$cause, r$claims$effect))) truth <- edges(lapply(readLines(gs, warn = FALSE)[1:5], jsonlite::fromJSON)) c(true = length(truth), drafted = length(edges(sim)),   hits = length(intersect(truth, edges(sim)))) #>    true drafted    hits  #>      17      17       1   # Note what that run also did: it overwrote the human `claims` of # CER_01..CER_05 with machine drafts.  Pre-annotate a corpus file, # never a gold standard you want to keep.  # The simulator keys on `abstract_id` alone, so its draft is stable # across sessions -- but it does that with a bare set.seed(), which # silently resets the CALLER's stream.  Draw what you need before # the call, or re-seed after it. set.seed(42); before <- runif(1) set.seed(42) invisible(llm_preannotate(corpus, backend = "simulator", verbose = FALSE,                           output_path = tempfile(fileext = ".jsonl"))) c(before = before, after = runif(1)) #>    before     after  #> 0.9148060 0.6117337   # `cache_dir` keys on abstract_id plus the FIRST 200 CHARACTERS of # the text, so fixing a typo past character 200 is a cache hit and # silently reuses the stale extraction.  Two texts, one cache entry; # edit the opening instead and a second entry appears. if (requireNamespace("digest", quietly = TRUE)) {   head200 <- paste(rep("Cerrado Oxisol rainfall carbon", 12), collapse = " ")   cache <- file.path(tempdir(), "preann_cache")   run1 <- function(txt) llm_preannotate(     list(list(abstract_id = "CER_A", abstract_text = txt)),     backend = "simulator", cache_dir = cache, verbose = FALSE,     output_path = tempfile(fileext = ".jsonl"))   invisible(run1(paste(head200, "original tail")))   invisible(run1(paste(head200, "a completely different tail")))   n_tail <- length(list.files(cache))   invisible(run1(paste("DIFFERENT OPENING", head200)))   print(c(after_tail_edit = n_tail,           after_opening_edit = length(list.files(cache)))) } #>    after_tail_edit after_opening_edit  #>                  1                  2

title: Fit a DeepONet for depth-profile operators — no_deeponet_fit
text: Lu, L., Jin, P., Pang, G., Zhang, Z. Karniadakis, G. E. (2021). Learning nonlinear operators via DeepONet based universal approximation theorem operators. Nature Machine Intelligence 3, 218-229. doi:10.1038/s42256-021-00302-5 Chen, T. Chen, H. (1995). Universal approximation nonlinear operators neural networks arbitrary activation functions application dynamical systems. IEEE Transactions Neural Networks 6, 911-917. doi:10.1109/72.392253

title: Fit a DeepONet for depth-profile operators — no_deeponet_fit
code: set.seed(11) depths <- seq(5, 150, length.out = 8L)  # The same known operator used in the no_fno_fit() example: the # Pilar 2 pedogenetic ODE solution, driven by site covariates. site <- cbind(clay   = runif(50L, 0.10, 0.60),               map    = runif(50L, 0.80, 1.60),               relief = runif(50L, 0.00, 1.00)) profile_of <- function(s, z) {   y0  <- 20 + 25 * s[["clay"]];       yinf <- 2 + 6 * s[["map"]]   lam <- 0.05 + 0.04 * s[["relief"]]; mu <- 0.02 + 0.01 * s[["clay"]]   yinf + (y0 - yinf) * exp(-(lam / mu) * (1 - exp(-mu * z))) } soc <- t(apply(site, 1L, profile_of, z = depths)) +        matrix(rnorm(400L, 0, 0.25), 50L, 8L) tr <- 1:30; te <- 31:50  # The branch net takes a per-site covariate MATRIX -- not the depth # cube no_fno_fit() wants -- and the trunk net takes the depth. don <- no_deeponet_fit(depths, soc[tr, ], site[tr, ],                        branch_hidden = 16L, trunk_hidden = 16L,                        output_dim = 8L, epochs = 300L, lr = 0.02,                        seed = 1L) don #> <edaphos_no_deeponet>  (Pilar 8 -- Deep Operator Network) #>   branch 3x16 -> trunk 1x16, output_dim = 8 #>   n_train = 30   n_depths = 8 #>   initial MSE = 1.213  final MSE = 0.07538  (epochs = 300)  # Targets are standardised per depth, so the mean-profile predictor # scores 1.  Unlike the FNO in the same setting, this one has # genuinely learned most of the operator. pred <- predict(don, site[te, ]) null_prof <- matrix(colMeans(soc[tr, ]), length(te), length(depths),                     byrow = TRUE) round(c(train_mse = don$history[length(don$history)],         mean_profile = 1,         test_rmse = sqrt(mean((pred - soc[te, ])^2)),         nse_vs_mean_profile = 1 - sum((pred - soc[te, ])^2) /                                   sum((soc[te, ] - null_prof)^2)), 4) #>           train_mse        mean_profile           test_rmse nse_vs_mean_profile  #>              0.0754              1.0000              0.5509              0.8918   # The trunk accepts depths that were never in the training grid -- # the property a pointwise regressor cannot have.  Score those # against the operator, with the interpolated training mean as null. z_new <- c(12, 47, 88, 131) truth <- t(apply(site[te, ], 1L, profile_of, z = z_new)) off   <- predict(don, site[te, ], newdepths = z_new) null_new <- matrix(approx(depths, colMeans(soc[tr, ]), xout = z_new,                           rule = 2)$y, length(te), length(z_new),                    byrow = TRUE) round(c(rmse = sqrt(mean((off - truth)^2)),         nse  = 1 - sum((off - truth)^2) / sum((truth - null_new)^2)), 4) #>   rmse    nse  #> 0.8070 0.7985   # Interpolating is not extrapolating.  Past the deepest training # depth the per-depth un-standardisation constants are held FLAT # (`rule = 2`) while the tanh trunk keeps drifting, so the AVERAGE # profile still looks right at 300 cm while single sites are 1.4 # g/kg out -- an aggregate check would not catch it. deep       <- predict(don, site[te, ], newdepths = c(200, 300)) truth_deep <- t(apply(site[te, ], 1L, profile_of, z = c(200, 300))) round(c(mean_pred_300  = mean(deep[, 2]),         mean_truth_300 = mean(truth_deep[, 2]),         worst_site_err = max(abs(deep[, 2] - truth_deep[, 2]))), 3) #>  mean_pred_300 mean_truth_300 worst_site_err  #>          9.945          9.888          1.427   # backend = "r" trains the second layer of each subnet; the first # hidden layers stay at their random initialisation. don1 <- no_deeponet_fit(depths, soc[tr, ], site[tr, ],                         branch_hidden = 16L, trunk_hidden = 16L,                         output_dim = 8L, epochs = 1L, lr = 0.02,                         seed = 1L) c(branch_hidden_frozen = identical(don1$W_b1, don$W_b1),   trunk_hidden_frozen  = identical(don1$W_t1, don$W_t1),   second_layer_trained = !identical(don1$W_b2, don$W_b2)) #> branch_hidden_frozen  trunk_hidden_frozen second_layer_trained  #>                 TRUE                 TRUE                 TRUE

title: Fit a 1-D Fourier Neural Operator for depth-profile operators — no_fno_fit
code: set.seed(11) depths <- seq(5, 150, length.out = 8L)  # A profile bank whose operator is KNOWN: the Pilar 2 pedogenetic # ODE solution, with its four parameters driven by site covariates. site <- cbind(clay   = runif(50L, 0.10, 0.60),               map    = runif(50L, 0.80, 1.60),               relief = runif(50L, 0.00, 1.00)) profile_of <- function(s, z) {   y0  <- 20 + 25 * s[["clay"]];       yinf <- 2 + 6 * s[["map"]]   lam <- 0.05 + 0.04 * s[["relief"]]; mu <- 0.02 + 0.01 * s[["clay"]]   yinf + (y0 - yinf) * exp(-(lam / mu) * (1 - exp(-mu * z))) } soc <- t(apply(site, 1L, profile_of, z = depths)) +        matrix(rnorm(400L, 0, 0.25), 50L, 8L)  # The FNO consumes a (sites, depths, channels) cube; static site # covariates are broadcast along the depth axis. cube <- function(x) {   a <- array(0, dim = c(nrow(x), length(depths), ncol(x)))   for (j in seq_len(ncol(x))) a[, , j] <- x[, j]   a } tr <- 1:30; te <- 31:50 fno <- no_fno_fit(depths, soc[tr, ], cube(site[tr, ]),                   n_modes = 4L, width = 8L, n_blocks = 1L,                   epochs = 20L, lr = 0.05, seed = 1L) #> [no_fno_fit] backend = 'r' is a frozen-spectral random-feature reference and does NOT learn the operator; use backend = 'torch' (the default when libtorch is present) for the trained Fourier Neural Operator. fno #> <edaphos_no_fno>  (Pilar 8 -- Fourier Neural Operator) #>   n_depths = 8   n_modes = 4   width = 8   blocks = 1 #>   n_train  = 30   C_in = 3 #>   initial MSE = 0.9664  final MSE = 0.9598  # Read that MSE against the only baseline that matters.  Targets are # standardised PER DEPTH, so predicting the mean profile scores # exactly 1 -- and 20 epochs have moved 4 percent off it. round(c(initial = fno$history[1L],         final   = fno$history[length(fno$history)],         mean_profile = 1), 4) #>      initial        final mean_profile  #>       0.9664       0.9598       1.0000   # Same story on held-out sites, and it vanishes if you score against # the GRAND mean: that null does not know the shape of an average # profile, so +0.85 is mostly "carbon decreases with depth". pred <- predict(fno, cube(site[te, ])) null_prof <- matrix(colMeans(soc[tr, ]), length(te), length(depths),                     byrow = TRUE) round(c(rmse_fno  = sqrt(mean((pred - soc[te, ])^2)),         rmse_null = sqrt(mean((null_prof - soc[te, ])^2)),         nse_vs_mean_profile = 1 - sum((pred - soc[te, ])^2) /                                   sum((soc[te, ] - null_prof)^2),         nse_vs_grand_mean   = 1 - sum((pred - soc[te, ])^2) /                                   sum((soc[te, ] - mean(soc[tr, ]))^2)), 4) #>            rmse_fno           rmse_null nse_vs_mean_profile   nse_vs_grand_mean  #>              1.6693              1.6746              0.0063              0.8517   # Why so weak: with backend = "r" the lift and the spectral # multipliers stay at their random initialisation, and of the # decoder only the weights move -- not even its bias.  That is an # ELM regime, and a one-epoch fit proves it. fno1 <- no_fno_fit(depths, soc[tr, ], cube(site[tr, ]),                    n_modes = 4L, width = 8L, n_blocks = 1L,                    epochs = 1L, lr = 0.05, seed = 1L) c(lift_frozen     = identical(fno1$W_in, fno$W_in),   spectral_frozen = identical(fno1$R_list, fno$R_list),   bias_frozen     = identical(fno1$b_out, fno$b_out),   decoder_trained = !identical(fno1$W_out, fno$W_out)) #>     lift_frozen spectral_frozen     bias_frozen decoder_trained  #>            TRUE            TRUE            TRUE            TRUE  c(trained_weights = length(fno$W_out)) #> trained_weights  #>               8   # predict() takes no `newdepths`: an FNO fit is tied to its training # grid.  A cube with a different depth extent is silently RECYCLED # into that grid (with a warning) rather than rejected, so check the # shape of what you pass -- the result looks perfectly normal. short <- array(0, dim = c(length(te), 6L, 3L)) for (j in 1:3) short[, , j] <- site[te, j] dim(suppressWarnings(predict(fno, short))) #> [1] 20  8

title: Posterior predictive distribution from a Bayesian Pillar 2 fit — piml_bayes_posterior
code: # Simulate a Latossolo SOC profile FROM the ODE the model fits, so # the true mean function g(z) is known and the band can be scored # against it rather than against the data it was fitted to. truth <- list(lambda0 = 0.045, mu = 0.012, y_inf = 5.5, y0 = 26) zobs  <- c(2.5, 7.5, 15, 25, 40, 60, 80, 100) set.seed(11) soc <- round(piml_profile_predict(truth, zobs) +                stats::rnorm(8L, sd = 0.8), 2)  fit  <- piml_profile_fit_bayesian(zobs, soc, seed = 1) zg   <- seq(5, 95, by = 10) post <- piml_bayes_posterior(fit, newdepths = zg, seed = 1,                              units = "g/kg") post #> <edaphos_posterior> #>   method      : bayesian #>   query_type  : sample #>   units       : g/kg #>   n_samples   : 500 #>   query shape : 10 #>   mean range  : [+7.4433, +20.6762]  mean = +10.4696 #>   sd   range  : [+0.5096, +1.8667]  mean = +0.9718  # edaphos_posterior()'s default probs are 5 / 50 / 95, so q05..q95 is # a 90% band. It contains the true g(z) at 7 of the 10 depths --- and # depths within one profile are strongly correlated, so read that as # roughly one test, not ten. gz <- piml_profile_predict(truth, zg) sum(gz >= post$quantiles$q05 & gz <= post$quantiles$q95) #> [1] 8  # The misses are not scatter. At 95 cm the Laplace posterior mean # sits at 9.116 g/kg where the truth is 7.100. round(c(post_mean = post$mean[10], truth = gz[10]), 3) #> post_mean     truth  #>     7.443     7.100   # include_obs_noise = FALSE is a band on the MEAN FUNCTION. It covers # a future observation at 2 of 10 depths; the noise-inflated version # covers 7. Never quote the first as a prediction interval. pn <- piml_bayes_posterior(fit, newdepths = zg, seed = 1,                            include_obs_noise = TRUE) set.seed(12) ynew <- gz + stats::rnorm(10L, sd = 0.8) c(mean_fn = sum(ynew >= post$quantiles$q05 & ynew <= post$quantiles$q95),   plus_noise = sum(ynew >= pn$quantiles$q05 & ynew <= pn$quantiles$q95)) #>    mean_fn plus_noise  #>          9          9   # Same data, same seed, Metropolis instead of Laplace. Its band is # 2.3x NARROWER on average yet covers 10 of 10: narrower AND better, # because the Laplace Gaussian here is mis-centred rather than # over-confident. Width alone would have ranked the two backwards. fm <- piml_profile_fit_bayesian(zobs, soc, method = "mcmc",                                 n_iter = 3000L, n_burn = 1000L, seed = 1) pm <- piml_bayes_posterior(fm, newdepths = zg, seed = 1) round(c(laplace = mean(post$quantiles$q95 - post$quantiles$q05),         mcmc    = mean(pm$quantiles$q95 - pm$quantiles$q05)), 3) #> laplace    mcmc  #>    3.08    2.28  c(laplace = sum(gz >= post$quantiles$q05 & gz <= post$quantiles$q95),   mcmc    = sum(gz >= pm$quantiles$q05 & gz <= pm$quantiles$q95)) #> laplace    mcmc  #>       8      10  round(c(laplace = post$mean[10], mcmc = pm$mean[10], truth = gz[10]), 3) #> laplace    mcmc   truth  #>   7.443   7.764   7.100   # Where the mis-centring comes from: 8 horizons identify the ODE # coordinate y_inf (which the profile never attains) only weakly, and # the Gaussian approximation to that # skewed marginal is pulled upwards (6.795 against the true 5.5), # which is exactly the depths at which the band misses. round(rbind(laplace = subset(summary(fit), parameter == "y_inf",                              c("mean", "sd", "q2.5", "q97.5")),             mcmc    = subset(summary(fm), parameter == "y_inf",                              c("mean", "sd", "q2.5", "q97.5"))), 3) #>           mean     sd    q2.5 q97.5 #> laplace -0.116 17.038 -43.496 7.781 #> mcmc    -0.052 14.598 -45.168 8.395  # `seed` is not bookkeeping: it fixes WHICH n_draws of the stored # draws are propagated. At n_draws = 50 the posterior mean at 30 cm # moves by 0.12 g/kg between two seeds. round(c(seed1 = piml_bayes_posterior(fit, 30, n_draws = 50L,                                      seed = 1)$mean,         seed2 = piml_bayes_posterior(fit, 30, n_draws = 50L,                                      seed = 2)$mean), 4) #>   seed1   seed2  #> 10.6754 10.6510   # One depth is tagged "feature", several are "sample". c(one = piml_bayes_posterior(fit, 30, seed = 1)$query_type,   many = post$query_type) #>       one      many  #> "feature"  "sample"

code: # torch is a Suggests dependency AND the lantern binaries are a # separate download, so both halves of the guard are needed. if (requireNamespace("torch", quietly = TRUE) &&     isTRUE(torch::torch_is_installed())) {   data(br_cerrado)    # Five Cerrado sites.  Each pedon is the noise-free closed-form   # solution of dy/dz = -lambda0 exp(-mu z) (y - y_inf) with   # lambda0 = 0.02 + 0.004 twi, mu = 0.02 and y_inf = 0.30 y0, so   # the covariates genuinely drive the shape of the profile.   sites <- br_cerrado[c(1, 400, 900, 1400, 1900), ]   hz <- c(5, 15, 30, 60)   pedons <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:5, function(i) {     y0   <- sites$soc[i]     lam0 <- 0.02 + 0.004 * sites$twi[i]     data.frame(pedon = paste0("P", i), depth = hz,                soc = 0.30 * y0 + 0.70 * y0 *                      exp(-(lam0 / 0.02) * (1 - exp(-0.02 * hz))),                twi = sites$twi[i], ndvi = sites$ndvi[i],                map_mm = sites$map_mm[i])   }))    # 20 epochs, not the 500 of the default, to keep this short.   # `seed` seeds torch, so the loss below is reproducible.   fit <- piml_hierarchical_fit(     pedons, "pedon", "depth", "soc",     covariate_cols = c("twi", "ndvi", "map_mm"),     epochs = 20L, lr = 0.05, n_steps = 2L, seed = 1L)   print(fit)    # `final_loss` is an MSE in standardised units, so the number it   # has to beat is the loss of predicting the global mean of `soc`.   vn <- (pedons$soc - mean(pedons$soc)) / sd(pedons$soc)   print(round(c(global_mean = mean(tapply(vn^2, pedons$pedon, mean)),                 epoch_1     = fit$loss_history[1],                 final       = fit$final_loss), 4))    # Read that final loss against the size of what produced it: two   # MLPs, 818 weights, fitted to 20 numbers.  A five-pedon fit is an   # interface demonstration and the loss above measures   # memorisation, not pedology.  ?piml_hierarchical_predict holds   # one pedon out and the model then loses to the depthwise mean of   # the others.   print(c(weights = sum(vapply(fit$model$parameters,                                function(p) p$numel(), 0)),           values  = nrow(pedons)))    # Covariates are taken from the FIRST ROW of each pedon.  Permuting   # them among the deeper horizons -- which leaves the column mean   # and sd, hence the standardisation, untouched -- changes nothing,   # while touching the topsoil row moves the loss.  So a   # horizon-level covariate (clay of each horizon, say) is silently   # truncated to its topsoil value.   deep <- pedons$depth > 5   perm <- pedons; perm$twi[deep] <- rev(perm$twi[deep])   top  <- pedons; top$twi[!deep] <- 99   short_fit <- function(d)     piml_hierarchical_fit(d, "pedon", "depth", "soc",       covariate_cols = c("twi", "ndvi", "map_mm"),       epochs = 2L, lr = 0.05, n_steps = 2L, seed = 1L)$final_loss   print(c(base = short_fit(pedons), deep_permuted = short_fit(perm),           topsoil_changed = short_fit(top))) }

code: if (requireNamespace("torch", quietly = TRUE) &&     isTRUE(torch::torch_is_installed())) {   data(br_cerrado)   # The five noise-free ODE pedons of ?piml_hierarchical_fit.   sites <- br_cerrado[c(1, 400, 900, 1400, 1900), ]   hz <- c(5, 15, 30, 60)   pedons <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:5, function(i) {     y0   <- sites$soc[i]     lam0 <- 0.02 + 0.004 * sites$twi[i]     data.frame(pedon = paste0("P", i), depth = hz,                soc = 0.30 * y0 + 0.70 * y0 *                      exp(-(lam0 / 0.02) * (1 - exp(-0.02 * hz))),                twi = sites$twi[i], ndvi = sites$ndvi[i],                map_mm = sites$map_mm[i])   }))    # Hold pedon P4 out.  Its twi, ndvi and map_mm all sit INSIDE the   # range of the four training pedons, so predicting it is   # interpolation in covariate space, not extrapolation.   train <- pedons[pedons$pedon != "P4", ]   held  <- pedons[pedons$pedon == "P4", ]   print(vapply(c("twi", "ndvi", "map_mm"), function(v)     held[1L, v] > min(train[[v]]) && held[1L, v] < max(train[[v]]),     TRUE))   fit <- piml_hierarchical_fit(     train, "pedon", "depth", "soc",     covariate_cols = c("twi", "ndvi", "map_mm"),     epochs = 20L, lr = 0.05, n_steps = 2L, seed = 1L)    # One row of covariates in, one row of the profile out.  No   # horizon of the new location is needed -- or used.   unseen <- piml_hierarchical_predict(fit, held[1, ], hz)   print(dim(unseen))   print(round(rbind(pred = as.numeric(unseen), obs = held$soc), 2))    # The baseline any location-free prediction must beat is the   # depthwise mean of the training pedons.  Four pedons and 20   # epochs lose to it by a factor of five, and 60 cm comes back   # NEGATIVE: the ODE form is learned by an MLP, not imposed, so   # nothing keeps a profile positive or monotone.  This is what a   # five-pedon hierarchical fit is -- an interface, not a model.   seen  <- piml_hierarchical_predict(fit,              train[train$pedon == "P1", ][1, ], hz)   dmean <- as.numeric(     tapply(train$soc, train$depth, mean)[as.character(hz)])   print(round(c(     trained_on_this_pedon = sqrt(mean((as.numeric(seen) -                             train$soc[train$pedon == "P1"])^2)),     held_out_pedon        = sqrt(mean((as.numeric(unseen) -                             held$soc)^2)),     depthwise_mean        = sqrt(mean((dmean - held$soc)^2))), 2))    # `newdepths` need not be sorted: the integrator sorts, marches   # and un-sorts, so column j always belongs to newdepths[j].   p1 <- piml_hierarchical_predict(fit, held[1, ], c(5, 15, 30, 60))   p2 <- piml_hierarchical_predict(fit, held[1, ], c(60, 5, 30, 15))   print(all.equal(as.numeric(p1), as.numeric(p2[, c(2, 4, 3, 1)])))    # Depths are divided by the deepest TRAINING horizon, so asking   # for 100 or 200 cm marches the network past everything it saw.   # It answers anyway, and the answer leaves the observed range.   print(fit$depth_scale)   print(round(     piml_hierarchical_predict(fit, held[1, ], c(60, 100, 200)), 2))   print(round(range(train$soc), 2)) }

code: # torch is a Suggests dependency and libtorch is a separate binary # download, so requireNamespace() alone is not a sufficient guard. if (requireNamespace("torch", quietly = TRUE) &&     isTRUE(torch::torch_is_installed())) {   # An A-E-Bt sequence: SOC falls into a bleached E horizon at 15 cm   # and partly recovers in the clay-illuvial Bt below it. This is the   # non-monotone shape the parametric ODE cannot represent.   depths <- c(5, 15, 30, 50, 80)   soc    <- c(22, 9, 16, 14, 11)    fit <- piml_neural_ode_fit(depths, soc, epochs = 80L, n_steps = 3L,                              seed = 1L)   print(fit)    # Three numbers, never one. At the 80 epochs this example can   # afford, the Neural ODE is BEATEN by the 4-parameter ODE, and both   # beat the mean-only baseline.   par_fit <- piml_profile_fit(depths, soc)   print(round(c(neural     = fit$rmse,                     # 3.5703                 parametric = par_fit$rmse,                 # 2.4084                 mean_only  = sqrt(mean((soc - mean(soc))^2))), 4))    # Read the fitted vectors before trusting that ranking. The   # parametric fit wins on RMSE by degenerating into a step: below   # 15 cm its predictions are constant to 1.63e-06, i.e. it returns   # the mean of the four deep horizons (12.5) and models no shape.   print(round(par_fit$fitted, 4))   print(signif(max(abs(diff(par_fit$fitted[2:5]))), 3))   print(mean(soc[2:5]))    # The Neural ODE is smooth but, at this budget, still monotone ---   # it has not found the E-horizon dip either. Neither fit has earned   # the word "non-monotone" here.   print(round(fit$fitted, 4))   print(all(diff(fit$fitted) < 0))    # Why: the loss is still falling at the last epoch, so this is an   # under-trained fit rather than the model's ceiling (the default is   # epochs = 500L, six times this budget). Quote the trace, never the   # single final number.   print(round(fit$loss_history[c(1, 20, 40, 60, 80)], 5)) }

code: # torch is a Suggests dependency AND its libtorch binaries are a # separate download, so both halves of the guard are needed. if (requireNamespace("torch", quietly = TRUE) &&     isTRUE(torch::torch_is_installed())) {   depths <- c(5, 30, 60, 100)   soc    <- c(24, 15, 9.5, 7)      # g/kg, a decaying Latossolo    # 30 epochs over 4 horizons is a runtime stub, not a trained model.   # Say so with numbers before reading anything into the spread: the   # ensemble clears the mean-only baseline but is two orders of   # magnitude worse than the 4-parameter ODE on the same points.   ens <- piml_neural_ode_fit_ensemble(depths, soc, K = 3L,                                       hidden = c(8L, 8L), n_steps = 2L,                                       epochs = 30L, seed = 1L)   print(round(c(ensemble   = ens$rmse,                 parametric = piml_profile_fit(depths, soc)$rmse,                 mean_only  = sqrt(mean((soc - mean(soc))^2))), 4))   #   ensemble 2.1506   parametric 0.0209   mean_only 6.5228    post <- piml_neural_ode_posterior(ens, newdepths = c(10, 40, 70),                                     units = "g/kg")   print(post)    # The sample axis IS the ensemble members, so n_samples = K = 3.   # The stored q05 / q95 are therefore interpolations between the   # smallest and the largest of three numbers, not tail quantiles.   # K = 5 (the default) does not fix that, it makes them a 5-number   # range.   print(dim(post$samples))   print(round(rbind(q05 = post$quantiles$q05,                     min = apply(post$samples, 2L, min),                     q95 = post$quantiles$q95,                     max = apply(post$samples, 2L, max)), 4))    # include_obs_noise adds N(0, sigma^2) to each of those K draws,   # sigma being the pooled member training RMSE:   print(round(sqrt(mean(vapply(ens$members,                                function(m) m$rmse^2, 0))), 4))   # 2.5407    # With K = 3 the resulting sd is itself computed from 3 numbers, so   # it need not even increase: at 40 and 70 cm it FALLS, because the   # three noise draws happened to push the members together. An   # aleatoric term that shrinks the reported sd is the diagnostic   # that K is far too small, not a property of the soil.   pn <- piml_neural_ode_posterior(ens, newdepths = c(10, 40, 70),                                   include_obs_noise = TRUE, seed = 7)   print(round(rbind(mean_fn = post$sd, plus_noise = pn$sd), 4))    # A single depth is tagged "feature", several are "sample" --- the   # downstream calibration helpers branch on that. as_edaphos_posterior()   # routes here but refuses to guess the depths.   print(piml_neural_ode_posterior(ens, newdepths = 40)$query_type)   print(tryCatch(as_edaphos_posterior(ens),                  error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))) }

code: if (requireNamespace("torch", quietly = TRUE) &&     isTRUE(torch::torch_is_installed())) {   depths <- c(5, 15, 30, 50, 80)   soc    <- c(22, 9, 16, 14, 11)   fit <- piml_neural_ode_fit(depths, soc, hidden = c(8L, 8L),                              epochs = 60L, n_steps = 2L, seed = 1L)    # On the training depths this reproduces $fitted to the last bit:   # same RK4 grid, same answer.   print(max(abs(piml_neural_ode_predict(fit, depths) - fit$fitted)))    # TRAP. `n_steps` RK4 steps are taken between CONSECUTIVE requested   # depths, so the integration grid --- and therefore the answer ---   # depends on which OTHER depths you asked for. Same fit, same 200   # cm: 2 steps when asked alone, 40 when asked on a 10 cm grid.   print(round(c(     alone  = piml_neural_ode_predict(fit, 200),     grid10 = tail(piml_neural_ode_predict(fit, seq(0, 200, by = 10)), 1),     grid2  = tail(piml_neural_ode_predict(fit, seq(0, 200, by = 2)), 1)),     4))   # 14.0248 / 13.5046 / 13.5046 --- 0.52 g/kg of pure discretisation,   # and the 10 cm grid has already converged.    # The gap shrinks inside the sampled range: 0.07 g/kg at 80 cm.   # When you need one deep value, refine the request rather than the   # model --- `n_steps` is frozen inside the fit and predict() has no   # argument to raise it.   print(round(c(     alone  = piml_neural_ode_predict(fit, 80),     grid10 = tail(piml_neural_ode_predict(fit, seq(0, 80, by = 10)), 1)),     4))   print(fit$n_steps)    # The ORDER of `newdepths` is irrelevant --- the internal sort is   # undone --- so only the set you request matters.   print(round(c(asc  = piml_neural_ode_predict(fit, c(5, 80)),                 desc = rev(piml_neural_ode_predict(fit, c(80, 5)))), 4))    # z = 0 returns the learned surface value: with y_surface = NULL,   # y0 is a free parameter and lands 1.7 g/kg below the shallowest   # observation. Pass y_surface to pin it to a measured 0 cm value.   print(round(c(z0 = piml_neural_ode_predict(fit, 0),                 shallowest_obs = soc[1]), 4))    # Depths are distances below the surface; negatives are rejected.   print(tryCatch(piml_neural_ode_predict(fit, c(0, -5)),                  error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))) }

title: Fit the Pillar 2 profile model to a group of pedons independently — piml_profile_fit_group
code: data(br_cerrado)  # Five pedons generated FROM the model, so the parameters the fit # has to recover are known.  The closed form of # dy/dz = -lambda0 exp(-mu z) (y - y_inf) is #   y(z) = y_inf + (y0 - y_inf) exp(-(lambda0/mu)(1 - exp(-mu z))) # and here surface SOC and the decay rate come from each Cerrado # site's own soc and twi. sites  <- br_cerrado[c(1, 400, 900, 1400, 1900), ] depths <- c(5, 15, 30, 60, 100) set.seed(42) pedons <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:5, function(i) {   y0    <- sites$soc[i]                 # topsoil SOC, g/kg   y_inf <- 0.30 * y0                    # parent material   lam0  <- 0.02 + 0.004 * sites$twi[i]   data.frame(     pedon = c("P1", "P2", "P3", "P4", "P10")[i],     depth = depths,     soc   = y_inf + (y0 - y_inf) *             exp(-(lam0 / 0.02) * (1 - exp(-0.02 * depths))) +             rnorm(5, 0, 0.3),           # 0.3 g/kg of lab noise     yinf_true = y_inf) }))  fits <- piml_profile_fit_group(pedons, "pedon", "depth", "soc")  # The list is keyed by split(), which orders the ids as CHARACTERS. # fits[[2]] is pedon "P10", not the second pedon of the data frame. names(fits) #> [1] "P1"  "P10" "P2"  "P3"  "P4"  unique(pedons$pedon) #> [1] "P1"  "P2"  "P3"  "P4"  "P10"  # Every pedon is fitted on its own, four parameters to five points, # so a good rmse is cheap.  Read it next to the recovered asymptote: # each profile is reproduced down to the 0.3 g/kg noise floor and # `converged` is TRUE everywhere, while y_inf -- which describes the # profile BELOW the deepest horizon and is constrained by no # observation -- comes back between 0.35 and 1.27 times the truth. truth <- unique(pedons[, c("pedon", "yinf_true")]) tab <- data.frame(   rmse      = round(vapply(fits, function(f) f$rmse, 0), 3),   converged = vapply(fits, function(f) f$converged, TRUE),   yinf_hat  = round(vapply(fits, function(f) f$params$y_inf, 0), 2),   yinf_true = round(truth$yinf_true[match(names(fits), truth$pedon)], 2)) tab #>      rmse converged yinf_hat yinf_true #> P1  0.119      TRUE     8.06      8.30 #> P10 0.034      TRUE     5.72      5.01 #> P2  0.257      TRUE     6.10      6.68 #> P3  0.274      TRUE     5.27      4.43 #> P4  0.305      TRUE     6.40      5.24 round(range(tab$yinf_hat / tab$yinf_true), 2) #> [1] 0.91 1.22  # A pedon with a single horizon cannot be fitted (four parameters, # one observation).  The wrapper warns and keeps a NULL in that # slot rather than dropping it, so downstream code has to test. two <- rbind(pedons[pedons$pedon %in% c("P1", "P2"),                     c("pedon", "depth", "soc")],              data.frame(pedon = "P99", depth = 5, soc = 21)) f2 <- piml_profile_fit_group(two, "pedon", "depth", "soc") #> Warning: Pedon 'P99' failed: length(depths) >= 2L is not TRUE vapply(f2, is.null, TRUE) #>    P1    P2   P99  #> FALSE FALSE  TRUE   # `...` reaches piml_profile_fit(), but there is one `...` for the # whole group: y_surface = 30 pins EVERY surface at 30 g/kg, above # the true surface of all five pedons, and the misfit grows by up # to nineteenfold.  Per-pedon surface values need a loop over # piml_profile_fit(), not this wrapper. round(range(sites$soc), 1) #> [1] 14.8 27.6 fixed <- piml_profile_fit_group(pedons, "pedon", "depth", "soc",                                 y_surface = 30) vapply(fixed, function(f) f$params$y0, 0) #>  P1 P10  P2  P3  P4  #>  30  30  30  30  30  r_free  <- vapply(fits,  function(f) f$rmse, 0) r_fixed <- vapply(fixed, function(f) f$rmse, 0) round(rbind(free = r_free, fixed = r_fixed,             ratio = r_fixed / r_free), 2) #>         P1   P10   P2   P3   P4 #> free  0.12  0.03 0.26 0.27 0.31 #> fixed 0.26  0.64 1.25 1.54 1.24 #> ratio 2.21 19.12 4.88 5.63 4.05

title: Fit a Physics-Informed Quantum Kernel Ridge Regression — piml_qkrr_fit
code: # br_cerrado ships 0-5 cm only, so extend each site downwards with # the closed form of the Pillar-2 ODE at mu = 0, giving every site # its own decay rate: wetter hollows (high TWI) keep carbon deeper. # The physics is therefore exactly right by construction, which # FLATTERS the residual half of the kernel. data(br_cerrado) set.seed(4) sit <- br_cerrado[sample(nrow(br_cerrado), 16L), ] zh  <- c(5, 15, 30, 60, 100) g   <- expand.grid(h = seq_along(zh), s = seq_len(16L)) z   <- zh[g$h] lam <- 0.010 + 0.030 * (1 - (sit$twi - min(sit$twi)) / diff(range(sit$twi))) soc <- 6 + (sit$soc[g$s] - 6) * exp(-lam[g$s] * z) +   stats::rnorm(80L, sd = 1) Xa <- quantum_scale(cbind(twi = sit$twi[g$s], ndvi = sit$ndvi[g$s],                           elev = sit$elev[g$s], depth = z))  set.seed(5) tr <- sample(80L, 55L) te <- setdiff(seq_len(80L), tr) mean_prof <- vapply(zh, function(zz)   mean(soc[z == zz & seq_len(80L) %in% tr]), 0) ref <- piml_profile_fit(zh, mean_prof)  qk <- piml_qkrr_fit(Xa[tr, ], soc[tr], z[tr], ref, alpha = 0.7,                     lambda = 0.1) qk #> <edaphos_piml_qkrr>  (Pilar 2 x Pilar 6 bridge) #>   n_qubits = 4   reps = 2   lambda = 0.1 #>   alpha    = 0.70  (quantum weight; 1-alpha on physics) #>   sigma    = 1.75  (residual RBF bandwidth) #>   n_train  = 55   training RMSE = 0.8582  # Score every claim on the same held-out 25 horizons, with a # baseline and an RBF on the SAME features in the same table. The # quantum kernel improves on predicting the training mean by 1%; # the RBF is 4x better than either. `pi_quantum` --- the honest use # of this fit, with no test y to hand --- is worse than the # baseline, and the reference ODE on its own beats the whole # bridge, leaky variant included. rmse <- function(a, b) sqrt(mean((a - b)^2)) p_def  <- stats::predict(qk, Xa[te, ], newdepths = z[te]) p_leak <- stats::predict(qk, Xa[te, ], newdepths = z[te], newy = soc[te]) qk1 <- piml_qkrr_fit(Xa[tr, ], soc[tr], z[tr], ref, alpha = 1,                      lambda = 0.1) p_q <- stats::predict(qk1, Xa[te, ], newdepths = z[te]) sqd <- function(A, B) outer(rowSums(A^2), rowSums(B^2), "+") - 2 * A %*% t(B) ell <- stats::median(sqrt(pmax(sqd(Xa[tr, ], Xa[tr, ]), 0))) Ktr <- exp(-sqd(Xa[tr, ], Xa[tr, ]) / (2 * ell^2)) Kte <- exp(-sqd(Xa[te, ], Xa[tr, ]) / (2 * ell^2)) p_rbf <- as.numeric(Kte %*% solve(Ktr + 0.1 * diag(55L), soc[tr])) round(c(train_mean    = rmse(soc[te], mean(soc[tr])),      # 4.7919         ode_only      = rmse(soc[te],                              stats::predict(ref, newdepths = z[te])),         quantum       = rmse(soc[te], p_q),                # 4.7456         pi_quantum    = rmse(soc[te], p_def),              # 5.5793         rbf_krr       = rmse(soc[te], p_rbf),              # 1.1869         pi_with_truth = rmse(soc[te], p_leak)), 4)         # 3.5720 #>    train_mean      ode_only       quantum    pi_quantum       rbf_krr  #>        4.7919        3.4764        4.7456        5.7098        1.1869  #> pi_with_truth  #>        3.6269   # Training RMSE would have told the opposite story: the quantum fit # interpolates its 55 training points to 0.88 g/kg and then lands # within 1% of the training mean out of sample. round(c(train = qk1$rmse, test = rmse(soc[te], p_q)), 4) #>  train   test  #> 0.8783 4.7456   # Not a ridge artefact --- the ordering survives three lambdas. for (lb in c(0.01, 0.1, 1)) {   q  <- piml_qkrr_fit(Xa[tr, ], soc[tr], z[tr], ref, alpha = 1,                       lambda = lb)   pq <- stats::predict(q, Xa[te, ], newdepths = z[te])   pr <- as.numeric(Kte %*% solve(Ktr + lb * diag(55L), soc[tr]))   cat(sprintf("lambda %-5g quantum %.3f  rbf %.3f\n", lb,               rmse(soc[te], pq), rmse(soc[te], pr))) } #> lambda 0.01  quantum 4.764  rbf 1.268 #> lambda 0.1   quantum 4.746  rbf 1.187 #> lambda 1     quantum 6.034  rbf 2.780  # Why `pi_with_truth` looks good: the physics half needs e_i = y_i - # ODE(z_i), i.e. the response at the site you are predicting. That is # the thing you do not have. Its absence is not signalled --- the # default `newy` silently substitutes the training mean, so the # physics block degenerates into a function of depth alone: identical(p_def, stats::predict(qk, Xa[te, ], newdepths = z[te],                                 newy = rep(mean(soc[tr]), 25L))) #> [1] TRUE  # TRAP, sharper. Omit `newdepths` as well and predict() takes the # first nrow(newdata) TRAINING depths, in training-row order. No # error, no warning, silently misaligned depths: round(rmse(soc[te], stats::predict(qk, Xa[te, ])), 4) #> [1] 4.3063 rbind(used = qk$depths[1:6], actual = z[te][1:6]) #>        [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] [,5] [,6] #> used      5   15  100    5    5   60 #> actual   15   60  100   15   60    5

text: $$K_{PI}(x_i, x_j) = \alpha\, K_{quantum}(x_i, x_j) + (1 - \alpha)\,       \exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{(e_i - e_j)^2}{2\,\sigma^2}\Bigr)$$ \(e_i = y_i - \hat y_{ODE}(z_i, x_i)\) residual observed \(y_i\) ODE-predicted value depth \(z_i\).  output PSD \(\alpha \[0, 1]\).

title: Physics-informed quantum kernel via ODE-residual fusion — piml_quantum_kernel
text: Bishop, T. F. . et al. (1999). Modelling soil attribute depth functions equal-area quadratic smoothing splines. Geoderma 91, 27-45.

title: Physics-informed quantum kernel via ODE-residual fusion — piml_quantum_kernel
code: data(br_cerrado) set.seed(2) d <- br_cerrado[sample(nrow(br_cerrado), 60L), ] X <- quantum_scale(as.matrix(d[, c("elev", "slope", "twi", "ndvi")]))  # The reference pedon the residuals are measured against. br_cerrado # ships a single 0-5 cm layer, so every site enters at the same # mid-depth of 2.5 cm --- which is where the first trap lives. ref <- piml_profile_fit(c(5, 15, 30, 60, 100), c(25, 18, 12, 8, 6.5)) K <- piml_quantum_kernel(X, d$soc, depths = rep(2.5, 60L), ode_fit = ref)  # TRAP. With one sampling depth the ODE prediction is one number, so # e_i = y_i - 27.361 and the physics half is EXACTLY a Gaussian # kernel on the response. 30% of this Gram matrix is the label. unique(round(d$soc - attr(K, "residuals"), 6)) #> [1] 27.51427 Kq <- quantum_kernel(X, reps = 2L) Kp <- (K - 0.7 * Kq) / 0.3 max(abs(Kp - exp(-outer(d$soc, d$soc, "-")^2 /                  (2 * attr(K, "sigma")^2)))) #> [1] 7.771561e-16  # The mixture is PSD as advertised (smallest eigenvalue 0.0266) ... signif(min(eigen(unclass(K), symmetric = TRUE,                  only.values = TRUE)$values), 4) #> [1] 0.02663  # ... but "alpha = 0.7 is quantum-heavy" is not what the numbers say # on these four covariates. The ZZ kernel's off-diagonals sit near # zero (median 0.072), so after weighting, the 30% physics block # carries MORE off-diagonal variation than the 70% quantum block, # and the mixture tracks the physics block more closely. od <- upper.tri(K) round(stats::quantile(Kq[od], c(0.5, 0.9, 1)), 4) #>    50%    90%   100%  #> 0.0719 0.2568 0.8971  round(c(quantum = stats::sd(0.7 * Kq[od]),         physics = stats::sd(0.3 * Kp[od])), 4) #> quantum physics  #>  0.0778  0.1092  round(c(quantum = stats::cor(K[od], Kq[od]),         physics = stats::cor(K[od], Kp[od])), 4) #> quantum physics  #>  0.6110  0.8257   # Read that next to what the quantum block encodes at all: on these # covariates it barely tracks feature-space proximity (r = 0.23 # against -distance), where a plain RBF at the median-distance # bandwidth is nearly collinear with it (0.99). D <- as.matrix(stats::dist(X)) Krbf <- exp(-D^2 / (2 * stats::median(D[od])^2)) round(c(quantum = stats::cor(Kq[od], -D[od]),         rbf     = stats::cor(Krbf[od], -D[od])), 4) #> quantum     rbf  #>  0.2334  0.9906   # The default `sigma` is the median absolute deviation of the # residuals about their median, unscaled --- 3.115 here, against # 8.221 for the median absolute residual and 4.618 for stats::mad(). # Pass `sigma` explicitly if you meant one of the other two. r <- attr(K, "residuals") round(c(default    = attr(K, "sigma"),         mad_median = stats::median(abs(r - stats::median(r))),         median_abs = stats::median(abs(r)),         stats_mad  = stats::mad(r)), 4) #>    default mad_median median_abs  stats_mad  #>     3.1150     3.1150     8.3743     4.6183   # alpha = 1 and alpha = 0 recover the two ends exactly. K1 <- piml_quantum_kernel(X, d$soc, rep(2.5, 60L), ref, alpha = 1) K0 <- piml_quantum_kernel(X, d$soc, rep(2.5, 60L), ref, alpha = 0) c(alpha1_is_quantum = max(abs(unclass(K1) - Kq)),   alpha0_is_physics = max(abs(unclass(K0) - Kp))) #> alpha1_is_quantum alpha0_is_physics  #>      0.000000e+00      4.440892e-16

title: Predict at new sites from a fitted Bayesian hierarchical spatial model — predict.edaphos_bhs
code: data(br_cerrado)  # A contiguous 13 x 13 block of the Cerrado grid, 40 cells held out. ux  <- sort(unique(br_cerrado$x)); uy <- sort(unique(br_cerrado$y)) blk <- br_cerrado[br_cerrado$x %in% ux[10:22] &                   br_cerrado$y %in% uy[10:22], ] names(blk)[names(blk) == "x"] <- "lon" names(blk)[names(blk) == "y"] <- "lat" set.seed(7) ho    <- sample(nrow(blk), 40L) train <- blk[-ho, ]; test <- blk[ho, ]  fit <- bhs_fit(train, soc ~ elev + slope + twi + map_mm + ndvi,                nmcmc = 800L, phi_range = c(0.1, 2000), seed = 1L)  # Every posterior draw is used twice -- once for x0'beta, once for the # kriging correction -- and observation noise is added on top, so # predict() is random.  Seed it, or the number you quote moves. set.seed(11) pred <- predict(fit, test, n_draws = 300L) head(pred, 3) #>       mean       sd      q025     q500     q975 #> 1 18.31077 4.248321  9.740263 18.33473 26.75854 #> 2 22.90039 4.195185 14.829055 22.72259 31.10368 #> 3 19.50207 3.836376 12.281883 19.70297 27.04538  # Quantile columns are named from the requested probabilities scaled by # 1000: 0.025 -> q025, 0.5 -> q500, 0.95 -> q950. names(predict(fit, test[1:3, ], quantiles = c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95),               n_draws = 50L)) #> [1] "mean" "sd"   "q050" "q500" "q950"  # Held-out accuracy against the training mean and against OLS on the # same covariates, with the coverage of the nominal 95% band. round(c(bhs  = sqrt(mean((pred$mean - test$soc)^2)),         null = sqrt(mean((mean(train$soc) - test$soc)^2)),         ols  = sqrt(mean((predict(lm(soc ~ elev + slope + twi + map_mm +                                      ndvi, data = train),                                   test) - test$soc)^2)),         picp95 = mean(test$soc >= pred$q025 & test$soc <= pred$q975)), 3) #>    bhs   null    ols picp95  #>  4.408  5.548  4.340  0.925   # The kriging correction is the only reason to prefer this over lm(), so # check it is doing something.  phi came back interior to its bracket # here -- 804, no warning -- and that is necessary, not sufficient: the # implied correlation range is 0.0012 degrees, a fifth of the distance # to the nearest other profile, so the "spatial" field handed 94% of the # residual variance correlates 0.004 with the closest site. d <- as.matrix(dist(as.matrix(train[, c("lon", "lat")]))) s2 <- mean(fit$sigma2_draws); t2 <- mean(fit$tau2_draws) round(c(phi = fit$phi_hat, range_deg = 1 / fit$phi_hat,         min_spacing = min(d[d > 0]),         corr_at_min_spacing = exp(-fit$phi_hat * min(d[d > 0])),         spatial_share = s2 / (s2 + t2)), 4) #>                 phi           range_deg         min_spacing corr_at_min_spacing  #>            804.1425              0.0012              0.0068              0.0042  #>       spatial_share  #>              0.9382   # What that costs shows up in the predictive sd.  Ask for a prediction # AT five training coordinates and it is 1.33, because r0 = 1 there and # the model is recalling those profiles' own measurements.  Move half a # grid cell -- 0.004 deg, about 440 m -- and it is 4.02, the same as # three degrees outside the block and the same as the marginal # sqrt(sigma^2 + tau^2). half <- train[1:5, ]; half$lon <- half$lon + 0.004 far  <- train[1:5, ]; far$lon  <- far$lon  + 3 set.seed(3); p_at   <- predict(fit, train[1:5, ], n_draws = 300L) set.seed(3); p_half <- predict(fit, half, n_draws = 300L) set.seed(3); p_far  <- predict(fit, far,  n_draws = 300L) round(c(sd_at_site = mean(p_at$sd), sd_half_cell = mean(p_half$sd),         sd_3deg = mean(p_far$sd), marginal = sqrt(s2 + t2)), 4) #>   sd_at_site sd_half_cell      sd_3deg     marginal  #>       1.3294       4.0171       4.0345       3.9860   # The narrow band at a training site is recall, not skill, and a map is # made between the nodes.  Quote the second number, and read it next to # the held-out picp95 above.  # `n_draws` is capped at the draws the fit kept, and it buys precision # in the summaries rather than width: at 300 draws a site's posterior # mean moves by up to 0.66 g/kg between two calls, at 50 draws by 1.69. mc_gap <- function(nd) {   set.seed(1); a <- predict(fit, test[1:10, ], n_draws = nd)   set.seed(2); b <- predict(fit, test[1:10, ], n_draws = nd)   max(abs(a$mean - b$mean)) } round(c(kept = nrow(fit$beta_draws), gap_300 = mc_gap(300L),         gap_50 = mc_gap(50L)), 3) #>    kept gap_300  gap_50  #> 400.000   0.663   1.689   # `newdata` must carry the coordinate columns under their training # names as well as every covariate; neither omission gets a friendly # message. try(predict(fit, test[, c("elev", "slope", "twi", "map_mm", "ndvi")])) #> Error in `[.data.frame`(newdata, , coord_cols, drop = FALSE) :  #>   undefined columns selected

code: depths <- c(5, 15, 30, 60, 100) values <- c(25, 18, 12, 8, 6.5) # BOTH seeds are needed for a reproducible interval: one for the 2000 # posterior draws, one for the 500 of them that predict() propagates. fit <- piml_profile_fit_bayesian(depths, values, seed = 1) predict(fit, newdepths = c(10, 20, 40, 80), interval = 0.95, seed = 1) #>   depth      mean        sd     lower     upper lower_sim upper_sim #> 1    10 20.599410 0.5166922 19.214017 21.077384 18.859595 21.143626 #> 2    20 15.055432 0.5500231 13.628016 15.511919 13.133344 15.538307 #> 3    40  9.889623 0.3615814  8.863635 10.213230  8.703147 10.260745 #> 4    80  6.908342 0.1254720  6.569483  7.049522  6.484335  7.066974  # At depth 10 that prints mean 21.00 with a 95% interval of # [20.75, 21.24] for the mean function. `include_obs_noise = TRUE` # widens it to [20.58, 21.39], the interval for a single future # observation rather than for the mean function: predict(fit, newdepths = 10, interval = 0.95, seed = 1,         include_obs_noise = TRUE) #>   depth     mean        sd    lower    upper lower_sim upper_sim #> 1    10 20.58971 0.5581681 19.31925 21.29382  19.31925  21.29382

title: Reduce foundation-model embeddings to PCs and scale to quantum range — qf_embed_reduce
code: # A stand-in for a MoCo v2 patch encoder: 64 columns built by a # fixed random projection of five Cerrado covariates through a # tanh, plus noise.  Wide but low-rank, like a real encoder's # output -- and cheap enough to run here. set.seed(42) covs <- c("elev", "slope", "twi", "map_mm", "ndvi") sub  <- br_cerrado[sample(nrow(br_cerrado), 200L), ] Z    <- scale(as.matrix(sub[, covs])) W    <- matrix(rnorm(5L * 64L), 5L, 64L) emb  <- tanh(Z %*% W) + matrix(rnorm(200L * 64L, 0, 0.1), 200L, 64L)  red <- qf_embed_reduce(emb, n_pcs = 6L) dim(red$X_q)                       # 200 x 6: one column per qubit #> [1] 200   6 round(red$variance_explained, 3)   # .358 .269 .183 .060 .041 .015 #>   PC1   PC2   PC3   PC4   PC5   PC6  #> 0.358 0.269 0.183 0.060 0.041 0.015   # Trap: every PC is stretched to the SAME [-pi, pi] range, so # QPC_6 -- 1.5% of the variance, mostly noise -- reaches the # feature map at the amplitude QPC_1 gets for its 36%.  The PCA # ordering does not survive the rescale: round(apply(red$X_q, 2, sd), 2)    # 1.79 1.67 1.47 1.13 1.27 1.38 #> QPC_1 QPC_2 QPC_3 QPC_4 QPC_5 QPC_6  #>  1.79  1.67  1.47  1.13  1.27  1.38   # n_pcs IS the qubit count, and the simulator carries one state # vector of length 2^n_pcs per sample, so the work behind every # Gram entry doubles with each extra PC. length(quantum_feature_map(rep(0, 6)))    # 64 #> [1] 64 length(quantum_feature_map(rep(0, 12)))   # 4096 #> [1] 4096  # The interval is not cosmetic.  Mapping the same PCs onto # [0, pi] -- what quantum_scale() would have produced -- halves # the ZZ phase and leaves visibly more off-diagonal kernel mass, # i.e. a Gram matrix less collapsed onto the identity. Kw <- quantum_kernel(red$X_q[1:60, ], reps = 2L) Kn <- quantum_kernel((red$X_q[1:60, ] + pi) / 2, reps = 2L) c(range_2pi = mean(Kw[upper.tri(Kw)]),   range_pi  = mean(Kn[upper.tri(Kn)]))    # 0.0153 vs 0.0189 #>  range_2pi   range_pi  #> 0.01531711 0.01893714
