title: Compare quantum, RBF, and linear kernels on the same feature set — qf_kernel_compare
code: # Same stand-in MoCo encoder output as in qf_embed_reduce(), on # 60 Cerrado pixels so the three Gram matrices stay 60 x 60. set.seed(42) covs <- c("elev", "slope", "twi", "map_mm", "ndvi") sub  <- br_cerrado[sample(nrow(br_cerrado), 60L), ] Z    <- scale(as.matrix(sub[, covs])) W    <- matrix(rnorm(5L * 64L), 5L, 64L) emb  <- tanh(Z %*% W) + matrix(rnorm(60L * 64L, 0, 0.1), 60L, 64L)  cmp <- qf_kernel_compare(qf_embed_reduce(emb, n_pcs = 6L)$X_q) names(cmp)          # K_quantum, K_rbf, K_linear, rbf_sigma, ... #> [1] "K_quantum"   "K_rbf"       "K_linear"    "rbf_sigma"   "diagnostics" cmp$diagnostics #>                pair   frob effrank_quantum effrank_rbf effrank_linear #> 1    quantum_vs_rbf 37.158           59.22        4.62           5.79 #> 2 quantum_vs_linear 62.070           59.22        4.62           5.79 #> 3     rbf_vs_linear 62.449           59.22        4.62           5.79  # Read that table carefully.  Only `pair` and `frob` vary by row; # the three effrank_* columns are per-KERNEL and are repeated # identically on all three rows. nrow(unique(cmp$diagnostics[, c("effrank_quantum", "effrank_rbf")])) #> [1] 1  # And effrank_quantum ~ 59 out of n = 60 is not evidence that the # quantum kernel is richer than the RBF's ~ 4.6.  It is evidence # that it is nearly the IDENTITY: at 6 qubits the ZZFeatureMap # states are close to mutually orthogonal, so K -> I, whose # entropy-based effective rank is exactly n. frob <- function(A, B) sqrt(sum((A - B)^2)) c(to_identity = frob(cmp$K_quantum, diag(60)),   # 1.33   to_rbf      = frob(cmp$K_quantum, cmp$K_rbf))  # 37.16 #> to_identity      to_rbf  #>    1.325009   37.157898   # The collapse is driven by the qubit count, not by `reps`.  Off- # diagonal kernel mass roughly halves per PC added, while the RBF # on the identical features holds at 0.61-0.63 throughout. off <- function(K) mean(K[upper.tri(K)]) t(vapply(2:6, function(p) {   k <- qf_kernel_compare(qf_embed_reduce(emb, n_pcs = p)$X_q)   c(n_pcs = p, quantum = off(k$K_quantum), rbf = off(k$K_rbf)) }, numeric(3)))                  # quantum .314 .137 .065 .032 .016 #>      n_pcs    quantum       rbf #> [1,]     2 0.31388334 0.6091690 #> [2,]     3 0.13679924 0.6297054 #> [3,]     4 0.06548216 0.6296694 #> [4,]     5 0.03222972 0.6262061 #> [5,]     6 0.01583906 0.6259345  # Deepening the circuit does not undo it -- `reps` leaves the # off-diagonal mass where 6 qubits put it: X6 <- qf_embed_reduce(emb, n_pcs = 6L)$X_q vapply(c(1L, 2L, 4L), function(r)   off(qf_kernel_compare(X6, reps = r)$K_quantum), numeric(1)) #> [1] 0.01622202 0.01583906 0.01610353  # A kernel that close to the identity gives kernel ridge nothing # to interpolate with: see the qf_krr_fit() example, where the # 6-PC fit reproduces its training set and then predicts the # training mean everywhere else.

title: Benchmark quantum-foundation KRR against classical baselines — qf_krr_benchmark
code: # Stand-in MoCo encoder output plus the five raw covariates it was # built from, over 200 Cerrado pixels, predicting SOC (g/kg). set.seed(42) covs <- c("elev", "slope", "twi", "map_mm", "ndvi") sub  <- br_cerrado[sample(nrow(br_cerrado), 200L), ] Z    <- scale(as.matrix(sub[, covs])) W    <- matrix(rnorm(5L * 64L), 5L, 64L) emb  <- tanh(Z %*% W) + matrix(rnorm(200L * 64L, 0, 0.1), 200L, 64L) y    <- sub$soc tr   <- 1:140; te <- 141:200  # set.seed() even with a fixed split: arm 1 draws 500 ranger trees # from the ambient RNG stream, so its RMSE moves without one. set.seed(7) bm <- qf_krr_benchmark(emb, as.matrix(sub[, covs]), y,                        train_ix = tr, test_ix = te,                        n_pcs = 5L, reps = 2L, lambda = 0.1) bm[, c("method", "rmse", "r2")] #>                             method     rmse          r2 #> rf         ranger (raw covariates) 5.051015  0.50603423 #> rbf      RBF-KRR on foundation PCs 4.981030  0.51962777 #> qraw Quantum KRR on raw covariates 6.798584  0.10509592 #> qf   Quantum KRR on foundation PCs 7.387175 -0.05656509 #   ranger (raw covariates)         5.02   0.513 #   RBF-KRR on foundation PCs       4.98   0.520 #   Quantum KRR on raw covariates   6.80   0.105 #   Quantum KRR on foundation PCs   7.39  -0.057  # The bridge's own arm comes last, and it loses to the null the # whole table has to clear first: edaphos_rmse(y[te], rep(mean(y[tr]), length(te)))   # 7.21 #> [1] 7.208675 # Only the two classical arms beat it.  The quantum lift over the # foundation PCs is worse than predicting the training mean here, # which is what a Gram matrix collapsed onto the identity looks # like downstream -- see qf_kernel_compare().  # Three things that make this table less of a head-to-head than # it reads: #  * arms 2 and 3 fit their preprocessing (the PCA, and #    quantum_scale()'s column min/max) on ALL rows, test included; #    arms 1 and 4 only ever see the training rows. #  * arm 3 quantum-encodes the FIRST n_pcs covariate columns, in #    whatever order the matrix happens to have -- not a selection. colnames(as.matrix(sub[, covs]))[1:5] #> [1] "elev"   "slope"  "twi"    "map_mm" "ndvi"   #  * if ncol(covariates) < n_pcs, arm 3 is dropped in silence and #    you get a three-row table with no warning: set.seed(7) nrow(qf_krr_benchmark(emb, as.matrix(sub[, covs[1:3]]), y,                       train_ix = tr, test_ix = te,                       n_pcs = 5L, reps = 2L, lambda = 0.1))   # 3 #> [1] 3

title: Quantum Kernel Ridge Regression on foundation embeddings — qf_krr_fit
code: # Stand-in MoCo encoder output over 200 Cerrado pixels; the # target is the bundled SOC column (g/kg, 0-5 cm). set.seed(42) covs <- c("elev", "slope", "twi", "map_mm", "ndvi") sub  <- br_cerrado[sample(nrow(br_cerrado), 200L), ] Z    <- scale(as.matrix(sub[, covs])) W    <- matrix(rnorm(5L * 64L), 5L, 64L) emb  <- tanh(Z %*% W) + matrix(rnorm(200L * 64L, 0, 0.1), 200L, 64L) y    <- sub$soc tr   <- 1:140; te <- 141:200  fit <- qf_krr_fit(emb[tr, ], y[tr], n_pcs = 6L, reps = 2L,                   lambda = 0.1) fit #> <edaphos_qf_krr>  (Pillar 4 x Pillar 6 bridge) #>   n_pcs  = 6  (qubits = 6) #>   reps   = 2 #>   lambda = 0.100 #>   n_train = 140 pred <- predict(fit, emb[te, ])  # The only number that matters is next to the achievable null -- # predicting the training mean at every unseen pixel. c(qf_krr = edaphos_rmse(y[te], pred),   train_mean = edaphos_rmse(y[te], rep(mean(y[tr]), length(te)))) #>     qf_krr train_mean  #>   7.449385   7.208675  # 7.45 vs 7.21 g/kg: the fit is WORSE than the mean, and edaphos_r2(y[te], pred)                       # -0.074, i.e. < 0 #> [1] -0.07443565  # Two diagnostics that have to be read side by side to see why. # In sample the fit is near-perfect; out of sample its predictions # barely move off the training mean.  With a 6-qubit Gram matrix # this close to the identity (see qf_kernel_compare()), KRR can # only memorise: every test pixel is near-orthogonal to every # training pixel, so the kernel expansion contributes ~ nothing # and prediction falls back on the intercept. c(rmse_in_sample = fit$fit$rmse,              # 0.63   rmse_held_out  = edaphos_rmse(y[te], pred)) # 7.45 #> rmse_in_sample  rmse_held_out  #>      0.6322467      7.4493853  c(sd_pred = sd(pred), sd_truth = sd(y[te]))   # 1.11 vs 7.25 #>  sd_pred sd_truth  #> 1.113525 7.247360   # Fewer qubits concentrate less, but do not rescue it: over # n_pcs 3-6, reps 1-2 and lambda 1e-3..1 the best held-out R2 # this fixture produced was 0.012 -- the training mean, again. fit4 <- qf_krr_fit(emb[tr, ], y[tr], n_pcs = 4L, reps = 2L,                    lambda = 1) edaphos_r2(y[te], predict(fit4, emb[te, ]))   # 0.012 #> [1] 0.01240346  # Trap in predict(): the PCA centre, rotation and pi-rescale all # come from the TRAINING rows, so a held-out pixel can encode # outside the [-pi, pi] the feature map was scaled for.  Nothing # errors and nothing warns -- the encoding just extrapolates, and # the stored bounds are the only way to notice: rng <- range(fit$reduction$range_min, fit$reduction$range_max) rng                              # training PC span, pre-rescale #> [1] -8.441388  8.382292  # Keep column names on newdata as well: an unnamed matrix against # a named training embedding falls back to positional alignment # and warns "NAs introduced by coercion".

title: Quantum KRR over GAT node embeddings (Pilar 6 x Pilar 10) — qf_krr_on_gat_embeddings
code: set.seed(1) sub <- br_cerrado[sample(nrow(br_cerrado), 150L), ] names(sub)[names(sub) == "x"] <- "lon" names(sub)[names(sub) == "y"] <- "lat" g <- gnn_build_graph(sub, k = 6L,                      feature_cols = c("elev", "slope", "twi",                                       "map_mm", "ndvi"))  # Pillar 10 transductively: the graph spans all 150 pixels, the # regression head sees only the first 100 SOC labels. tr <- 1:100; te <- 101:150 y_obs <- sub$soc; y_obs[te] <- NA gat <- gnn_fit(g, y_obs, hidden = 8L, n_heads = 2L, n_layers = 1L,                epochs = 40L, seed = 1L) c(gat        = edaphos_rmse(sub$soc[te], predict(gat)[te]),   train_mean = edaphos_rmse(sub$soc[te], rep(mean(sub$soc[tr]), 50))) #>        gat train_mean  #>   4.740551   6.271455  # 4.77 vs 6.27 g/kg -- the GAT is ahead of the null it must beat  # Now the hand-off, and the first thing it demands: one y per NODE. # There is no train_mask here, so the quantum KRR is fitted on all # 150 labels, including the 50 the GAT was never shown. qk <- qf_krr_on_gat_embeddings(gat, sub$soc, n_pcs = 5L, reps = 1L,                                lambda = 0.5) qk #> <edaphos_qf_krr_gat>  (Pilar 6 x Pilar 10) #>   GAT emb_dim   : 8 #>   qubits (PCs)  : 5 #>   reps          : 1   lambda = 0.5 #>   n_train       : 150 c(nodes = nrow(gat$emb), gat_trained_on = gat$n_train,   krr_trained_on = qk$n_train)                    # 150, 100, 150 #>          nodes gat_trained_on krr_trained_on  #>            150            100            150   # Which makes every number the returned object can produce an # in-sample one.  This looks held out and is not: edaphos_rmse(sub$soc[te], predict(qk, newdata = gat$emb[te, ]))  # 2.93 #> [1] 2.761911 edaphos_rmse(sub$soc, predict(qk))   # 2.73, predict() with no #> [1] 2.666344                                      # newdata scores the training                                      # embeddings  # The honest version: same embedding, KRR refitted on the 100 rows # the GAT actually trained on, read against the training mean. qk_tr <- qf_krr_fit(gat$emb[tr, ], sub$soc[tr], n_pcs = 5L,                     reps = 1L, lambda = 0.5) p <- predict(qk_tr, gat$emb[te, ]) c(qf_krr     = edaphos_rmse(sub$soc[te], p),   train_mean = edaphos_rmse(sub$soc[te], rep(mean(sub$soc[tr]), 50)),   r2         = edaphos_r2(sub$soc[te], p)) #>     qf_krr train_mean         r2  #>  6.5263153  6.2714550 -0.1192319  # 6.32, 6.27, -0.049: worse than predicting the mean everywhere. # The GAT embedding the bridge feeds the ZZFeatureMap is 8-dim and # nearly rank-2 -- the first two PCs hold 94 % of its variance -- # so five qubits are encoding almost no independent directions. round(qk$reduction$variance_explained, 3) #>   PC1   PC2   PC3   PC4   PC5  #> 0.622 0.324 0.040 0.013 0.002

title: Build a quantum Hamiltonian from Pauli-string coefficients — quantum_hamiltonian
code: if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{ # Everything in Pillar 6 talks to a live Qiskit stack through # reticulate; install it once with #   reticulate::py_install(c("qiskit", "qiskit-aer", #                            "qiskit-algorithms"), pip = TRUE)  # Two non-interacting spins with different Zeeman energies. h <- quantum_hamiltonian(c("ZI" = 1, "IZ" = 2)) h  # Qubit order is the trap.  The LEFTMOST character is the HIGHEST # qubit index, so the coefficient 2 sits on qubit 0, not qubit 1. # The diagonal, in Qiskit's |q1 q0> basis order (00, 01, 10, 11), # comes back as 3, -1, 1, -3: flipping qubit 0 costs 4 = 2 * 2, # flipping qubit 1 only 2 = 2 * 1. Re(diag(h$op$to_matrix()))  # `n_qubits` is inferred from the FIRST string alone, so a ragged # set of terms surfaces as an invalid-Pauli error naming the # second string, never as a length mismatch. try(quantum_hamiltonian(c("ZZI" = 1, "ZZ" = 1)))  # The alphabet is {I, X, Y, Z} and it is case sensitive. try(quantum_hamiltonian(c("zz" = 1)))  # An all-identity term is a pure energy offset: it shifts every # eigenvalue and no variational circuit can lower it. quantum_vqe_exact(quantum_hamiltonian(c("IIII" = -2.5)))   # -2.5  # Repeated Pauli strings are NOT rejected -- SparsePauliOp adds # them up, so this is the single term ZI with coefficient 3 and a # ground state at -3.  De-duplicate upstream if that is not what # you meant; nothing downstream will warn you. quantum_vqe_exact(quantum_hamiltonian(c("ZI" = 1, "ZI" = 2)))  # -3 } # }

Optionally, chemical core orbitals frozen FreezeCoreTransformer — cheap orbital-space-neutral reduction typically halves qubit count first-row organics. frontier orbitals projected (num_active_electrons, num_active_orbitals) active space via ActiveSpaceTransformer, keeping chemistry local coordination event user cares (e.g. Fe-O-C charge transfer organo-mineral complex). resulting second-quantised Hamiltonian mapped qubits chosen fermion--qubit transformation; default ParityMapper used known particle numbers, taper two qubits Z2 symmetry reduction.

code: if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{ h2 <- quantum_hamiltonian_h2() h2                                  # 2 qubits, 5 Pauli terms  # The reference every VQE run in this package is scored against: # the exact STO-3G ground state at 0.735 A. round(quantum_vqe_exact(h2), 6)                      # -1.857275  # -1.052373 of that is the "II" term, a constant no ansatz can # touch.  Only -0.804902 Ha is what the circuit actually has to # find, so a relative error quoted against -1.857 flatters the # fit by a factor of 2.31. h2_var <- quantum_hamiltonian(   h2$pauli_terms[names(h2$pauli_terms) != "II"]) round(quantum_vqe_exact(h2_var), 6)                  # -0.804902 round(quantum_vqe_exact(h2) / quantum_vqe_exact(h2_var), 2)  # 2.31  # Four levels only, so the whole spectrum is inspectable.  The # 0.6127 Ha gap to the first excited state is what makes H2 a # forgiving benchmark: shot noise of order 0.02 Ha cannot confuse # the two.  Read it next to the 0.1258 Ha gap of # quantum_hamiltonian_organo_mineral(), where it can. lv <- sort(Re(eigen(h2$op$to_matrix(), only.values = TRUE)$values)) round(lv, 6)     # -1.857275 -1.244584 -0.882722 -0.224911 round(lv[2] - lv[1], 4)                              # 0.6127 } # }

code: if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{ # The chain is OPEN: n - 1 couplings plus n field terms = 2n - 1. h <- quantum_hamiltonian_ising_1d(4) h$pauli_terms     # IIZZ IZZI ZZII IIIX IIXI IXII XIII length(h$pauli_terms)                                     # 7  # Two limits have closed forms and make good unit checks.  With # h = 0 the chain is classical, E0 = -J (n - 1) = -3; with J = 0 # the spins are free, E0 = -h n = -4. quantum_vqe_exact(quantum_hamiltonian_ising_1d(4, J = 1, h = 0))  # -3 quantum_vqe_exact(quantum_hamiltonian_ising_1d(4, J = 0, h = 1))  # -4  # At the critical point J = h = 1 neither limit applies. round(quantum_vqe_exact(quantum_hamiltonian_ising_1d(4)), 6)  # Finite size, not the solver, is what limits this benchmark. # Energy per site creeps towards the known infinite-chain value # -4/pi = -1.273240 but is still 0.035091 Ha per site above it at # n = 10, because both end spins of an open chain are missing a # neighbour.  Do not compare a 4-qubit run to a textbook number. eps <- vapply(c(2, 4, 6, 8, 10), function(n)   quantum_vqe_exact(quantum_hamiltonian_ising_1d(n)) / n, numeric(1)) round(eps, 6)     # -1.118034 -1.189693 -1.216038 -1.229744 -1.238149 round(eps[5] - (-4 / pi), 6)                          # 0.035091  # The sign of J is invisible in the spectrum of an open chain -- # flipping every second spin gauges it away -- so the "antiferro- # magnetic" chain returns the identical ground-state energy. round(quantum_vqe_exact(quantum_hamiltonian_ising_1d(4, J = -1)), 6)  # `n_qubits` is truncated, not validated: 3.7 silently builds a # 3-site chain (5 terms).  Only n < 2 is rejected. length(quantum_hamiltonian_ising_1d(3.7)$pauli_terms)     # 5 try(quantum_hamiltonian_ising_1d(1)) } # }

title: Toy organo-mineral Hamiltonian (4-qubit Fe + ligand coupling) — quantum_hamiltonian_organo_mineral
code: if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{ om <- quantum_hamiltonian_organo_mineral() om                                  # 4 qubits, 8 Pauli terms  # Switch the hopping off and the Hamiltonian is diagonal, i.e. a # classical Ising energy over z in {-1, +1}^4 that you can # minimise by hand.  Both routes give -1, all four spins up. g <- expand.grid(z3 = c(1, -1), z2 = c(1, -1),                  z1 = c(1, -1), z0 = c(1, -1)) min(-0.5 * (g$z3 + g$z2) - 0.3 * (g$z1 + g$z0) +      0.4 * g$z3 * g$z2 + 0.2 * g$z1 * g$z0)                  # -1 quantum_vqe_exact(quantum_hamiltonian_organo_mineral(t = 0))  # -1  # `t` is what makes the cluster quantum: Fe-ligand tunnelling # buys 0.215809 Ha of extra binding at the default t = 0.25 and # the ground state stops being a product state.  With t = 0 there # is nothing here a VQE could tell you that expand.grid() cannot. round(quantum_vqe_exact(om), 6)                     # -1.215809 round(quantum_vqe_exact(om) - (-1), 6)              # -0.215809  # Why this is a harder target than quantum_hamiltonian_h2(): the # first excited state sits only 0.125771 Ha above the ground # state and is doubly degenerate, so a fit must beat that before # "ground state" means anything.  H2's gap is 0.6127. lv <- sort(Re(eigen(om$op$to_matrix(), only.values = TRUE)$values)) round(lv[1:4], 6)   # -1.215809 -1.090038 -1.090038 -0.795228 round(lv[2] - lv[1], 6)                             # 0.125771  # Judged that way the default fit fails.  Twenty COBYLA restarts # of the EXACT statevector VQE -- no shot noise at all, about 1 s # a run -- spanned 0.031 to 0.123 Ha off: a quarter to nearly all # of the spectral gap, with not one run converging.  Read `gap` # against `lv[2] - lv[1]`, never against the energy, and never # report a single run. gaps <- replicate(5, quantum_vqe_fit(om, max_iter = 400L)$gap) round(range(gaps), 4) round(range(gaps) / (lv[2] - lv[1]), 2)  # Reaching the ground state takes a deeper ansatz and far more # iterations: reps = 3 with max_iter = 2000 (about 6 s a run) # brought five restarts down to a 0.0000-0.0450 Ha spread. round(quantum_vqe_fit(om, ansatz_reps = 3L, max_iter = 2000L)$gap, 4) } # }

code: if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{   # The gate that every other IBMQ entry point consults first.   quantum_ibmq_available()    # It is a three-part check and the third part is only   # nzchar(Sys.getenv("IBMQ_TOKEN")). Any non-empty string passes,   # so TRUE means "a token is present", never "the token   # authenticates": junk credentials return TRUE here and then   # fail at the first network call in quantum_ibmq_backends().   old <- Sys.getenv("IBMQ_TOKEN", "")   Sys.setenv(IBMQ_TOKEN = "not-a-real-token")   quantum_ibmq_available()                       # TRUE   if (nzchar(old)) Sys.setenv(IBMQ_TOKEN = old) else     Sys.unsetenv("IBMQ_TOKEN")    # When it is FALSE, decompose it. The three preconditions fail   # for unrelated reasons and only the third is fixed by editing   # ~/.Renviron.   c(reticulate = requireNamespace("reticulate", quietly = TRUE),     runtime    = reticulate::py_module_available("qiskit_ibm_runtime"),     token      = nzchar(Sys.getenv("IBMQ_TOKEN", "")))    # The token is read from the environment and nowhere else, so   # keep it out of scripts: put IBMQ_TOKEN=<key from   # https://quantum.ibm.com/account> in ~/.Renviron and restart R. } # }

code: if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{   # Step 2 of the discovery path: preflight, list, then pick.   stopifnot(quantum_ibmq_available())   qpus <- quantum_ibmq_backends()   qpus    # TRAP: an unavailable service is reported as character(0), not   # as an error, so a length-0 result is indistinguishable from   # "this account has no operational processor". The preflight   # above is the only thing that tells the two apart -- without it   # a missing IBMQ_TOKEN looks exactly like an empty fleet.   length(quantum_ibmq_backends())    # The difference between the two calls is the calibration queue:   # `operational_only = FALSE` also lists processors paused for   # maintenance. Read it before blaming a stalled job on your   # circuit.   setdiff(quantum_ibmq_backends(operational_only = FALSE), qpus)    # `simulator = FALSE` is the default, i.e. real processors only.   # Flip it to see whatever simulated backends the account still   # exposes; IBM has been retiring them, so an empty answer here is   # a normal outcome rather than a misconfiguration.   quantum_ibmq_backends(simulator = TRUE)    # Feed a name straight into the dispatch layer. Pinning it is   # what makes two runs comparable -- see quantum_ibmq_least_busy()   # for why leaving `ibmq_backend = NULL` does not.   quantum_vqe_fit(quantum_hamiltonian_h2(), backend = "ibmq",                    ibmq_backend = qpus[1L],                    optimizer = "SPSA", max_iter = 50L) } # }

code: if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{   # Step 3 of the discovery path, for when you have no reason to   # prefer a particular processor.   name <- quantum_ibmq_least_busy()   name %in% quantum_ibmq_backends()        # TRUE: it is one of them    # `min_num_qubits` filters the DEVICE, and says nothing about the   # size of your problem. The 2-qubit preset from   # quantum_hamiltonian_organo_mineral_nature() is routed onto the   # full coupling map before submission, so the circuit that   # actually leaves R is as wide as the processor -- 127 qubits on   # an Eagle device. Width here is a capacity filter, not a limit.   quantum_ibmq_least_busy(min_num_qubits = 127L)    # TRAP: NA_character_ is the only failure signal and it covers   # three unrelated causes -- no token (returns before any network   # call), no backend matching the filter, and any API error (the   # service call is wrapped in tryCatch). Split them by hand:   if (is.na(quantum_ibmq_least_busy(min_num_qubits = 1000L))) {     if (!quantum_ibmq_available()) {       message("no IBMQ_TOKEN in this session")     } else {       message("token present; no backend that wide, or API error")     }   }    # "Least busy" is a queue-depth decision, not a fidelity one, and   # it can return a different processor minutes apart. Resolve it   # once and pin the name when two runs have to be comparable:   pinned <- quantum_ibmq_least_busy(min_num_qubits = 127L)   quantum_ibmq_submit(quantum_hamiltonian_h2(),                        parameters = rep(0.1, 12),                        backend_name = pinned, mitigation = "m3") } # }

title: Submit a single expectation-value PUB to IBM Quantum hardware — quantum_ibmq_submit
code: if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{   ham <- quantum_hamiltonian_h2()          # 2 qubits, 5 Pauli terms    # `parameters` must match the ansatz length exactly: there is no   # recycling, and nothing on the R side checks it. EfficientSU2   # carries n_qubits * 2 * (reps + 1) angles, so 2 * 2 * 3 = 12 at   # the default `ansatz_reps = 2`. Compute it, do not guess it.   theta <- rep(0.1, 12)    job <- quantum_ibmq_submit(ham, parameters = theta,                               shots = 4096L, mitigation = "m3")   job    # One PUB is ONE expectation value at ONE parameter point -- this   # is not an optimisation. The noiseless value at this theta is   # -1.029329 while the ground state is -1.857275, so theta = 0.1   # sits 0.83 Hartree above the minimum. A hardware number near   # -1.03 therefore means the device worked, NOT that the chemistry   # converged; quantum_vqe_fit(backend = "ibmq") does the latter.   ref <- quantum_vqe_fit(ham, backend = "aer_statevector",                           initial_point = theta)$history[1L]   c(hardware = job$expectation, noiseless = ref,     ground_state = quantum_vqe_exact(ham))    # `std_error` is shot noise ONLY -- the EstimatorV2 standard   # error, of order 1/sqrt(shots) (0.0156 at 4096 shots).   # Quadrupling `shots` halves it and does nothing whatsoever to   # the coherent gate error, which is the bias `mitigation`   # attacks. A tight std_error next to an untreated bias is the   # classic way to over-trust a hardware run.   c(std_error = job$std_error, shot_floor = 1 / sqrt(job$shots))    # So compare mitigation levels rather than trusting one run, and   # pin `backend_name` while doing it: the default picks the   # least-busy device afresh each call, which would confound the   # comparison with a change of processor. Two queue slots.   raw <- quantum_ibmq_submit(ham, parameters = theta, shots = 4096L,                               backend_name = job$backend,                               mitigation = "none")   c(none = raw$expectation, m3 = job$expectation, noiseless = ref)    # `mitigation` is match.arg()'d here, so it is case sensitive   # even though the internal level map is not: "zne" works, "ZNE"   # errors.    # Supplying your own circuit ignores `ansatz_reps` and is   # unchecked: a handle whose width differs from ham$n_qubits gets   # past the transpiler and dies later inside apply_layout() with   # "Number of qargs does not match (3 != 2)". Match the width to   # hamiltonian$n_qubits yourself.   names(job$metadata)                      # primitive's own report } # }

title: Fit a Quantum Kernel Ridge Regression (Pillar 6) — quantum_krr_fit
code: # \donttest{   ## The target is the sign of an interaction between two covariates -- a   ## checkerboard. In the population neither a linear rule nor a threshold   ## on a single column beats chance on it, so a score here reflects the   ## kernel and not the task. (A target such as y = sign(x1 - mean(x1))   ## is instead solved exactly by the one-line rule that defines it, and a   ## perfect score on it would say nothing about any estimator.)   set.seed(1)   u <- matrix(runif(2 * 400L), ncol = 2L)   y <- sign((u[, 1L] - 0.5) * (u[, 2L] - 0.5))   X <- quantum_scale(u)          # ZZFeatureMap needs features in [0, pi]   tr <- 1:200; te <- 201:400     # fit on 200 points, score on 200 unseen    fit <- quantum_krr_fit(X[tr, ], y[tr], reps = 2L, lambda = 0.1)   mean(predict(fit, X[te, ], type = "class") == y[te])   # 0.75, held out #> [1] 0.75    ## The two numbers 0.75 has to beat before it means anything:   max(table(y[te])) / length(te)                         # 0.53, majority class #> [1] 0.53    ## A fitted linear rule has no signal to latch onto here, so its held-out   ## accuracy is chance in expectation and swings widely from split to   ## split; on this split it happens to land above the majority class.   lin <- lm(y[tr] ~ X[tr, ])   mean(sign(cbind(1, X[te, ]) %*% coef(lin)) == y[te])   # 0.6 #> [1] 0.6    ## The same fit scored in sample instead -- optimistic, which is why the   ## held-out number above is the one to read:   mean(predict(fit, X[tr, ], type = "class") == y[tr])   # 0.78, in sample #> [1] 0.78    ## This is a demonstration on two simulated covariates, not a benchmark:   ## it shows the quantum kernel picks up an interaction a linear model   ## cannot, on data with no noise in the labels. Claiming it beats a   ## classical kernel would need the same held-out protocol run against,   ## say, an RBF-kernel ridge fit, repeated over splits, on real data. # }

title: GP-equivalent posterior for a Quantum Kernel Ridge Regression fit — quantum_krr_posterior
code: ## Soil organic carbon (g/kg) from three covariates: 60 calibration ## sites, 30 held out. set.seed(11) n    <- 90 clay <- runif(n,   8,  62) ph   <- runif(n, 4.5, 7.5) elev <- runif(n,  60, 340) soc  <- 24 + 0.10 * (clay - 35) + 2.2 * (ph - 6) -         0.010 * (elev - 200) + rnorm(n, 0, 1.5) X    <- quantum_scale(cbind(clay, ph, elev))  # ZZFeatureMap wants [0, pi] tr <- 1:60; te <- 61:90  fit  <- quantum_krr_fit(X[tr, ], soc[tr], reps = 2L, lambda = 0.1) set.seed(11)          # edaphos_posterior() synthesises Gaussian draws post <- quantum_krr_posterior(fit, X[te, ], units = "g/kg") post #> <edaphos_posterior> #>   method      : analytic #>   query_type  : sample #>   units       : g/kg #>   n_samples   : 500 #>   query shape : 30 #>   mean range  : [-2.6350, +3.6037]  mean = +0.5971 #>   sd   range  : [+3.4170, +3.4600]  mean = +3.4373 #>   epistemic sd: [+0.2940, +0.6184]  mean = +0.4669 #>   aleatoric sd: [+3.4043, +3.4043]  mean = +3.4043  ## TRAP -- `post$mean` is on the CENTRED scale. quantum_krr_fit() ## subtracts mean(y) and predict() adds it back; this function does ## not, so the posterior must be shifted by `fit$y_mean` before it ## meets an observation in g/kg. pred <- predict(fit, X[te, ]) round(c(post_mean = post$mean[1L], predict = pred[1L],         y_mean    = fit$y_mean), 3)          # 1.024, 24.430, 23.406 #> post_mean   predict    y_mean  #>     1.024    24.430    23.406   lo <- post$mean + fit$y_mean - 1.96 * post$sd up <- post$mean + fit$y_mean + 1.96 * post$sd round(c(unshifted = edaphos_picp(soc[te], post$mean - 1.96 * post$sd,                                  post$mean + 1.96 * post$sd),         shifted   = edaphos_picp(soc[te], lo, up)), 3)   # 0.000, 0.933 #> unshifted   shifted  #>     0.000     0.933   ## 0.933 against a nominal 0.95 reads like a calibrated model. It is ## not one: on this split the point predictions are WORSE than the ## training mean (negative R2), while an ordinary linear fit on the ## same three covariates is not. d   <- data.frame(soc, clay, ph, elev) lin <- lm(soc ~ clay + ph + elev, data = d[tr, ]) round(c(qkrr   = edaphos_r2(soc[te], pred),         linear = edaphos_r2(soc[te], predict(lin, d[te, ]))), 3) #>   qkrr linear  #>  -0.37   0.72  #  -0.37 and 0.72  ## PICP cannot see that; the interval score can. A constant band ## around the training mean -- no model at all -- is both narrower ## and better scored. nl <- rep(fit$y_mean - 1.96 * sd(soc[tr]), length(te)) nu <- rep(fit$y_mean + 1.96 * sd(soc[tr]), length(te)) round(c(is_qkrr = edaphos_interval_score(soc[te], lo, up),   # 16.90         is_null = edaphos_interval_score(soc[te], nl, nu),   # 11.82         w_qkrr  = mean(up - lo),                             # 13.47         w_null  = mean(nu - nl)), 2)                         # 10.59 #> is_qkrr is_null  w_qkrr  w_null  #>   16.90   11.82   13.47   10.59   ## Which half of the decomposition earned the coverage? The aleatoric ## one: it is a leave-one-out estimate, and it lands on the held-out ## residual sd while the training RMSE is 3.7x optimistic. round(c(aleatoric  = post$aleatoric_sd[1L],   # 3.404         heldout_sd = sd(soc[te] - pred),      # 3.351         train_rmse = fit$rmse), 3)            # 0.899 #>  aleatoric heldout_sd train_rmse  #>      3.404      3.351      0.899   ## The epistemic half is decoration here. k(x*, x*) = 1 for any ## normalised state, so the implied GP prior sd is 1 g/kg by ## construction and not from the data, and `lambda` stands in for a ## noise variance the same residuals put two orders of magnitude ## higher. Delete the epistemic term and nothing moves: a <- post$aleatoric_sd[1L] round(c(sigma_n2  = a^2, lambda = fit$lambda,          # 11.589, 0.100         picp_full = edaphos_picp(soc[te], lo, up),     # 0.933         picp_ale  = edaphos_picp(soc[te], pred - 1.96 * a,                                  pred + 1.96 * a),     # 0.933         is_full   = edaphos_interval_score(soc[te], lo, up),   # 16.905         is_ale    = edaphos_interval_score(soc[te], pred - 1.96 * a,                                            pred + 1.96 * a)), 3)  # 17.010 #>  sigma_n2    lambda picp_full  picp_ale   is_full    is_ale  #>    11.589     0.100     0.933     0.933    16.905    17.010   ## Nor does it flag extrapolation, the one job an epistemic term is ## usually hired for: the corners of the encoding cube, far from any ## calibration site, sit inside the range seen at the held-out sites. far <- X[te, ]; far[1L, ] <- 0; far[2L, ] <- pi set.seed(11) pf <- quantum_krr_posterior(fit, far) round(c(corner_0     = pf$epistemic_sd[1L],         corner_pi    = pf$epistemic_sd[2L],         interior_min = min(pf$epistemic_sd[-(1:2)]),         interior_max = max(pf$epistemic_sd[-(1:2)])), 3) #>     corner_0    corner_pi interior_min interior_max  #>        0.488        0.467        0.294        0.618  #  0.488, 0.467, 0.294, 0.618 -- the corners are not the extremes

title: Total molecular energy from an active-space VQE result — quantum_nature_total_energy
code: if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{   ham <- quantum_hamiltonian_organo_mineral_nature("formic_acid")    # `seed` does NOT pin quantum_vqe_fit(): it seeds NumPy, while   # the random starting point of the ansatz is drawn by Qiskit's   # own RNG. Five runs at seed = 1L give five different energies:   # the spread was 6e-06, 7e-05 and 8e-05 Hartree in three sessions   # here. Fix `initial_point` when you need a stable number.   reps <- vapply(1:5,                   function(i) quantum_vqe_fit(ham, seed = 1L)$energy,                   numeric(1))   diff(range(reps))                             # not 0    fit   <- quantum_vqe_fit(ham, seed = 1L, initial_point = rep(0.1, 12))   e_tot <- quantum_nature_total_energy(fit)   sprintf("%.6f", e_tot)                        # "-186.223195"    # The helper is arithmetic, not chemistry: <H> over the active   # space plus the three constants the Hamiltonian carries. The   # frozen-core term is two orders of magnitude larger than the   # part the VQE actually optimises, which is why fit$energy on its   # own is not an energy of anything.   all.equal(e_tot, fit$energy + attr(ham, "energy_shift"))   round(c(active_H = fit$energy,           nuclear  = attr(ham, "nuclear_repulsion_energy"),           frozen   = attr(ham, "frozen_core_shift"),           active_p = attr(ham, "active_space_shift")), 6)    # HONESTY CHECK -- read this next to the total energy, never the   # total energy alone. `reference_energy` is the full-molecule   # Hartree-Fock energy, so e_tot - E_HF is the correlation the   # (2e, 2o) active space recovered: -34.2 mHartree. CCSD/STO-3G on   # the same geometry is -183.1 mHartree below HF, so this 2-qubit   # carboxylate model captures 19% of the correlation energy. A   # working pipeline; not a chemistry-grade number.   pyscf <- reticulate::import("pyscf")   mf <- pyscf$scf$RHF(pyscf$gto$M(atom = attr(ham, "geometry"),                                    basis = attr(ham, "basis"),                                    verbose = 0L))   e_hf <- as.numeric(mf$kernel())   cc <- pyscf$cc$CCSD(mf); cc$verbose <- 0L; invisible(cc$kernel())   round(c(vqe_corr  = e_tot - e_hf,           ccsd_corr = as.numeric(cc$e_tot) - e_hf,           fraction  = (e_tot - e_hf) /                       (as.numeric(cc$e_tot) - e_hf)), 4)    # That fraction is a property of the chosen active space, not of   # the method, so it must never be quoted as "the accuracy of the   # VQE". The identical 2-qubit recipe on methanediol recovers   # -0.5 mHartree of a -144.4 mHartree CCSD correlation -- 0.3%,   # i.e. nothing -- because its frontier pair is essentially closed   # shell. Same qubit count, same runtime, no chemistry.   hm <- quantum_hamiltonian_organo_mineral_nature("methanediol")   round(quantum_vqe_exact(hm) + attr(hm, "energy_shift") -           attr(hm, "reference_energy"), 6)       # -0.000495    # The helper is class-gated: it stopifnot()s on   # `edaphos_quantum_hamiltonian_nature`, so a fit built from the   # toy quantum_hamiltonian_organo_mineral() or _h2() errors here   # instead of silently adding a shift that does not exist.   try(quantum_nature_total_energy(     quantum_vqe_fit(quantum_hamiltonian_h2(), seed = 1L))) } # }

title: Rescale a covariate matrix into [lower, upper] column-wise — quantum_scale
code: ## A clay sweep at constant pH, in field units. Holding pH fixed ## isolates one covariate, and shows the constant-column rule: a ## column with no spread is sent to the midpoint (lower + upper) / 2. clay <- seq(12, 58, by = 2)                      # % clay raw  <- cbind(clay = clay, ph = rep(6.0, length(clay))) X    <- quantum_scale(raw) round(apply(X, 2L, range), 4)   # clay -> [0, pi]; pH -> 1.5708 twice #>        clay     ph #> [1,] 0.0000 1.5708 #> [2,] 3.1416 1.5708  ## Why the rescaling is not cosmetic: the ZZFeatureMap encodes ## covariate i as Rz(2 x_i), so the kernel is PERIODIC in the ## covariate. With a single column the period is exactly pi, and two ## sites pi apart encode to the same state. quantum_kernel(matrix(c(0.7, 0.7 + pi), ncol = 1L), reps = 2L)[1, 2] #> [1] 1 #  1 -- not "similar", indistinguishable  ## Fed raw, clay spans 46 units = 14.6 periods, and kernel similarity ## stops tracking soil similarity. Row 1 is the 12% clay site; ## columns 2, 12 and 23 are the 14%, 34% and 56% sites. k_raw <- quantum_kernel(raw, reps = 2L)[1, ] k_sc  <- quantum_kernel(X,   reps = 2L)[1, ] rbind(raw    = round(k_raw[c(2, 12, 23)], 4),   # 0.2974 0.9967 0.9871       scaled = round(k_sc[ c(2, 12, 23)], 4))   # 0.9368 0.0005 0.0033 #>          [,1]   [,2]   [,3] #> raw    0.2974 0.9967 0.9871 #> scaled 0.9368 0.0005 0.0033  ## Raw, it is the 34% and 56% sites that come back near-identical to ## the 12% site while its actual neighbour at 14% does not. Over the ## whole sweep the raw encoding carries no distance information: c(raw    = round(cor(k_raw, -(clay - 12)), 4),   # 0.0223   scaled = round(cor(k_sc,  -(clay - 12)), 4))   # 0.5382 #>    raw scaled  #> 0.0223 0.5382   ## Read 0.5382 as "some", not "all". The ZZ kernel is not a distance ## kernel even on [0, pi] -- it revives at large gaps. Rescaling ## removes the exact aliasing; it does not buy monotonicity.  ## TRAP -- the map is refitted from whatever you pass, so scaling a ## validation set on its own puts the same soil at a different angle. ## Carry the CALIBRATION range across instead of calling ## quantum_scale() a second time. val <- cbind(clay = c(20, 34, 40), ph = rep(6.0, 3)) rng <- range(raw[, "clay"]) round(c(own_map   = unname(quantum_scale(val)[2L, "clay"]),   # 2.1991         train_map = (34 - rng[1L]) * pi / diff(rng)), 4)      # 1.5025 #>   own_map train_map  #>    2.1991    1.5025   ## One site scaled on its own is doubly broken: range() has no spread ## so every covariate collapses to pi/2, and apply() drops the result ## to a vector rather than the 1-row matrix. quantum_scale(val[1L, , drop = FALSE]) #>     clay       ph  #> 1.570796 1.570796

title: Exact ground-state energy via classical diagonalisation — quantum_vqe_exact
code: if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{ h2 <- quantum_hamiltonian_h2()  # This is the yardstick.  `$exact` inside an edaphos_quantum_vqe # object is literally this call and `$gap` is |energy - exact|; a # VQE energy means nothing except read next to it. round(quantum_vqe_exact(h2), 6)                      # -1.857275  # Dense diagonalisation, so cost is 2^n.  n = 14 (a 16384-square # operator) still returns in about 0.2 s; memory, not time, is # the wall shortly above that. system.time(quantum_vqe_exact(quantum_hamiltonian_ising_1d(14)))  # "Exact" is not bit-reproducible: repeated calls scatter by a # few times 1e-15 (H2) up to 6e-14 (a 10-qubit chain).  That is # six orders below the best VQE gap below, so it never matters # numerically -- but do not reach for identical() on it. v <- replicate(8, quantum_vqe_exact(h2)) diff(range(v))                       # order 1e-15, not 0 isTRUE(all(v == v[1]))               # FALSE  # 1) Exact statevector back end.  No sampling noise whatever, so #    the gap is pure optimiser error -- and wildly variable across #    restarts: 1e-9 to 1.5e-3 in one sweep of eight, median 3e-8, #    because the ansatz start point is random (see the caveat at #    the end).  Quote the median of restarts, not one run. fit <- quantum_vqe_fit(h2, backend = "aer_statevector") c(energy = fit$energy, exact = fit$exact, gap = fit$gap)  # 2) Shot-based Aer with SPSA -- the honest simulation.  4096 #    shots put a 1/sqrt(4096) = 0.0156 Ha standard error on every #    energy the optimiser sees, and the gap then runs 0.002-0.034 #    Ha: about five orders worse than the median of (1), none of #    it physics.  SPSA, not COBYLA, because the cost function is #    now stochastic. fs <- quantum_vqe_fit(h2, backend = "aer_shots", shots = 4096L,                       optimizer = "SPSA", max_iter = 60L) c(gap = fs$gap, shot_se = 1 / sqrt(4096))  # The trap: min(fs$history) is the luckiest of ~171 noisy draws, # not a variational bound.  It came out BELOW the exact energy in # 3 of 6 runs, which is physically impossible and diagnoses noise # rather than success; even fs$energy did so twice in eleven. # Report `energy`, judge it by `gap`, and treat any gap smaller # than shot_se as luck rather than convergence. c(min_history = min(fs$history), exact = fs$exact,   n_evals = length(fs$history))  # 3) Real hardware.  quantum_ibmq_available() is an offline probe #    (reticulate + qiskit_ibm_runtime + IBMQ_TOKEN) that touches #    no network.  `mitigation` is live only here: "m3" maps to IBM #    resilience_level 1, "zne" to 2; both Aer back ends ignore it #    and "aer_shots" says so out loud.  `ibmq_backend = NULL` #    picks the least-busy operational device.  Run (1) first and #    treat its gap as the floor device error sits on top of. if (quantum_ibmq_available()) {   fq <- quantum_vqe_fit(h2, backend = "ibmq",                         ibmq_backend = "ibm_brisbane",                         shots = 4096L, mitigation = "m3",                         optimizer = "SPSA", max_iter = 50L)   c(hardware = fq$gap, exact_sim = fit$gap) }  # Caveat for all three: `seed` does NOT make quantum_vqe_fit() # reproducible -- it seeds numpy's legacy global RNG, not the # generator qiskit-algorithms draws the initial point from, so # five runs at seed = 1L gave gaps from 5e-10 to 1e-4.  Pass an # explicit `initial_point` (12 angles for 2 qubits at reps = 2) # and `$energy` repeats to the last bit across sessions; `$gap` # still wobbles at 1e-15 because `exact` does. p0 <- rep(0.1, 12) a <- quantum_vqe_fit(h2, initial_point = p0)$energy b <- quantum_vqe_fit(h2, initial_point = p0)$energy identical(a, b)             # TRUE, both -1.857131658135603 } # }

title: Variational Quantum Eigensolver (Pillar 6 main entry point) — quantum_vqe_fit
text: Three execution back ends supported v0.9.0: "aer_statevector" (default) Exact noiseless statevector simulation via qiskit.primitives.StatevectorEstimator. ansatz transpiled. Deterministic; limited memory roughly 24 qubits. "aer_shots" Shot-based simulation via qiskit_aer.primitives.EstimatorV2. energy evaluation estimated shots circuit executions therefore carries finite-sample noise order 1/sqrt(shots). ansatz transpiled standard \{id, rz, sx, x, cx, u\} basis gate set Aer primitive can dispatch . "ibmq" Real hardware via qiskit_ibm_runtime.EstimatorV2 inside Runtime Session. Requires qiskit-ibm-runtime Python package IBMQ_TOKEN environment variable. Supports two mitigation strategies (Kim et al. 2023, see References): mitigation = "m3" — Matrix-free Measurement Mitigation (TREX + M3 readout correction), mapped IBM runtime resilience_level = 1; mitigation = "zne" — Zero-Noise Extrapolation gate-folding noise scales, mapped IBM runtime resilience_level = 2.

code: data(br_cerrado) xy <- br_cerrado[seq(1, nrow(br_cerrado), by = 20), c("x", "y")]  # Scale the buffer to the data. `br_cerrado` is a 0.3-degree demonstration # grid whose widest separation is about 47 km, so the 68 km default -- set # for the Cerrado-wide WoSIS extract -- would empty a fold, and the function # says so rather than returning one silently. try(spatial_block_folds(xy, k = 5, buffer_km = 68, seed = 1)) #> Error : buffer_km = 68 leaves fewer than two training rows in at least one fold. Reduce the buffer or the number of folds.  # Without a buffer, the nearest training neighbour of a test row can be # arbitrarily close to it. f0 <- spatial_block_folds(xy, k = 5, buffer_km = 0, seed = 1) round(min(f0$min_dist_km), 2) #> [1] 3.03  # With one, no training row is closer than the buffer, and the cost in # discarded training data is reported rather than hidden. f1 <- spatial_block_folds(xy, k = 5, buffer_km = 10, seed = 1) round(min(f1$min_dist_km), 2) #> [1] 10.73 f1$n_buffered #> [1] 24 25 27 28 41 f1 #> <edaphos_spatial_folds> #>   102 rows, 5 blocks, buffer 10 km #>   test rows per fold : 16, 19, 23, 25, 19 #>   training rows kept : 62, 58, 52, 49, 42 #>   discarded to buffer: 24, 25, 27, 28, 41 (28.4% of all rows) #>   realised min train-test distance: 10.7 km

title: Build a standalone ConvLSTM cell (Pillar 3 primitive) — temporal_convlstm_cell
code: # lantern is a separate binary download, so requireNamespace() alone # is not enough -- torch_is_installed() is the half that matters. if (requireNamespace("torch", quietly = TRUE) &&     isTRUE(torch::torch_is_installed())) {   torch::torch_manual_seed(1)   cell <- temporal_convlstm_cell(input_dim = 2, hidden_dim = 3)    # All four gates come out of ONE convolution: out_channels is   # 4 * hidden_dim and in_channels is input_dim + hidden_dim,   # because the input and the previous h are concatenated first.   print(dim(cell$conv$weight))          # 12 5 3 3    # init_state() returns (h, c) -- both zeros, both hidden_dim   # channels. Height and width are yours to supply; the cell is   # fully convolutional and has no built-in grid size.   state <- cell$init_state(batch = 1, height = 8, width = 8)   print(vapply(state, function(s) paste(dim(s), collapse = " x "), ""))   # "1 x 3 x 8 x 8" "1 x 3 x 8 x 8"    cube <- temporal_synth_soc_cube(H = 8, W = 8, T_total = 6, seed = 42)   tt   <- temporal_cube_to_tensor(cube)   x1 <- torch::torch_tensor(     tt$sequence[, 1, , , , drop = FALSE])$squeeze(2)   print(x1$shape)                       # 1 2 8 8 = (batch, C, H, W)    state <- cell(x1, state)   # The cell emits hidden_dim feature channels, NOT a prediction.   # The 1x1 head that turns them into one soil property lives in   # temporal_convlstm_fit()'s stack, not here.   print(state[[1]]$shape)               # 1 3 8 8    # h = o * tanh(c) with o in (0, 1), so |h| can never exceed   # |tanh(c)|. Read c as the retained memory and h as the part of   # it the next layer is allowed to see.   print(round(c(h_absmax = as.numeric(state[[1]]$abs()$max()$item()),                 c_absmax = as.numeric(state[[2]]$abs()$max()$item())), 4))   # h_absmax c_absmax   #   0.1323   0.2638    # Trap: padding is floor((kernel_size - 1) / 2), which preserves   # H and W only for ODD kernels. kernel_size = 2 gives padding 0,   # so the gates come back 7 x 7 while c_prev is still 8 x 8 and   # the cell dies on f * c_prev. There is no check for this.   torch::torch_manual_seed(1)   even <- temporal_convlstm_cell(2, 3, kernel_size = 2)   print(tryCatch(even(x1, even$init_state(1, 8, 8)),                  error = function(e) trimws(                    sub("Exception raised.*", "", conditionMessage(e)))))   # "The size of tensor a (7) must match the size of tensor b (8) at   #  non-singleton dimension 3" }

title: K-seed deep ensemble of stacked ConvLSTMs — temporal_convlstm_ensemble_fit
code: # Pillar 3 on a 12-month synthetic Cerrado SOC cube: 8 x 8 cells, # two channels (standardised elevation, monthly precipitation) and # SOC in g/kg. Months 1-9 are the training window. if (requireNamespace("torch", quietly = TRUE) &&     isTRUE(torch::torch_is_installed())) {    cube <- temporal_synth_soc_cube(H = 8L, W = 8L, T_total = 12L,                                   seed = 42L)   tt   <- temporal_cube_to_tensor(cube)   past_seq <- tt$sequence[, 1:9, , , , drop = FALSE]  # (1, 9, 2, 8, 8)   past_tgt <- tt$target[,   1:9, , , drop = FALSE]    # (1, 9, 8, 8)    # return_sequence = TRUE is not the default here, but it is what   # temporal_convlstm_ensemble_rollout() insists on further down.   ens <- temporal_convlstm_ensemble_fit(     sequence = past_seq, target = past_tgt,     hidden_dims = 4L, return_sequence = TRUE,     epochs = 20L, lr = 0.05, K_ens = 3L, base_seed = 7L)   print(ens)    # base_seed is the ONLY source of diversity: no bagging, no   # augmentation, every member sees the identical cube and differs   # purely by initialisation. At 20 epochs that has not settled --   # the worst member's loss is 2.1x the best member's. K_ens = 3 is   # kept here only for run time; it leaves the across-member sd with   # 2 degrees of freedom, which is why the default is 10.   print(round(ens$final_losses, 4))    # final_loss is MSE in the standardised units of tt$target, so   # quote it against the MSE of predicting the training-window mean.   # Even the worst member beats that trivial model 9x.   print(round(c(worst_member     = max(ens$final_losses),                 predict_the_mean = mean((past_tgt -                                          mean(past_tgt))^2)), 4))    # Rescaled, those are in-sample RMSEs of 1.8-2.6 g/kg on a cube   # whose SOC spans 16.7-52.2 g/kg. In-sample only -- the forecast   # picture is in ?temporal_convlstm_ensemble_rollout.   print(round(sqrt(ens$final_losses) * tt$scaling$soc_sd, 2))   print(round(range(cube$soc), 1))    # loss_histories keeps the full per-member Adam trace.   print(round(ens$loss_histories[[1L]][c(1L, 10L, 20L)], 4))    # Trap: the default return_sequence = FALSE trains happily on a   # (batch, H, W) target, and only the rollout helper complains.   flat <- temporal_convlstm_ensemble_fit(     sequence = past_seq,     target   = array(past_tgt[1L, 9L, , ], dim = c(1L, 8L, 8L)),     hidden_dims = 4L, epochs = 3L, K_ens = 2L, base_seed = 7L)   print(tryCatch(temporal_convlstm_ensemble_rollout(                    flat, past_seq,                    tt$sequence[, 10:12, , , , drop = FALSE]),                  error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))) }

title: Roll every ensemble member forward and stack the forecasts — temporal_convlstm_ensemble_rollout
code: # Forecast months 10-12 of the synthetic Cerrado SOC cube from an # ensemble trained on months 1-9, then score the across-member # spread as if it were a predictive interval. if (requireNamespace("torch", quietly = TRUE) &&     isTRUE(torch::torch_is_installed())) {    cube <- temporal_synth_soc_cube(H = 8L, W = 8L, T_total = 12L,                                   seed = 42L)   tt   <- temporal_cube_to_tensor(cube)   past_seq <- tt$sequence[, 1:9,   , , , drop = FALSE]   past_tgt <- tt$target[,   1:9,   , , drop = FALSE]   fut_seq  <- tt$sequence[, 10:12, , , , drop = FALSE]  # known drivers    ens <- temporal_convlstm_ensemble_fit(     sequence = past_seq, target = past_tgt, hidden_dims = 4L,     return_sequence = TRUE, epochs = 20L, lr = 0.05,     K_ens = 3L, base_seed = 7L)    rolls <- temporal_convlstm_ensemble_rollout(     ens, past_sequence = past_seq, future_drivers = fut_seq)   print(dim(rolls))                # (K_ens, T_future, H, W) = 3 3 8 8    # Undo the z-scaling so every number below is in g/kg.   gkg   <- rolls * tt$scaling$soc_sd + tt$scaling$soc_mu   truth <- cube$soc[10:12, , ]    # Spread and error, side by side, per lead time. The nominal-90%   # band is mean +/- 1.645 * across-member sd and `covered` is the   # PICP numerator out of the 64 grid cells.   print(round(t(vapply(1:3, function(h) {     mu <- apply(gkg[, h, , ], c(2, 3), mean)     sm <- apply(gkg[, h, , ], c(2, 3), stats::sd)     y  <- as.numeric(truth[h, , ])     c(spread  = mean(sm),       rmse    = edaphos_rmse(y, as.numeric(mu)),       bias    = edaphos_bias(y, as.numeric(mu)),       picp90  = edaphos_picp(y, as.numeric(mu - 1.645 * sm),                                 as.numeric(mu + 1.645 * sm)),       covered = sum(abs(y - as.numeric(mu)) <= 1.645 * as.numeric(sm)),       persistence_rmse = edaphos_rmse(y, as.numeric(cube$soc[9L, , ])))   }, numeric(6))), 3))    # Two readings. (1) The spread barely doubles across the horizon   # (4.13 -> 8.83 g/kg) while RMSE more than quadruples (3.35 ->   # 15.13), so coverage falls from 0.922 to 0.406. (2) Carrying   # month 9 forward unchanged has RMSE 3.23 g/kg at +3 months   # against this ensemble's 15.13: persistence wins by 4.7x. Treat   # the fit as a harness for the uncertainty API, not as a forecast.    # Why it drifts: the network sees elevation and precipitation, no   # calendar. Months 10-12 are the driest quarter and their drivers   # look like months 1-2, when SOC was 20 g/kg -- so the +3-month   # forecast lands 14.7 g/kg low, back at the month-5/6 level of the   # cube, instead of continuing the 20 -> 43 g/kg accumulation. A   # confounded driver, not a flaw in the ensembling.   print(round(rbind(precip = apply(cube$precip, 1L, mean),                     soc    = apply(cube$soc,    1L, mean)), 1))    mu <- apply(gkg[, 3L, , ], c(2, 3), mean)   sm <- apply(gkg[, 3L, , ], c(2, 3), stats::sd)   y  <- as.numeric(truth[3L, , ])    # At +3 months the error is almost pure bias: residuals scatter by   # 3.57 g/kg about a mean miss of 14.71, and the ensemble spread   # (8.83) is 2.5x that scatter. The members disagree plenty; they   # are simply all wrong in the same direction, because they share   # an architecture and a training window. A deep ensemble measures   # disagreement, never the bias its members hold in common.   b <- edaphos_bias(y, as.numeric(mu))   print(round(c(bias       = b,                 resid_sd   = stats::sd(y - as.numeric(mu)),                 ens_spread = mean(sm)), 2))    # So the interval score refuses the usual repair. Tripling the   # band buys PICP 1.000 and scores WORSE than the honest narrow one   # (87.11 vs 66.90); only recentring pays (29.04) -- and that used   # the truth, so it is a diagnosis, not something you can deploy.   sc <- function(lo, hi) c(     picp = edaphos_picp(y, as.numeric(lo), as.numeric(hi)),     IS   = edaphos_interval_score(y, as.numeric(lo), as.numeric(hi),                                   alpha = 0.10))   print(round(rbind(     as_is      = sc(mu - 1.645 * sm,     mu + 1.645 * sm),     widened_3x = sc(mu - 3 * 1.645 * sm, mu + 3 * 1.645 * sm),     debiased   = sc(mu + b - 1.645 * sm, mu + b + 1.645 * sm)), 3))    # The same rollout in the unified container. The adapter re-runs   # the rollout internally and keeps the LAST future step by default   # (time_step = 3 here), which is the worst-calibrated one.   post <- as_edaphos_posterior(ens, past_sequence = past_seq,                                future_drivers = fut_seq,                                units = "SOC z-units")   print(post)   print(unlist(post$metadata)) }

Length determines depth. Default c(4L) (single-layer). kernel_size Integer, spatial kernel size (odd). return_sequence Logical; see objectives . epochs, lr Adam hyperparameters. physics_lambda Numeric >= 0; weight physics-informed mass-balance regulariser. > 0 (return_sequence = TRUE), loss becomes $$\mathrm{MSE}(\hat y, y) + \lambda_{\text{phys}}\,        \mathrm{MSE}\!\left(\Delta\hat y_t,\,        k_{\text{}} P_t - k_{\text{}} \hat y_t P_t / \bar P\right),$$ .e. predicted per-step change \(\Delta\hat y_t = \hat y_{t+1} - \hat y_t\) pushed towards mass-balance increment implied driver channel. Setting zero collapses physics loss pure temporal smoothness penalty. physics_driver_channel Integer, index (1-based) input channel carries driver \(P_t\) (e.g. precipitation). physics_scaling scaling list returned temporal_cube_to_tensor() (soc_mu, soc_sd, prec_mu, prec_sd). Required whenever physics_lambda > 0. physics_k_in physics_k_out rates property's raw units, driver channel network sees standardised, whose mean zero machine precision — outflow term \(k_{} y P / \bar P\) formed without constants map two scales. earlier version guarded division 1e-6 instead, turned physics residual 1e6 amplification numerical noise: arrived 2.6e7 times heavier data-fit term, sign flipped seed, made fit 12 times worse rather regularising . title: Fit a stacked ConvLSTM on a 4D covariate cube — temporal_convlstm_fit
code: if (requireNamespace("torch", quietly = TRUE) &&     isTRUE(torch::torch_is_installed())) {   cube <- temporal_synth_soc_cube(H = 8, W = 8, T_total = 6, seed = 42)   tt   <- temporal_cube_to_tensor(cube)    # Sequence-to-one: six months of (elev, precip) -> the month-6 SOC   # map. `target` must keep its batch axis, so 3-D (1, H, W). The   # 2-D map that tt$target[1, 6, , ] returns is rejected by   # stopifnot(target$dim() == 3L).   y6  <- array(tt$target[1, 6, , ], dim = c(1, 8, 8))   fit <- temporal_convlstm_fit(tt$sequence, y6, hidden_dims = 4L,                                epochs = 150L, lr = 0.05, seed = 1L)   print(fit)    # A loss number alone means nothing. The reference that makes it   # readable is the constant map: mean(y6) predicted everywhere.   baseline <- mean((y6 - mean(y6))^2)   print(round(c(final = fit$final_loss, baseline = baseline,                 ratio = fit$final_loss / baseline), 4))   #   final baseline    ratio   #  0.0091   0.5382   0.0169    # Adam at lr = 0.05 is not monotone: 7 of the 149 steps go uphill,   # so never read final_loss as "the best loss reached".   print(sum(diff(fit$loss_history) > 0))          # 7    # And keep the ratio in proportion -- this fits 64 pixels with   # this many parameters and no held-out month, so 0.0169 measures   # capacity, not skill. temporal_convlstm_rollout() is where the   # same model has to face months it never saw.   print(sum(vapply(fit$model$parameters,                    function(p) prod(dim(p)), 0)))  # 885    # Trap 1: the physics regulariser is silently inert unless   # return_sequence = TRUE. physics_lambda is stored on the object   # either way, so loss_phys_history is the only proof it ever ran.   off <- temporal_convlstm_fit(tt$sequence, y6, epochs = 20L, lr = 0.05,                                seed = 1L, physics_lambda = 10)   print(c(lambda = off$physics_lambda,           phys_loss = max(off$loss_phys_history)))   #    lambda phys_loss   #        10         0    # Trap 2: the mass balance is written in RAW units -- physics_k_in   # and physics_k_out are the g/kg-per-mm rates of the generator --   # but temporal_cube_to_tensor() hands over a z-scored driver whose   # mean is zero to machine precision, so the outflow term   # k_out * y * P / mean(P) cannot be formed on that scale.   print(mean(as.numeric(tt$sequence[1, , 2, , ])))   # ~1.2e-16    # Supplying the scaling constants is therefore mandatory, not   # optional. Without them the fit refuses rather than guessing.   print(class(try(     temporal_convlstm_fit(tt$sequence, tt$target, return_sequence = TRUE,                           epochs = 2L, physics_lambda = 1, seed = 1L),     silent = TRUE)))                                 # "try-error"    on <- temporal_convlstm_fit(tt$sequence, tt$target, hidden_dims = 4L,                               return_sequence = TRUE, epochs = 30L,                               lr = 0.05, seed = 1L, physics_lambda = 1,                               physics_scaling = tt$scaling)   print(signif(c(fit   = on$loss_fit_history[1],                  phys  = on$loss_phys_history[1],                  ratio = on$loss_phys_history[1] /                          on$loss_fit_history[1]), 3))    # The physics term is now the same order of magnitude as the term it   # regularises, and it is itself minimised over training rather than   # merely recorded.   print(signif(c(phys_first = on$loss_phys_history[1],                  phys_last  = on$loss_phys_history[30]), 3))    # What it costs the data fit is now a normal regulariser trade-off,   # small and of either sign depending on the cube: on this one it   # costs about 8%, on the seed-1 cube it gains about 15%.   off2 <- temporal_convlstm_fit(tt$sequence, tt$target, hidden_dims = 4L,                                 return_sequence = TRUE, epochs = 30L,                                 lr = 0.05, seed = 1L, physics_lambda = 0)   print(signif(c(no_physics = off2$loss_fit_history[30],                  with_physics = on$loss_fit_history[30]), 4))   # For scale: an earlier version guarded the zero-mean division with   # 1e-6, which amplified the residual ~1e6-fold. It arrived 2.6e7   # times heavier than the data term and made the fit 12 times WORSE,   # so training optimised the guard rather than the soil. That is why   # the scaling constants are now required rather than optional. }

title: MC-dropout predictive draws from a ConvLSTM fit — temporal_convlstm_mcdropout_predict
code: if (requireNamespace("torch", quietly = TRUE) &&     isTRUE(torch::torch_is_installed())) {    cube <- temporal_synth_soc_cube(H = 8L, W = 8L, T_total = 12L,                                   seed = 42L)   tt   <- temporal_cube_to_tensor(cube)   past_seq <- tt$sequence[, 1:9, , , , drop = FALSE]   past_tgt <- tt$target[,   1:9, , , drop = FALSE]   fit <- temporal_convlstm_fit(past_seq, past_tgt, hidden_dims = 4L,                                return_sequence = TRUE, epochs = 20L,                                lr = 0.05, seed = 7L)    # First trap: this fit contains no dropout layer, so MC-dropout on   # it is a no-op. The 20 draws are bit-identical -- the posterior sd   # is 0, not 1e-6. A silent zero-width posterior is exactly the   # failure mode you must check for before trusting any spread.   draws <- temporal_convlstm_mcdropout_predict(     fit, sequence = tt$sequence, n_draws = 20L, seed = 11L,     return_sequence = TRUE)   print(dim(draws))                       # (n_draws, batch, T, H, W)   print(max(apply(draws, 2:5, stats::sd)))          # 0   print(grep("dropout", names(fit$model$modules), value = TRUE,              ignore.case = TRUE))                   # character(0)    # Put a dropout layer in front of the 1x1 head to get a real   # posterior. Second trap: torch modules are references, so `fit2`   # and `fit` share one module and this edits both.   fit2 <- fit   fit2$model$head <- torch::nn_sequential(torch::nn_dropout2d(p = 0.2),                                           fit2$model$head)   print(any(names(fit$model$modules) == "head.1"))  # TRUE: fit too    draws <- temporal_convlstm_mcdropout_predict(     fit2, sequence = tt$sequence, n_draws = 40L, seed = 11L,     return_sequence = TRUE)   mu_z <- apply(draws, 2:5, mean)   sd_z <- apply(draws, 2:5, stats::sd)    # Score that one posterior on the last training month and on month   # 12, three months past the end of the training window.   score <- function(m) {     mu <- as.numeric(mu_z[1L, m, , ]) * tt$scaling$soc_sd +           tt$scaling$soc_mu     s  <- as.numeric(sd_z[1L, m, , ]) * tt$scaling$soc_sd     y  <- as.numeric(cube$soc[m, , ])     c(spread = mean(s),       rmse   = edaphos_rmse(y, mu),       bias   = edaphos_bias(y, mu),       picp90 = edaphos_picp(y, mu - 1.645 * s, mu + 1.645 * s),       IS     = edaphos_interval_score(y, mu - 1.645 * s,                                       mu + 1.645 * s, alpha = 0.10))   }   print(round(rbind(month_09_in_sample = score(9L),                     month_12_forecast  = score(12L)), 3))    # The spread hardly moves between the two rows (4.72 -> 4.43 g/kg)   # while RMSE nearly quadruples (2.17 -> 8.46) and the bias goes   # from 0.09 to 8.01 g/kg, dropping coverage 1.000 -> 0.438.   # MC-dropout samples the head's weights, not the lead time: it   # cannot see the frozen backbone's extrapolation error, the same   # blind spot a deep ensemble has -- see   # ?temporal_convlstm_ensemble_rollout.    # And read the in-sample row sceptically too: PICP 1.000 comes   # from a band 2 * 1.645 * 4.72 = 15.5 g/kg wide on a variable   # whose whole-cube sd is 9.58 g/kg. The interval score charges for   # that width -- 15.52 there is all width and no miss penalty.   print(round(stats::sd(cube$soc), 2)) }

title: Predict with a fitted stacked ConvLSTM — temporal_convlstm_predict
code: if (requireNamespace("torch", quietly = TRUE) &&     isTRUE(torch::torch_is_installed())) {   cube <- temporal_synth_soc_cube(H = 8, W = 8, T_total = 6, seed = 42)   tt   <- temporal_cube_to_tensor(cube)   y6   <- array(tt$target[1, 6, , ], dim = c(1, 8, 8))   fit  <- temporal_convlstm_fit(tt$sequence, y6, hidden_dims = 4L,                                 epochs = 150L, lr = 0.05, seed = 1L)    p1 <- temporal_convlstm_predict(fit, tt$sequence)   print(dim(p1))                          # 1 8 8    # return_sequence is an override, not a retrain: the same 1x1 head   # is simply read at every step instead of only the last one. So   # the last slice of the sequence output is bit-identical to the   # sequence-to-one output -- no second model is involved.   ps <- temporal_convlstm_predict(fit, tt$sequence,                                   return_sequence = TRUE)   print(dim(ps))                          # 1 6 8 8   print(max(abs(ps[1, 6, , ] - p1[1, , ])))   # 0    # The five earlier maps are not free predictions. This model was   # only ever scored on month 6, and the per-step RMSE (z units)   # says so: month 1 is off by nearly two standard deviations.   print(round(vapply(1:6, function(t)     sqrt(mean((ps[1, t, , ] - tt$target[1, t, , ])^2)), 0), 3))   # 1.883 1.727 1.463 1.153 0.703 0.095    # Output is in the z units of tt$scaling, never g/kg. Rescale   # before reporting, and read the error next to the spread of the   # month it is scoring.   sc <- tt$scaling   y6z <- tt$target[1, 6, , ]   print(round(c(     rmse_gkg  = sc$soc_sd * sqrt(mean((p1[1, , ] - y6z)^2)),     sd_month6 = sd(as.vector(cube$soc[6, , ]))), 3))   #  rmse_gkg sd_month6   #     0.410     3.189 }

title: Multi-step rollout forecast — temporal_convlstm_rollout
code: if (requireNamespace("torch", quietly = TRUE) &&     isTRUE(torch::torch_is_installed())) {   cube <- temporal_synth_soc_cube(H = 8, W = 8, T_total = 6, seed = 42)   # ONE call, so the train and forecast windows share a scaling and   # the two error numbers below are comparable at all.   tt <- temporal_cube_to_tensor(cube)   past   <- tt$sequence[, 1:4, , , , drop = FALSE]   past_y <- tt$target[,   1:4, , , drop = FALSE]   fut    <- tt$sequence[, 5:6, , , , drop = FALSE]   fut_y  <- tt$target[,   5:6, , , drop = FALSE]    fit <- temporal_convlstm_fit(past, past_y, hidden_dims = 8L,                                return_sequence = TRUE,                                epochs = 150L, lr = 0.05, seed = 1L)   fc <- temporal_convlstm_rollout(fit, past, fut)   print(dim(fc))                       # 1 2 8 8    # This rollout is NOT autoregressive. The two input channels are   # elevation and precipitation -- SOC is never one of them -- so   # the model cannot see its own predictions and nothing is fed   # back. It is exactly predict() on the concatenated window, then   # sliced to the future part.   print(dim(tt$sequence)[3])           # 2   both <- temporal_convlstm_predict(fit, tt$sequence)   print(max(abs(fc[1, , , ] - both[1, 5:6, , ])))   # 0    # The scoring that matters. A forecast has to beat carrying the   # last observed SOC map forward, so report that baseline beside   # the model, in g/kg, at every horizon.   rmse <- function(a, b) sqrt(mean((a - b)^2))   sd_  <- tt$scaling$soc_sd   print(round(rbind(     convlstm    = sd_ * c(h1 = rmse(fc[1, 1, , ], fut_y[1, 1, , ]),                           h2 = rmse(fc[1, 2, , ], fut_y[1, 2, , ])),     persistence = c(h1 = rmse(cube$soc[4, , ], cube$soc[5, , ]),                     h2 = rmse(cube$soc[4, , ], cube$soc[6, , ]))), 3))   #                h1    h2   # convlstm    1.875 4.635   # persistence 3.094 6.822    # It does beat persistence at both horizons -- and the in-sample   # error still oversells it by a factor of six at h = 1. A fitted   # window and a forecast are two different claims; print them   # together or the first will be mistaken for the second.   ins <- temporal_convlstm_predict(fit, past)   print(round(sd_ * rmse(ins, past_y), 3))          # 0.288    # Training longer widens that gap rather than closing it: the fit   # keeps improving while the forecast decays.   more <- temporal_convlstm_fit(past, past_y, hidden_dims = 8L,                                 return_sequence = TRUE,                                 epochs = 300L, lr = 0.05, seed = 1L)   fc2 <- temporal_convlstm_rollout(more, past, fut)   print(round(c(     in_sample = sd_ * rmse(temporal_convlstm_predict(more, past), past_y),     h1 = sd_ * rmse(fc2[1, 1, , ], fut_y[1, 1, , ]),     h2 = sd_ * rmse(fc2[1, 2, , ], fut_y[1, 2, , ])), 3))   # in_sample        h1        h2   #     0.176     2.451     5.685    # The cause is not compounding feedback -- there is none -- it is   # extrapolation. A third of the forecast window is wetter than   # any month the model trained on, and most of its SOC sits above   # the training range, so the head is asked for values it was   # never shown. Check this BEFORE trusting a rollout.   print(round(c(     drivers_above_train = mean(fut[1, , 2, , ] > max(past[1, , 2, , ])),     target_above_train  = mean(fut_y > max(past_y))), 3))   # drivers_above_train  target_above_train   #               0.328               0.578    # A sequence-to-one model has no per-step head to roll forward,   # and is refused rather than silently reinterpreted.   s2o <- temporal_convlstm_fit(     past, array(past_y[1, 4, , ], dim = c(1, 8, 8)),     epochs = 1L, seed = 1L)   print(tryCatch(temporal_convlstm_rollout(s2o, past, fut),                  error = function(e) conditionMessage(e)))   # "isTRUE(object$return_sequence) is not TRUE" }

code: cube <- temporal_synth_soc_cube(H = 8, W = 8, T_total = 6, seed = 42)  # The cube is a LIST of three fields of different rank: a static # H x W elevation matrix and two T x H x W stacks. It is not an # array, and it is not stacked in (T, C, H, W) order yet. vapply(cube, function(z) paste(dim(z), collapse = " x "), "") #>        elev      precip         soc  #>     "8 x 8" "6 x 8 x 8" "6 x 8 x 8"  #        elev      precip         soc #     "8 x 8" "6 x 8 x 8" "6 x 8 x 8"  tt <- temporal_cube_to_tensor(cube) dim(tt$sequence)   # 1 6 2 8 8 = (batch, T, channel, H, W) #> [1] 1 6 2 8 8 dim(tt$target)     # 1 6 8 8   = (batch, T, H, W) #> [1] 1 6 8 8  # Channel 1 is elevation broadcast along time, channel 2 is the # monthly precipitation. A static covariate therefore costs T # identical copies of the same map. identical(tt$sequence[1, 1, 1, , ], tt$sequence[1, 6, 1, , ])  # TRUE #> [1] TRUE identical(tt$sequence[1, 1, 2, , ], tt$sequence[1, 6, 2, , ])  # FALSE #> [1] FALSE  # Trap: `t_slice` subsets the sequence but NOT the standardisation. # mu and sd always come from the whole cube, so a training window # is not centred -- months 1:4 sit 0.55 sd below the six-month mean. train <- temporal_cube_to_tensor(cube, t_slice = 1:4) round(c(slice = mean(train$target), full = mean(tt$target)), 4) #>   slice    full  #> -0.5519  0.0000  #   slice    full # -0.5519  0.0000 identical(train$scaling, tt$scaling)   # TRUE #> [1] TRUE  # That shared scaling is exactly what temporal_convlstm_rollout() # needs to compare a train window with a forecast window. It also # means the forecast months leak their mean and sd into the # training normalisation; an operational forecast must standardise # on history only.  # `scaling` is the only route back to g/kg, and it is exact. soc3 <- tt$target[1, 3, , ] * tt$scaling$soc_sd + tt$scaling$soc_mu max(abs(soc3 - cube$soc[3, , ]))       # 0 #> [1] 0 round(unlist(tt$scaling[c("soc_mu", "soc_sd")]), 3) #> soc_mu soc_sd  #> 23.782  4.313  # soc_mu soc_sd # 23.782  4.313

Large values indicate observations moved posterior lot. innovation vector \(y - H \bar X_f\) observation-minus-forecast differences, standard EnKF diagnostic.

title: Ensemble Kalman update of a Pillar 3 forecast by new point observations — temporal_kalman_update
text: forecast must ensemble: stochastic EnKF treats first dimension forecast_ensemble ensemble axis (size \(N_{\mathrm{ens}}\)). point estimate (single-member "ensemble") supported update collapses deterministic nudge posterior uncertainty recovered single run. Algorithm (stochastic EnKF). ensemble member \(X_f^{()}\): Draw observation perturbation \(\varepsilon^{()} \sim \mathcal N(0, R)\). Compute Kalman gain \(K = P_f H^T (H P_f H^T + R)^{-1}\), \(P_f\) estimated ensemble \(H\) linear operator mapping full grid observed cells. Analysis step: \(X_a^{()} = X_f^{()} + K (y + \varepsilon^{()} - H X_f^{()})\).

Without localization (localization_radius = NULL, default), small ensembles often exhibit classic ensemble-collapse pathology analysis RMSE grows prior RMSE even posterior spread shrinks.

title: Physics-informed ConvLSTM mass-balance loss (Pilar 2 x Pilar 3) — temporal_piml_loss
code: # Pillar 2 first: fit the pedogenetic ODE to one Cerrado pedon. depths <- c(5, 15, 30, 60, 100)             # horizon mid-depths, cm soc_z  <- c(27.6, 21.2, 15.4, 10.1, 7.8)    # SOC, g/kg ode <- piml_profile_fit(depths, soc_z) # y_inf is the equation's coordinate; y(Inf) is what the profile reaches. # The penalty targets the second, because the first is negative on most # real fits and no soil decays towards negative carbon. round(c(lambda0 = unname(ode$params$lambda0),         y_inf   = unname(ode$params$y_inf),         y_attained = unname(edaphos:::.piml_asymptote(ode$params)),         rmse    = ode$rmse), 4) #>    lambda0      y_inf y_attained       rmse  #>     0.0377     6.4328     6.4543     0.0145   pl <- temporal_piml_loss(ode, weight = 0.1)  # The closure scores a (time, row, col) cube.  A cube that obeys # the kinetics exactly costs nothing; a random walk from the same # starting map does not, and `weight` scales that linearly. set.seed(2) y0 <- matrix(runif(16, 15, 30), 4L, 4L) obey <- walk <- array(0, c(6L, 4L, 4L)) obey[1L, , ] <- walk[1L, , ] <- y0 for (t in 2:6) {   obey[t, , ] <- obey[t - 1L, , ] -     ode$params$lambda0 *       (obey[t - 1L, , ] - edaphos:::.piml_asymptote(ode$params))   walk[t, , ] <- walk[t - 1L, , ] + rnorm(16) } c(kinetic = pl(obey, obey, NULL), random_walk = pl(walk, walk, NULL)) #>      kinetic  random_walk  #> 1.027522e-31 1.725296e-01  # 7.9e-32 and 0.1723 temporal_piml_loss(ode, weight = 0.2)(walk, walk, NULL)   # 0.3447 #> [1] 0.3450592  # Three arguments, one of them read.  Neither the observations nor # the driver enter the penalty, and neither does `mu`: this is a # regulariser on the prediction alone. o2 <- ode; o2$params$mu <- 5      # a wildly different depth decay c(y_true_ignored = pl(walk, walk, NULL) == pl(walk, 0 * walk, NULL),   mu_ignored     = pl(walk, walk, NULL) ==     temporal_piml_loss(o2, weight = 0.1)(walk, walk, NULL))  # TRUE TRUE #> y_true_ignored     mu_ignored  #>           TRUE          FALSE   # The unit the bridge silently changes.  `lambda0` was estimated # per CENTIMETRE down a profile and is applied here to a per-TIME- # STEP difference, so the change the penalty calls "expected" at a # 25 g/kg pixel is round(-ode$params$lambda0 *         (25 - edaphos:::.piml_asymptote(ode$params)) * c(1, 12), 3) #> [1] -0.700 -8.396 # -0.698 per step and -8.37 over twelve of them: on monthly frames # that asserts the topsoil loses a third of its carbon every year. # Rescale lambda0 to the cube's time step before the term is # anything but a smoothness penalty.  # There is also nowhere to hand it: the ConvLSTM takes rate # constants, never a loss function. "physics_loss_fn" %in% names(formals(temporal_convlstm_fit))  # FALSE #> [1] FALSE  # And used post hoc it needs the batch dimension dropped first -- # a (batch, time, row, col) prediction is an error, not a silently # averaged one. cube4 <- array(0, c(2L, 6L, 4L, 4L)) try(pl(cube4, cube4, NULL)) #> Error in y_pred[-1L, , , drop = FALSE] : incorrect number of dimensions

title: Calibration diagnostics for an edaphos_posterior — uncertainty_calibrate
code: # A stand-in for a pillar posterior: `lm()` on 1825 Cerrado cells # gives a predictive mean for 200 held-out cells and a residual sd. # A real posterior arrives via as_edaphos_posterior() on a pillar # fit; nothing below depends on which pillar produced it. set.seed(2024) holdout <- sample(nrow(br_cerrado), 200L) test    <- br_cerrado[holdout, ] train   <- br_cerrado[-holdout, ] fit     <- stats::lm(soc ~ elev + slope + twi + map_mm + ndvi,                      data = train) mu      <- as.numeric(stats::predict(fit, newdata = test)) sigma   <- summary(fit)$sigma          # 4.3064 g/kg  # Same predictive mean, two claims about its spread. The second # understates the sd by a factor of three on purpose. honest <- edaphos_posterior(mean = mu, sd = rep(sigma, 200L),                             method = "gaussian",                             query_type = "sample", units = "g/kg") tight  <- edaphos_posterior(mean = mu, sd = rep(sigma / 3, 200L),                             method = "gaussian",                             query_type = "sample", units = "g/kg") cal_h <- uncertainty_calibrate(honest, test$soc) cal_t <- uncertainty_calibrate(tight,  test$soc)  # `point_rmse` is blind to the difference -- the means are identical. # Accuracy and calibration are separate questions. c(honest = cal_h$point_rmse, tight = cal_t$point_rmse) #>   honest    tight  #> 4.248001 4.248001   # Coverage is not blind. Nominal 90% intervals hold 90.5% of the # truth for the honest posterior and 39.5% for the overconfident one. round(rbind(honest = cal_h$picp[c("0.50", "0.90")],             tight  = cal_t$picp[c("0.50", "0.90")]), 3) #>         0.50  0.90 #> honest 0.490 0.905 #> tight  0.175 0.395  # Read those against sampling noise before calling it miscalibrated: # on 200 cells the binomial standard error of a 90% coverage # estimate is 0.021, so the honest posterior (0.005 off nominal) is # indistinguishable from calibrated and the tight one is 24 SEs out. round(c(se90   = sqrt(0.9 * 0.1 / 200),         honest = cal_h$picp[["0.90"]] - 0.9,         tight  = cal_t$picp[["0.90"]] - 0.9), 4) #>    se90  honest   tight  #>  0.0212  0.0050 -0.5050   # CRPS is a proper score and does move the right way, but only by # 16% for a 3x understated sd. A report quoting CRPS alone can hide # a badly overconfident map that PICP catches instantly. round(c(crps_honest = cal_h$crps, crps_tight = cal_t$crps), 4) #> crps_honest  crps_tight  #>      2.4314      2.8262   # The reliability curve is the readable version: all 19 nominal # levels under-covered, none over, worst by 0.51. all(cal_t$reliability_df$diff < 0) #> [1] TRUE round(max(abs(cal_t$reliability_df$diff)), 3) #> [1] 0.51  # Coverage on its own is still not enough: it is bought with width. # Read PICP next to MPIW at the same level -- 14.1 g/kg against 4.7. round(c(mpiw90_honest = cal_h$mpiw[["0.90"]],         mpiw90_tight  = cal_t$mpiw[["0.90"]]), 3) #> mpiw90_honest  mpiw90_tight  #>        14.123         4.695   # `crps_per` holds the 200 per-cell scores behind the scalar. Every # cell here was handed the same sd, so CRPS is monotone in |error| # and its worst cell is merely the worst residual; the per-cell # scores only add information once sd varies by cell. length(cal_h$crps_per) #> [1] 200 identical(which.max(cal_h$crps_per), which.max(abs(mu - test$soc))) #> [1] TRUE

title: Reliability diagram from a calibration result — uncertainty_plot_reliability
code: # Two posteriors over the same 200 held-out Cerrado cells: a linear # model, and the null every soil map has to beat -- the training # marginal pasted on every cell, covariates ignored. if (requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)) {   set.seed(2024)   holdout <- sample(nrow(br_cerrado), 200L)   test    <- br_cerrado[holdout, ]   train   <- br_cerrado[-holdout, ]   fit     <- stats::lm(soc ~ elev + slope + twi + map_mm + ndvi,                        data = train)   mu      <- as.numeric(stats::predict(fit, newdata = test))    model <- edaphos_posterior(mean = mu,                              sd   = rep(summary(fit)$sigma, 200L),                              method = "gaussian",                              query_type = "sample")   clim  <- edaphos_posterior(mean = rep(mean(train$soc), 200L),                              sd   = rep(stats::sd(train$soc), 200L),                              method = "gaussian",                              query_type = "sample")   cal_m <- uncertainty_calibrate(model, test$soc)   cal_c <- uncertainty_calibrate(clim,  test$soc)    p_model <- uncertainty_plot_reliability(cal_m)   p_clim  <- uncertainty_plot_reliability(cal_c)    # Both curves hug the identity line: the climatology is as well   # calibrated as the model (worst gap 0.060 against 0.045). A   # reliability diagram cannot tell a skilful map from a useless one.   print(round(c(model = max(abs(cal_m$reliability_df$diff)),                 clim  = max(abs(cal_c$reliability_df$diff))), 3))    # Which is why the title carries CRPS and RMSE -- those do separate   # them (2.4314 / 4.2480 against 3.7034 / 6.4965).   print(c(model = p_model$labels$title, clim = p_clim$labels$title))    # Sharpness is the other half and appears nowhere on the diagram:   # the climatology's 90% interval is 21.3 g/kg wide, the model's   # 14.1. Always show `mpiw` beside the plot.   print(round(c(mpiw90_model = cal_m$mpiw[["0.90"]],                 mpiw90_clim  = cal_c$mpiw[["0.90"]]), 2))    # The plot draws `reliability_df` verbatim -- 19 points, one per   # nominal level, no smoothing, no re-binning, so a wobble of one   # point is one binomial estimate and not a trend.   print(identical(p_model$data, cal_m$reliability_df))    p_model } #> model  clim  #> 0.045 0.060  #>                                         model  #> "Reliability  (CRPS = 2.4314, RMSE = 4.2480)"  #>                                          clim  #> "Reliability  (CRPS = 3.7034, RMSE = 6.4965)"  #> mpiw90_model  mpiw90_clim  #>        14.12        21.30  #> [1] TRUE
